articles.title: Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain
articles.text:
Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain
- Date:
- October 26, 2026
- Source:
- Norwegian University of Science and Technology
- Summary:
- Scientists have filmed tiny magnetic vortices called skyrmions melting out of an organized lattice for the first time, revealing new ways to manipulate these unusual structures. The breakthrough could help make brain-like computers a reality, potentially enabling dramatically smaller and more energy-efficient technology.
- Share:
Tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a new generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity. Although most people have never heard of skyrmions, these microscopic magnetic vortices may eventually play an important role in how computers store and process data.
A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides new insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them. The findings could help researchers develop smaller, more efficient computing systems and advance emerging quantum technologies.
Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).
"Skyrmions are small, magnetic vortices that can store information in a completely new way," explained Asle Sudbø, who leads NTNU's Centre for Quantum Spintronics (QuSpin).
Unlike conventional technologies, which require increasing amounts of space and energy to handle growing quantities of data, skyrmions could offer a much more efficient alternative.
"Instead of the current technology, where we constantly need more space and energy to process data, skyrmions could make it possible to build much smaller and more energy-efficient data storage systems," explained Sudbø.
Tiny Magnetic Vortices Could Enable Brain-Like Computers
The potential applications of skyrmions extend well beyond conventional data storage. They are also important to spintronics, which explores ways to use the magnetic properties of electrons in electronic devices, and to research involving topological quantum effects.
One particularly promising possibility is the development of computers that operate in ways similar to biological brains.
"These nanoscale vortices could help develop computers that resemble biological brains," said Sudbø.
Rather than relying on conventional transistor-based computing, such systems could use magnetism to process information. In principle, this approach could dramatically reduce electricity consumption, potentially allowing future computers to perform complex tasks with very little energy.
Turning that possibility into practical technology, however, requires scientists to understand exactly how skyrmions behave and how to manipulate them reliably.
The latest research represents an important advance toward that goal.
Scientists Film Magnetic Skyrmion Lattices Melting for the First Time
Skyrmions do not always exist as isolated magnetic structures. Under certain conditions, they organize themselves into repeating patterns known as lattices, resembling the orderly arrangement of atoms in a crystal, but on a much smaller scale.
Scientists can manipulate these arrangements, a capability that could be essential for using skyrmions in future computing devices.
In the new study, researchers achieved something that had not been demonstrated before. They recorded the melting of a magnetic skyrmion lattice as it happened while simultaneously controlling individual skyrmions.
"For the first time, researchers have managed to film how a magnetic skyrmion lattice melts in real time, while simultaneously being able to manipulate each individual skyrmion directly as they film it. For example, both their shape and size can be changed 'on the fly'," said Sudbø.
The ability to observe this process directly provides a clearer picture of how skyrmions respond when their organized structures break apart. It also allows researchers to study how changing the size and shape of individual magnetic vortices affects their behavior.
A New Step Toward Energy-Efficient Computing
Understanding how skyrmions behave during the breakdown of their lattices could help scientists develop more precise ways to control them. That control is particularly important if these magnetic structures are to become useful components in future computer systems.
The findings therefore offer more than a new way to observe an unusual magnetic phenomenon. They provide information that could help researchers overcome challenges involved in developing practical skyrmion-based technologies.
"The findings give us new insight into how these types of particles behave. This could therefore become important for the development of more energy-efficient computer technology in the future," said Sudbø.
Although substantial development is still needed before skyrmions can be used in everyday computing devices, the research highlights their potential for improving data storage, enabling new computing architectures, and supporting advances in quantum technology.
By learning to observe and manipulate these tiny magnetic vortices in real time, scientists are gaining capabilities that could eventually help reshape the design of computers.
"This could revolutionize the way we think about computers," concluded Sudbø.
Story Source:

Journal Reference:

articles.title: Archaeologists may have just found the world's oldest shipwreck
articles.text:
Archaeologists may have just found the world's oldest shipwreck
- Date:
- October 26, 2026
- Source:
- The Conversation
- Summary:
- A mysterious shipwreck off Turkey’s coast may be the oldest ever discovered, dating back approximately 4,500 years to the age of the Egyptian pyramids. Although the wooden vessel has disappeared, its surviving pottery cargo reveals clues about an ancient trading network that may have connected distant Mediterranean civilizations. Researchers believe the ship may have crashed against rocks during a storm while transporting valuable goods such as oil, wine, or tree resin.
- Share:
A shipwreck off the coast of Turkey is the oldest shipwreck in the world, our team of archaeologists believes.
There’s little left of the ship itself but based on clues from its cargo – including pottery vessels – a research team I was part of has tentatively dated the wreck to around 2700–2400 BCE.
That’s about 4,500 years ago. Prior to this discovery, the world’s oldest shipwreck was a wreck off the coast of Dokos, in Greece, thought to have been from about 4,200 years ago.
Much work remains to be done to finesse the conclusions, and a paper outlining the results is yet to be published in a peer-reviewed journal. Yet the discovery could transform our understanding of ancient Mediterranean connections during the Early Bronze Age.
Here, and perhaps even earlier, lie the foundations of extensive trade routes as we know them today.
Searching for clues
Associate Professor Hakan Öniz of Akdeniz University, Antalya, has worked along this coastline for decades excavating ancient shipwrecks.
Acting on clues from local seafarers, Öniz found a shipwreck in shallow waters off Kekova, west of Antalya in Turkey, in 2024. Earlier this year, he contacted me and asked if I would help date some of the pottery vessels found on this wreck.
As an archaeologist specializing in desert sites, this was a singular experience. New technology, water-logged methods of excavation and laborious conservation techniques were the new normal. Yet there is always room for learning new skills in life.
Of the ship itself there is now nothing to see, owing to underwater exposure. Yet the research team has now estimated the ship and its cargo dates to around 2700–2400 BCE. However, the precise dating is still under consideration. Earlier or later dates on either side of this initial determination are also possible.
A time capsule of ancient trade
This discovery promises to re-write our understanding of early trade networks from around 4,500 years ago.
The ship is a “missing piece” in the story of networks, trade and commodity exchange in the wider eastern Mediterranean. This era includes the pyramid age of Giza and its mighty pharaohs.
What remains under the sea is a time capsule of ancient trade.
Although its direction was not known, the boat was evidently traveling along the coast of southern Turkey.
Now resting on the seabed between two islands, it is apparent the ship likely sought refuge in the lee waters during a storm. One could imagine the terror of the sailors – possibly coastal people from the Levant region – as their ship crashed against the rocks.
While timbers from the ship disappeared long ago, the remains of its precious cargo were embedded in the rocky slope along the Kekova coast.
Divers worked over the past four months to extract its pottery from barnacles clinging to the rocky underwater slope.
A closer look at pottery
Pottery is like plastic: it never goes away and just breaks down into smaller and smaller pieces.
Yet humble pottery vessels hold many clues about the past.
In this case, the cargo included large ceramic storage vessels or amphorae which once contained products from regions of the eastern Mediterranean.
The pots were large ovoid, flat-based jars with two handles, many featuring a raised horizontal clay “belt” around the widest part of the jar.
Through these vessels was possible to ascertain many pieces of information. This includes the likely origin of the jars and the contents exchanged across the region.
Importantly, the shape and manufacturing technique of the pots themselves help us date the cargo. By extension, this includes also the date of other pottery, and the ship itself.
The bigger picture
Compared to later periods, trade and exchange in the eastern Mediterranean during the third millennium (3000–2000 BCE) is poorly understood.
Maritime voyages during the that period are known from Egyptian texts, pottery vessels and raw materials from ancient tombs.
Around the same time as this ship struck the rocks, the ancient Egyptians were trading in the eastern Mediterranean through the port of Byblos in Lebanon.
Commodities such as cedar, tin/lead, oils, tree resins, lapis lazuli and silver, all materials that Egypt lacked, were imported by the Egyptian state.
Recent scientific research also reveals that silver was acquired by the Egyptian state around 2600 BCE. Analyses showed this silver was acquired from the Lavrion mines east of modern Athens.
While it is unlikely Egyptian ships made this journey, boats like the Kekova ship may have used the route as part of an extended international maritime network.
And what was in the jars? Remarkably there were still residues visible to the naked eye. Again, scientific analyses are pending, but could be some of the products mentioned in the Egyptian texts, possibly olive oil, wine or tree resin.
The ship may have acquired its pottery from several ports on their journey. Our best assessment at this stage of research is that some of the “belted” jars (or clays used to make them) may have originated in the Central Jordan Valley.
The coast of southern Turkey is littered with ancient shipwrecks. While maritime archaeology is a relatively recent phenomenon, some of the world’s most famous wrecks have been discovered there. Who knows what other secrets these waters hold.
The research on which this article is based was led by Associate Professor Hakan Öniz, head of the Division of Mediterranean Underwater Cultural Heritage Research, and the Department of Restoration and Conservation of Cultural Heritage in the Faculty of Art at the Akdeniz University, Antalya, Turkey.
Story Source:

articles.title: AI detects “invisible” signs of pancreatic cancer years before diagnosis
articles.text:
AI detects “invisible” signs of pancreatic cancer years before diagnosis
- Date:
- October 26, 2026
- Source:
- BMJ Group
- Summary:
- A powerful new AI system could help doctors detect pancreatic cancer years before it becomes visible on conventional scans. The technology, called REDMOD, identified hidden warning signs an average of 475 days before diagnosis and was nearly twice as sensitive as experienced radiologists. By spotting cancer-related changes at their earliest stages, it could dramatically improve the chances of successful treatment for one of the deadliest forms of cancer.
- Share:
An artificial intelligence model called REDMOD can identify extremely subtle changes in pancreatic tissue that may signal cancer long before the disease becomes visible to doctors or conventional imaging technology. According to research published online in the journal Gut, the system can detect early signs of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, the most common type of pancreatic cancer.
Researchers believe this technology could help transform pancreatic cancer detection by identifying the disease at a much earlier stage (stage 0), when treatment is more likely to succeed. Instead of receiving a diagnosis after the cancer has progressed to an advanced, potentially terminal stage, patients might have an opportunity to begin treatment while the disease is still treatable.
Although REDMOD outperformed experienced radiologists in the study, more research is necessary before it can be introduced into routine medical care. In particular, the scientists emphasize the need to test the system in patients at high risk, including those experiencing unexplained weight loss or recently diagnosed diabetes.
Why Pancreatic Cancer Is So Difficult to Detect Early
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma has a low survival rate, largely because it is often discovered only after the disease has advanced. Early pancreatic cancer typically produces few noticeable symptoms, and the changes it causes in pancreatic tissue can be too subtle to detect through standard medical imaging. The cancer can also progress rapidly, making timely diagnosis especially important.
To address these challenges, researchers created an artificial intelligence framework known as Radiomics-based Early Detection MODel (REDMOD). The system analyzes extremely fine patterns in the texture of pancreatic tissue, known as radiomics (radiomics), that are not readily visible on conventional computed tomography (CT) scans.
REDMOD also automatically identifies and outlines the pancreas, separating it from nearby organs and tissues. This process eliminates the need for specialists to manually trace the organ's boundaries, reducing the inconsistencies that can arise when different people perform the task.
AI Finds Hidden Cancer Signals Years Before Diagnosis
To evaluate the system, the researchers examined abdominal CT scans from 219 patients treated at multiple hospitals. At the time of their scans, experienced radiologists had found no evidence of pancreatic cancer. However, every patient in this group was subsequently diagnosed with the disease.
The scans had been taken at different intervals before diagnosis. For 87 patients (40%), the images were obtained 3 to 12 months earlier. Another 76 patients (35%) had been scanned 12 to 24 months before diagnosis, while 56 (25%) had undergone imaging more than 24 months earlier (up to around 3 years). In nearly two thirds (64%) of the patients, the cancer developed in the head of the pancreas.
The researchers compared these images with CT scans from 1243 people who remained free of pancreatic cancer for up to three years afterward. The comparison group was matched according to age, sex, and the dates of their scans.
Patients who eventually developed pancreatic cancer had an average age of 69, with ages ranging from 34 to 88. Those in the comparison group were 64 years old on average, with the same age range of 34 to 88.
REDMOD successfully identified subtle imaging signatures associated with pancreatic cancer an average of 475 days before patients received their clinical diagnoses. These early warning signs had previously gone undetected during routine radiological assessments.
"This temporal window holds profound significance, as attaining such early detection would substantially augment the probability of cure and improved survival," highlight the researchers.
"In fact, modelling studies indicate that increasing the proportion of localized [pancreatic ductal carcinomas] from 10% to 50% would more than double survival rates, thereby underscoring that the timing of diagnosis is the single most critical determinant of survival outcomes," they add.
AI Outperforms Experienced Radiologists
The results also showed that REDMOD was substantially better than experienced radiologists at recognizing early cancer signals.
The AI achieved a sensitivity of 73%, compared with 39% for radiologists. Sensitivity measures how effectively a diagnostic method identifies people who actually have the disease, rather than overlooking genuine cases.
The difference was even more pronounced when researchers examined scans taken more than two years before the patients were diagnosed. In these cases, REDMOD achieved a detection rate of 68%, nearly three times the 23% recorded by radiologists.
The researchers also assessed how well the system could recognize scans from people without pancreatic cancer. In an independent group of 539 patients from several hospitals, REDMOD correctly classified just over 81% of scans as cancer free. It performed even better on the publicly available US National Institutes of Health NIH-PCT dataset (80 patients), correctly identifying 87.5% as free of pancreatic cancer.
Additional testing suggested that the early warning signs detected by REDMOD were consistent over time. When the researchers analyzed scans taken from the same patients several months apart, the system produced matching results in 90 to 92% of cases. This consistency strengthened the evidence that the AI was identifying meaningful changes associated with the disease.
Could AI Transform Early Pancreatic Cancer Detection?
Despite the promising findings, the researchers caution that several questions remain unanswered. One limitation is that the study population did not include a sufficiently diverse range of ethnic backgrounds, which could affect how well the technology performs across different populations.
The system must also undergo prospective testing, particularly among people at increased risk of pancreatic cancer, before researchers can determine whether it will be effective in everyday clinical practice.
Even with these limitations, the findings suggest that AI could eventually help doctors identify pancreatic cancer while it is still at a much more treatable stage, potentially improving survival for patients who would otherwise receive a late diagnosis.
The researchers conclude: "This study validates REDMOD as a fully automated AI framework capable of identifying the imaging signatures of stage 0 [pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma] in normal pancreas, achieving this with substantial lead times and performance superior to expert radiologists."
They add: "While prospective validation is paramount to confirm clinical utility, the REDMOD framework represents a significant advance towards shifting the paradigm for sporadic [pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma] from a late-stage symptomatic diagnosis to proactive pre-clinical interception, offering tangible hope for improving outcomes in this challenging disease."
Story Source:
Materials provided by BMJ Group. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Sovanlal Mukherjee, Ajith Antony, Nandakumar G Patnam, Kamaxi H Trivedi, Aashna Karbhari, Khurram Khaliq Bhinder, Armin Zarrintan, Joel G Fletcher, Mark Truty, Matthew P Johnson, Suresh T Chari, Ajit Harishkumar Goenka. Next-generation AI for visually occult pancreatic cancer detection in a low-prevalence setting with longitudinal stability and multi-institutional generalisability. Gut, 2026; gutjnl-2025-337266 DOI: 10.1136/gutjnl-2025-337266

articles.title: Scientists discover Arctic sea ice loss could be far worse than predicted
articles.text:
Scientists discover Arctic sea ice loss could be far worse than predicted
- Date:
- October 26, 2026
- Source:
- University of Cambridge
- Summary:
- Arctic winter sea ice could disappear much faster than scientists previously expected, according to new research using climate clues from 6,000 years ago. By comparing ancient ocean sediments with modern climate models, researchers found that future winter ice coverage may be roughly one million square kilometers smaller than earlier predictions suggested.
- Share:
The Arctic could lose roughly one million square kilometers more winter sea ice than scientists previously predicted, according to new research that draws on evidence from a warmer Arctic 6,000 years ago. By using ancient climate records to refine modern computer models, researchers have produced more reliable estimates of how much ice may disappear in the coming decades.
The findings, published in Nature Geoscience, could also have important consequences for winter weather in the United Kingdom and other parts of Europe.
Much of the attention surrounding Arctic ice loss has focused on the dramatic retreat of summer sea ice. Winter ice, however, has received considerably less scrutiny, even though climate models show their greatest disagreements when predicting how much ice will cover the Arctic during the colder months.
Why Arctic Winter Sea Ice Matters for Global Weather
Winter sea ice influences weather far beyond the Arctic by controlling how much heat and moisture escape from the ocean into the atmosphere. Declining ice cover has been associated with colder winters and increased snowfall in the United Kingdom, northern Europe, and North America.
Recent observations have also highlighted the Arctic's changing conditions. In March 2025, winter sea ice reached the lowest annual maximum extent recorded since modern monitoring began. The Arctic matched that record again in 2026.
To improve predictions of future ice loss, scientists at the University of Cambridge and Mexico's Centro de Investigación en Matematicas (CIMAT) turned to evidence preserved beneath the Arctic Ocean.
The team assembled the largest database of its kind containing a chemical marker produced by algae that live within sea ice. The evidence came from sediment cores deposited during the mid-Holocene, approximately 6,000 years ago, when small changes in Earth's orbit helped create a warmer Arctic with less extensive ice cover.
These ancient conditions offered a valuable opportunity to investigate how Arctic sea ice responds to warming and to test whether today's climate models accurately represent that response.
Ancient Ocean Sediments Reveal What Climate Models Missed
The researchers examined concentrations of a biomarker known as IP25, which is produced by algae associated with sea ice. They combined these measurements with other chemical markers left behind by organisms living in open water, allowing them to reconstruct Arctic ice conditions thousands of years in the past.
Next, they compared those reconstructions with simulations generated by 27 climate models for the same ancient period.
Using a statistical method called Bayesian weighting, the researchers assigned greater importance to models that more closely matched the historical evidence. Models that performed less accurately received less influence over the final predictions.
Because the underlying physical processes controlling sea ice remain consistent across different climate conditions, the team could apply these same weights to simulations of both the recent past and the future.
The comparison revealed a significant problem: collectively, the climate models predicted more winter sea ice than the ancient evidence supported.
"When we apply the model weights to historical simulations, we completely eliminated the positive bias," said lead author Crystal Fu, from Cambridge's Scott Polar Research Institute. "The future projections similarly end up being lower than previous estimates, by about a million square kilometers."
More Accurate Arctic Ice Forecasts Reduce Uncertainty by 85%
Scientists have collected substantial evidence about Earth's ancient climates, but translating that information into reliable forecasts remains difficult. Both historical reconstructions and future climate simulations contain uncertainties that complicate direct comparisons.
"The scientific community has amassed lots of paleoclimate records over recent decades, but it's remained a challenge to directly link these records to future projections, since there is uncertainty at both ends," said Fu.
The team's new approach substantially narrowed those uncertainties, reducing the range of possible outcomes in some projections by as much as 85%.
"By using evidence from the past, we can now produce more reliable maps of where Arctic winter sea ice is likely to disappear," said co-author Marco Aquino-López, of CIMAT. "These give us a much clearer picture of what the Arctic might look like in the coming decades, and how much uncertainty remains."
Although the warming that occurred during the mid-Holocene was driven by changes in Earth's orbit rather than the human activities responsible for today's warming, Fu emphasized that the response of sea ice to rising temperatures follows the same basic physical principles.
"It doesn't matter if the warming is natural variation or caused by human activity: if it warms, sea ice is going to melt," she said.
Arctic Ice Loss Could Have Wider Consequences for Europe
The findings may have implications that extend beyond the disappearance of Arctic sea ice itself.
When the researchers applied their improved model weighting to projections of precipitation, they found indications that current climate models may also underestimate future snowfall in southeastern Greenland and rainfall across the Mediterranean region.
Greater snowfall over Greenland could affect the stability of the Greenland ice sheet, while increased Mediterranean rainfall could influence future flooding risks in southern Europe.
These potential effects suggest that the consequences of a warming Arctic may be more extensive than existing predictions indicate. The revised simulations offer researchers a clearer foundation for investigating those risks and understanding how changing Arctic conditions could influence weather elsewhere.
The research received partial funding from the US National Science Foundation and the Cambridge Trust. Crystal Fu is a Member of Girton College, Cambridge.

Materials provided by University of Cambridge. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- C. Y. Fu, M. B. Osman, M. A. Aquino-López. Palaeoclimate constraints narrow uncertainty in future Arctic winter sea ice projections. Nature Geoscience, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41561-026-02123-w

articles.title: A simple liquid can stop cavities without drilling, major study confirms
articles.text:
A simple liquid can stop cavities without drilling, major study confirms
- Date:
- October 25, 2026
- Source:
- University of Michigan
- Summary:
- A simple liquid painted onto teeth in seconds can stop cavities without drilling, injections, or anesthesia, according to a major clinical trial involving young children. The inexpensive treatment could spare thousands of children painful dental procedures and surgery while paving the way for broader FDA-approved use.
- Share:
A cavity doesn't always have to mean drilling, injections, or an uncomfortable visit to the dentist. A major clinical trial has confirmed that a simple, inexpensive liquid can stop tooth decay in young children, potentially preventing painful infections and the need for dental surgery.
The treatment, called silver diamine fluoride (SDF), takes only seconds to apply to each affected tooth. Rather than removing damaged tooth material and placing a filling, a dentist uses a tiny sponge tipped applicator to paint the liquid directly onto the cavity. The process requires no drilling, injections, or sedation.
The findings could have enormous implications for childhood dental care. Every year, thousands of young children in the United States visit emergency departments because of untreated cavities. Emergency physicians generally cannot provide the dental procedures needed to address the underlying problem, leaving some children with ongoing pain and infections. Others ultimately need dental surgery under general anesthesia, which makes them completely unconscious during the procedure.
Now, researchers led by the University of Michigan have produced compelling evidence that a much simpler approach can stop many cavities from getting worse.
Major Clinical Trial Confirms Silver Diamine Fluoride Works
Published in JAMA Pediatrics, the Phase III clinical trial included 830 children younger than 6. Participants were recruited through dental clinics, pediatric medical practices, and Head Start and Early Head Start programs in Michigan, New York, and Iowa.
Head Start and Early Head Start are federally supported programs that provide early childhood education and related services to eligible families.
The results showed that a solution containing 38% silver diamine fluoride successfully stopped decay in more than half of the affected baby teeth when treatment was provided at six month intervals.
Dentists refer to this as arresting tooth decay, meaning the damaged area stops deteriorating. Unlike a traditional filling, the treatment does not replace lost tooth structure. Instead, it helps prevent existing decay from progressing.
SDF works through the combined effects of silver and fluoride. Silver helps combat bacteria associated with tooth decay, while fluoride helps strengthen the mineral structure of teeth and resist further damage.
"This is a very effective and safe treatment -- even in children as young as 1," said Margherita Fontana, professor of dentistry at the University of Michigan School of Dentistry and the study's lead investigator.
A Simple Treatment Could Help Millions Avoid Dental Pain
Tooth decay is the most common chronic disease among children, affecting more than 40% of American children. Although cavities may initially cause few noticeable symptoms, untreated decay can eventually lead to severe toothaches, infections, problems eating and sleeping, missed school days, and repeated medical appointments.
For young children, conventional dental treatment can also be particularly challenging. Some are too young to remain still throughout a procedure, while others experience significant fear or anxiety.
SDF offers an alternative for many of these patients because it can be applied quickly without the equipment and procedures required for a traditional filling.
Fontana said the benefits could extend well beyond young children. Older adults, people with developmental or physical disabilities, individuals with severe dental anxiety, and patients who have difficulty obtaining conventional dental care could also benefit.
There is, however, one important tradeoff. SDF permanently turns the decayed portion of a treated tooth dark, which can be especially noticeable on front teeth. The discoloration is primarily cosmetic, but it may influence whether patients and families choose the treatment.
For many people, avoiding pain, drilling, or more invasive procedures may outweigh that drawback.
Why This Decades-Old Treatment Could Soon Reach More Patients
Silver diamine fluoride is not a newly invented substance. Dentists have successfully used it to manage cavities in numerous countries for decades.
In the United States, the FDA approved SDF as a medical device for treating tooth sensitivity in 2014. Dentists have also used it off-label to stop cavities, meaning they apply an authorized product for a purpose beyond its original approved indication.
What has been missing is large-scale clinical evidence from U.S. populations establishing its safety and effectiveness for treating tooth decay, a key step toward obtaining FDA approval for that specific use.
The University of Michigan trial was designed to help fill that gap.
"If we want more children and families to benefit from this treatment, we need rigorous evidence showing both that it works and that it's safe. From a public health perspective, if we want broader implementation across the United States, including in medical settings, we need carefully collected data in U.S. populations, and we now have that," Fontana said.
The investigation began in 2018 and continued despite the major disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic.
The researchers believe stronger clinical evidence could make SDF more widely available, including in pediatric medical settings where children often receive care long before their first dental appointment.
"In medicine, clinicians want high-quality evidence before changing practice," Fontana said. "It is important to have data they can refer to because young children often see pediatricians years before they ever visit a dentist, broader acceptance could allow many more cavities to be treated while a referral to a dental home is successful, and before they become painful, infected or require surgery."
A dental home refers to an ongoing relationship with a dental care provider who can deliver preventive care, treatment, and follow-up services.
Expanding access to SDF could allow more children to receive early intervention before relatively manageable cavities develop into serious dental problems.
FDA Approval Could Expand Access to Cavity Treatment
The trial brought together researchers from the University of Michigan, New York University, the University of Iowa, and Indiana University. The National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research, part of the National Institutes of Health, provided more than $12 million in funding.
The product tested was Advantage Arrest 38% SDF, supplied by Elevate Oral Care.
The findings provide clinical trial evidence that the manufacturer can use in an application seeking FDA approval of SDF as a drug for arresting dental caries, the medical term for tooth decay.
Amr Moursi, a professor of pediatric dentistry at New York University College of Dentistry and a co-principal investigator, emphasized the potential importance of that regulatory change.
"Our results support FDA approval of SDF for managing arrest of tooth decay in young children. Removing SDF from off-label status would be an important innovation which could lead to increased utilization by providers, enhanced payments by insurers and more consistent product quality," said Moursi, a co-principal investigator on the study.
For some children, receiving another application of SDF every few months could be sufficient to keep a cavity under control until the affected baby tooth naturally falls out.
Adults could also benefit, either by using SDF to manage decay over a longer period or as a temporary solution until a filling or another restorative procedure becomes affordable or practical.
The treatment is not suitable for every cavity, and stopping decay does not necessarily eliminate the need for future dental work. Nevertheless, the findings suggest that a procedure requiring only seconds to perform could help many patients avoid more complicated treatment.
"For almost anyone, this can arrest the decay and stop the infection and the pain it causes," Fontana said. "This could benefit many people."

articles.title: Scientists overcome a hidden obstacle to more powerful quantum computers
articles.text:
Scientists overcome a hidden obstacle to more powerful quantum computers
- Date:
- October 25, 2026
- Source:
- RIKEN
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a way to operate multiple silicon qubits simultaneously with remarkable accuracy, overcoming a major challenge in scaling up quantum computers. Their new technique maintained accuracy of approximately 99.9% even when all five qubits were running at once, opening the door to larger and more powerful quantum processors.
- Share:
Silicon spin qubits could play a major role in the future of quantum computing because they can be produced using the same semiconductor manufacturing methods that make today's computer chips. However, researchers have faced a significant challenge. When multiple silicon qubits are controlled at the same time, their operations tend to become less accurate. Building practical, large quantum computers will require scientists to control many qubits simultaneously while keeping errors to a minimum.
Researchers at the RIKEN Center for Emergent Matter Science and their collaborators have now made important progress toward solving this problem. In a study published in Nature Physics, the team demonstrated highly accurate control of several silicon spin qubits operating simultaneously. Their experiments used an array of five qubits connected to a shared microwave control line. By identifying a major cause of errors during simultaneous operation, the scientists developed a technique to reduce those errors and maintain precision.
Leon Camenzind, a RIKEN research scientist and co-first author who supervised the experiments, explains the significance of the results: "This shows that high-fidelity control can be maintained even when several qubits are operated at the same time and represents an important step toward scaling up silicon-based quantum processors."
Scientists Identify a Hidden Source of Quantum Computing Errors
Unlike conventional computers, which store information as bits representing either 0 or 1, quantum computers use quantum bits, or qubits, that can exist in combinations of both states. Silicon spin qubits store this information using the spin of individual electrons confined within silicon. Performing reliable quantum calculations requires extremely precise control over these electron spins.
Microwave signals provide that control, but operating multiple qubits simultaneously can create unwanted effects that interfere with their accuracy. The researchers traced much of this problem to a phenomenon called the AC Stark shift.
This effect occurs when microwave control signals alter a qubit's effective energy levels, producing changes in the phase of its quantum state. Those phase shifts can disrupt the intended operation of individual qubits, particularly when several are being controlled at once.
To counteract the problem, the team created a calibration method that compensates for these unwanted shifts. Rather than separately calibrating every possible combination of qubits, the technique relies on calibrations performed between pairs of qubits. This makes the approach more practical for systems containing larger numbers of quantum bits.
"Rather than requiring an entirely separate calibration procedure for every possible combination of qubits, our method uses calibrations between pairs of qubits to compensate for the unwanted phase shifts," explains Yi-Hsien Wu, the first author who carried out the experiments as part of his PhD research.
Quantum Qubits Achieve Accuracy Above 99.99%
The researchers combined their calibration technique with an improved device design and carefully adjusted microwave control pulses. Their results showed that exceptionally high accuracy could be maintained even when multiple qubits were operating simultaneously.
When the five qubits were tested individually, each achieved single-qubit gate fidelity well above 99.99%, with the highest approaching 99.999%. Fidelity describes how closely a quantum operation matches its intended result.
The team then tested how well the system performed when several qubits were active together. With as many as three qubits operating simultaneously, fidelity remained above 99.99%. Even when all five qubits were controlled at once, accuracy stayed at approximately 99.9%, approaching the levels needed for practical fault-tolerant quantum computing.
Although the calibration method greatly reduced errors, it did not eliminate them entirely. The researchers found that the remaining loss of accuracy was linked to drive-induced decoherence, an effect caused by the greater microwave power required to operate multiple qubits simultaneously.
Unlike the unwanted phase shifts corrected by the new technique, decoherence involves the loss of the delicate quantum coherence needed for reliable operations.
According to Camenzind, "This is a limitation, but further improvements to device design could help mitigate this source of error."
A New Path Toward Larger Quantum Processors
The findings show that controlling several silicon spin qubits at the same time does not necessarily require a major sacrifice in accuracy. By correcting a key source of errors, the researchers have demonstrated a promising approach for operating more qubits through shared microwave control lines.
This is especially important for the development of large quantum processors. Giving every qubit its own independent control system would make increasingly complex devices difficult to manage. Shared control lines could offer a more practical way to expand these systems while maintaining the precision needed for quantum calculations.
"By addressing a key source of control errors through pairwise calibration," says Camenzind. "Our study supports the use of shared control lines as a practical approach to scaling up quantum processors. Combined with silicon's compatibility with established semiconductor manufacturing, we believe that this advance could help pave the way toward larger quantum processors capable of performing increasingly complex computations."
The broader objective is to develop quantum computers that can reliably perform calculations despite the errors and disturbances that affect quantum systems. Such machines, known as fault-tolerant quantum computers, will require precise, dependable control over large numbers of qubits.
"Our long-term goal is to build a fault-tolerant quantum computer based on silicon spin qubits, and reliable parallel control is an essential step toward that goal," adds Seigo Tarucha, project manager of a silicon quantum computing project under JST's Moonshot Goal 6.

articles.title: Scientists reveal the hidden danger of missing blood pressure medication
articles.text:
Scientists reveal the hidden danger of missing blood pressure medication
- Date:
- October 25, 2026
- Source:
- European Society of Cardiology
- Summary:
- Missing blood pressure medication could mean losing much of its protection against heart attacks and strokes, according to an analysis of more than 91,000 people. Patients who consistently took their medication experienced an 11% reduction in major cardiovascular events, while those who missed too many doses saw little or no measurable benefit.
- Share:
Missing doses of blood pressure medication could significantly reduce its ability to protect against heart attacks, strokes, and other serious cardiovascular problems, according to findings presented at ESC Congress 2026.
An estimated 1.4 billion adults worldwide between the ages of 30 and 79 have high blood pressure (hypertension), a major contributor to illness and death. Although medications that lower blood pressure are proven to reduce the risk of cardiovascular complications, approximately half of patients do not take their prescriptions as directed.
"We have evidence that poor adherence to antihypertensive medication is associated with worse outcomes," explained presenter, Miss Qianqian Yang from the University of Oxford, UK. "However, previous data has come from observational studies and could be confounded by other factors. We undertook an analysis of randomized trial data to assess the true impact of adherence on the benefits of antihypertensive treatment."
Major Study Examines the Impact of Missed Blood Pressure Medication
To better understand how consistently taking medication affects its benefits, researchers analyzed individual patient data from 91,339 participants across nine clinical trials. Each trial compared a blood pressure treatment (intervention group) with an alternative approach (comparator group: either placebo or a less-intensive regimen).
The researchers divided participants into two categories based on how closely they followed their prescribed treatment. Those who took at least 80% of their assigned medication were considered to have higher adherence, while those who took less than 80% were placed in the lower adherence group.
Even with the regular monitoring and structured conditions of clinical trials, patients became less consistent about taking their medication as time passed.
"A decline in adherence over time was apparent, even in the structured setting of trials," noted Miss Yang. Overall, 88% of participants met the higher adherence threshold during the first year, but that figure had dropped to just 79% by the fifth year.
Skipping Blood Pressure Pills Reduces Treatment Benefits
The difference in medication adherence was reflected in how much patients' blood pressure improved.
Among participants with higher adherence, systolic blood pressure, the top number in a blood pressure reading, was 5.2 mmHg lower in the intervention group than in the comparator group. For those with lower adherence, the difference was considerably smaller at just 3.0 mmHg.
Researchers then examined whether these differences translated into protection against major cardiovascular problems. The outcomes included strokes, heart attacks (myocardial infarction), ischemic heart disease, and heart failure that resulted in hospitalization or death.
The findings revealed a striking contrast. Among patients who consistently followed their treatment plans, the intervention group experienced an 11% lower incidence of major cardiovascular events compared with the comparator group. However, among patients with lower adherence, there was no statistically significant reduction in these events.
"Notably, our results reinforce the saying that 'drugs don't work in patients who don't take them.' Patients with lower adherence derived little or no cardiovascular benefit, whereas those with higher adherence had greater reductions in blood pressure and prevention of cardiovascular events," said Miss Yang.
Helping Patients Get Lifesaving Heart Protection
The researchers believe that helping people take their medication consistently should become a greater priority in the treatment of high blood pressure. They recommend more routine assessments of medication adherence, along with better patient education and practical strategies to make treatment easier to follow.
Possible approaches include simplifying medication schedules, combining multiple treatments into a single pill, and prescribing longer-acting drugs that can help limit the consequences of an occasional missed dose.
Professor Felix Mahfoud, Chair of the ESC Communication Committee, emphasized that missed medication has received too little attention as a contributor to poorly controlled blood pressure.
"For years, we have neglected non-adherence to medication as a cause for uncontrolled hypertension. Assessment of adherence should become a routine part of hypertension care so patients do not miss out on life-saving benefits. As healthcare providers, we are here to have open, non-judgmental conversations with our patients about any barriers they may have to taking medication, to help improve adherence."

articles.title: Just two drinks a day may be far riskier than you think
articles.text:
Just two drinks a day may be far riskier than you think
- Date:
- October 25, 2026
- Source:
- Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs
- Summary:
- A major new study reveals that drinking just two alcoholic beverages a day is associated with a 1 in 25 lifetime risk of death from alcohol-related causes, challenging the idea that moderate drinking is harmless. Researchers also found no significant overall health benefits from alcohol, with risks rising as consumption increases.
- Share:
Even alcohol consumption that many Americans would describe as moderate may carry significant health risks, including a greater likelihood of premature death, disability, cancer, and heart disease. That is the conclusion of a new study published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs, a journal published at Rutgers University.
The research, known as the Alcohol Intake and Health Study, was originally commissioned by the U.S. federal government to help shape updated national dietary recommendations. Researchers estimated that people who consume an average of 14 alcoholic drinks per week face a 1 in 25 lifetime risk of dying from alcohol-related causes. By comparison, consuming up to seven drinks weekly was linked to only small increases in risk for most health conditions.
"Even low levels of alcohol use come with health risks," says lead study author Kevin Shield, Ph.D., an associate professor at the University of Toronto and a senior scientist who leads the World Health Organization (WHO)/Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) Collaborating Centre in Addiction and Mental Health. "And that risk continues to increase the more someone drinks."
How Scientists Measured the Health Risks of Alcohol
To better understand the long-term consequences of drinking, Shield and his colleagues in the United States and Canada investigated how alcohol consumption over a lifetime contributes to disease and premature death among Americans.
Medical experts first examined more than 7,200 scientific publications covering illnesses and injuries associated with alcohol. Using this evidence, they estimated the risks for individual health conditions and combined those findings with large national health data sets. Statistical models then allowed the team to calculate how different levels of alcohol consumption affect the likelihood of developing serious health problems or dying prematurely.
The findings provide specific estimates that are missing from the latest U.S. Dietary Guidelines. The updated recommendations simply encourage Americans to "limit alcoholic beverages" without identifying a particular consumption threshold. Earlier versions advised men to drink no more than two alcoholic beverages per day and women no more than one.
"While the new U.S. Dietary Guidelines contain a useful 'less-is-best' message, they provide no quantitative framework. Our study was designed to do just that across the drinking spectrum," says study co-author Timothy Naimi, M.D., M.P.H., director of the University of Victoria's Canadian Institute for Substance Use Research and an adjunct professor at Boston University.
"It turns out that two drinks per day, which might be considered 'moderate' from a social standpoint, is associated with a substantially elevated risk of a premature death caused by alcohol," explains Naimi.
Moderate Drinking Offers No Significant Overall Health Benefits
The researchers looked beyond the risk of premature death to examine alcohol's connection to a wide range of immediate and long-term health problems. These included cancers (e.g., esophageal, oral, and breast), cardiovascular disease, liver disease, and injuries.
One of the study's most important findings challenges the longstanding belief that consuming small amounts of alcohol can improve health, particularly heart health.
"We did not observe a significant protective effect of alcohol on health at any level of consumption," says Shield. "At low levels, alcohol may be associated with a reduced risk of ischemic heart disease and stroke. But when you look across the full range of health outcomes, including cancer and other chronic diseases, those potential benefits are outweighed by the risks even at 7 drinks per week."
In other words, while some studies have suggested that light drinking may benefit certain aspects of cardiovascular health, those possible advantages do not translate into an overall health benefit once alcohol's links to cancer and other diseases are taken into account.
Why Individual Alcohol Risks Can Differ
Although the analysis drew on extensive scientific evidence, the researchers emphasize that its estimates describe risks across populations rather than predicting precisely what will happen to any particular person.
Shield says the statistical calculations relied on "the best possible data." However, he cautions that individual circumstances can substantially influence the results.
"However, we can't assume that means one person's individual health risk is the same as what is reported here -- that depends on other factors like lifestyle, genetics, drinking patterns, and other choices that differ person to person."
To estimate alcohol's overall impact, the researchers calculated risks for health conditions already known to be caused by alcohol and combined them into a broader assessment. However, scientists are continuing to investigate additional possible consequences of drinking, including emerging evidence connecting alcohol consumption to pancreatic cancer.
"Understanding those relationships, and how much alcohol contributes to those risks, is an area that still needs further work," says Shield.
What the Findings Mean for U.S. Drinking Guidelines
The results suggest that alcohol-related health risks become more pronounced when consumption exceeds one drink per day, regardless of whether the person is male or female. This provides a more specific reference point for people trying to understand how their drinking habits might affect their long-term health.
Rather than suggesting that any particular amount is completely safe, the findings show how risks increase with greater consumption and why drinking less generally reduces exposure to alcohol-related harm.
"Having a clearer threshold helps people better understand what level of drinking is associated with increased risk and make more informed decisions when drinking," says Shield.
The study has also raised questions about how scientific evidence was incorporated into federal dietary recommendations.
In an accompanying editorial, Robert M. Vincent, a former Associate Administrator for the U.S. Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, offers his perspective on the circumstances surrounding the research and its role in the development of national guidance.
"The Alcohol Intake and Health report was explicitly invited to inform alcohol guidance during development of the Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2025-2030," he writes. "Despite the study's adherence to its mandate, its findings were sidelined."

articles.title: Three giant black holes discovered in a galaxy from the dawn of time
articles.text:
Three giant black holes discovered in a galaxy from the dawn of time
- Date:
- October 25, 2026
- Source:
- Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics, Garching
- Summary:
- Astronomers have discovered three actively feeding black holes inside a single galaxy more than 12.5 billion light-years away, revealing a remarkable scene from the universe’s infancy. Two of the black holes are separated by just 620 light-years and are expected to eventually merge, while a third lurks farther away. One weighs an astonishing 80 million suns, and another is growing faster than conventional theories predict.
- Share:
Astronomers have discovered three actively feeding supermassive black holes in a single galaxy more than 12.5 billion light-years from Earth. The finding, made by an international research team led by the Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics (MPE), offers a rare glimpse of how enormous black holes grew and interacted during the universe's earliest stages.
The black holes are located in a galaxy known as J0148-4214. All three are actively accumulating matter, which spirals toward them through surrounding disks of gas and other material. Because the galaxy is so distant, its light has traveled through space for approximately 12.5 billion years before reaching Earth. This means astronomers are observing it as it existed just 1.2 billion years after the Big Bang.
Over such vast distances, the expansion of the universe stretches light to longer, redder wavelengths. Astronomers measure this effect through a property called redshift. For J0148-4214, the researchers measured a redshift of z=5.02, allowing them to determine its remarkable distance.
Three Black Holes in One Ancient Galaxy
"This is the first evidence of three active black holes in a single galaxy in the distant Universe," says Hannah Übler, research group leader at MPE and lead author of the study.
Two of the black holes lie near the galaxy's center, separated by a projected distance of just 620 light-years. The third is much farther out, approximately 5,500 light-years from the center.
The discovery provides important evidence about how massive black holes came together in the young universe.
"It suggests that processes in the early Universe were efficient at bringing massive black holes together, setting the stage for the massive black hole mergers we expect to detect with future gravitational wave observatories," says Übler.
Astronomers believe that galaxy collisions and mergers were common during the universe's early history. As galaxies combined, their central black holes could also move closer together and eventually merge. These mergers would produce increasingly massive black holes at the centers of the newly formed galaxies, potentially helping explain how some grew to enormous sizes so soon after the Big Bang.
How Astronomers Detected the Hidden Black Holes
The researchers identified the three black holes by examining distinctive patterns in the light emitted by hydrogen gas. Near a black hole, powerful gravitational forces cause gas to move at extremely high speeds. These movements leave recognizable signatures in the spectrum of light, allowing astronomers to detect black hole activity even when the objects themselves cannot be seen directly.
In the center of J0148-4214, the team found a particularly complicated hydrogen emission pattern. The best explanation was the presence of two closely spaced black holes rather than a single source.
To distinguish between them, the scientists used a precise measurement technique called spectro-astrometry. By tracking subtle changes in the positions of spectral emissions across the galaxy, they were able to identify the locations of both central black holes, even though the telescope could not resolve them as two separate points of light.
The observations also revealed the third active black hole in the galaxy's outer region.
Three Black Holes With Remarkably Different Masses
The three black holes vary dramatically in size. According to the researchers' calculations, their masses are approximately 80 million, 600,000, and 2 million times that of the Sun.
Surprisingly, the largest black hole is not the one feeding most aggressively. Its smaller neighbor, with a mass of roughly 600,000 suns, is accumulating matter at a much higher rate. In fact, its estimated feeding rate exceeds the maximum predicted by basic models of black hole growth (the Eddington limit).
This unusually rapid growth may offer clues to how some black holes became extraordinarily massive during the relatively short time available in the early universe.
"The JWST data allowed us not only to identify the three black holes, but also to estimate their masses, accretion rates, and the stellar mass of the galaxy," says Dr. Giovanni Mazzolari, second author of the study and researcher at MPE. "We find a total stellar mass of about 1.3 billion suns, and the black holes represent a significant fraction of that."
An Ancient Black Hole Merger in the Making
The two black holes near the galaxy's center are expected to merge within the next few hundred million years. Their eventual collision could help produce an even more massive black hole, illustrating a process that may have been essential to the growth of the universe's earliest cosmic giants.
"These results are extremely exciting," adds Roberto Maiolino, professor at the University of Cambridge and co-author of the study. "They suggest that black hole merging may be an additional, fast route for their rapid growth in the early Universe."
The third black hole presents another intriguing puzzle. Located well outside the galaxy's center, it could be a remnant of an earlier merger that was pushed outward by a powerful gravitational recoil. Such a kick can occur when merging black holes emit gravitational waves unevenly, sending the resulting black hole in the opposite direction.
Another possibility is that the third black hole is gradually moving toward the galaxy's center, where it may eventually interact with the other two.
James Webb Reveals Black Holes That Might Otherwise Remain Hidden
The discovery highlights the remarkable capabilities of the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) for studying black holes in distant galaxies.
In particular, the findings demonstrate the importance of integral field spectroscopy, which allows astronomers to examine how light and its spectral signatures vary across different parts of a galaxy.
Using Webb's Near Infrared Spectrograph in its integral field spectroscopy mode (NIRSpec-IFS), the researchers were able to separate signals that would otherwise have appeared to come from a single black hole.
Without that detailed spatial information, astronomers likely would have identified only one of the galaxy's three active black holes.
The results suggest that other distant galaxies may contain multiple growing black holes that have gone undetected. Finding more of these hidden systems could help scientists reconstruct the history of black hole mergers and better understand how the universe produced its most massive black holes so early in cosmic history.

articles.title: New evidence suggests spinosaurus spent most of its life underwater
articles.text:
New evidence suggests spinosaurus spent most of its life underwater
- Date:
- October 25, 2026
- Source:
- Yale University
- Summary:
- Millions of years after animals first conquered land, some took an extraordinary evolutionary U-turn and returned to the water. Using machine learning and thousands of fossil measurements, Yale scientists have uncovered surprising clues about which prehistoric creatures truly became aquatic. Their findings suggest that Spinosaurus spent most of its life underwater, while some ancient marine reptiles previously thought to be fully aquatic actually spent considerable time on land.
- Share:
For millions of years, evolution helped animals make the transition from life in the ocean to life on land. But the journey did not always move in one direction. Many species eventually returned to the water, developing new adaptations that allowed them to thrive in aquatic environments.
Dozens of major groups of mammals and reptiles made this remarkable evolutionary reversal. Now, a new study from Yale University is shedding light on when and how these transitions occurred, as well as which ancient animals became fully aquatic and which continued to depend on land.
The findings were published in the journal Current Biology.
"These secondarily aquatic groups adapted in strikingly similar ways to their new aquatic home -- evolving flippers and a suite of other features that made them better swimmers," said lead author Caleb Gordon, who completed his doctorate at Yale's Graduate School of Arts and Sciences (GSAS) earlier this year and is now a postdoctoral researcher at the Florida Museum of Natural History. "As a result, they've become textbook examples of convergent evolution, which can tell us a lot about the processes driving and constraining adaptive change in response to similar environmental cues."
Using Ancient Fossils and AI to Reconstruct Evolution
To investigate these evolutionary changes, the researchers examined hundreds of fossil and modern specimens housed at the Yale Peabody Museum and dozens of other institutions worldwide. They collected extensive new data, including measurements (more than 11,000), photographs, and CT scans.
The team combined traditional paleontological techniques with machine learning models that account for evolutionary relationships. They also incorporated a statistical approach originally used by naval forces during World War II. Together, these methods offered a new way to investigate one of the most remarkable transitions in vertebrate evolution.
"Reconstructing the lives of extinct life forms in a scientifically rigorous way, as opposed to just telling stories, is a precise and delicate undertaking," said Bhart-Anjan Bhullar, senior author of the study. Bhullar is an associate professor of Earth and planetary sciences in Yale's Faculty of Arts and Sciences (FAS) and an associate curator of vertebrate paleontology and vertebrate zoology at the Peabody Museum.
"It requires a careful interweaving of data from modern organisms, of which our understanding is necessarily far deeper, and knowledge of these living organisms' genealogy relative to fossil forms," he said. "Caleb's work accomplishes all of this and more, and on a massive evolutionary scale."
For decades, scientists have disagreed about when particular groups of prehistoric animals became fully adapted to life underwater. The fossil record often provides incomplete or conflicting clues, making it difficult to determine whether an extinct species primarily lived on land, in water, or in both environments.
Some skeletal features may indicate an aquatic lifestyle, while others suggest that the same animal remained capable of moving and feeding on land. These contradictions have led researchers to different conclusions about how ancient species behaved.
"In these cases, paleontologists are often stuck, as different lines of evidence disagree about what the ancient animal was like," Gordon said.
To address this uncertainty, Gordon developed a method using relatively simple but effective machine learning models trained on living animals. By identifying relationships between skeletal proportions and known lifestyles, the models can estimate how extinct species used aquatic environments. They can also predict soft tissue adaptations, including swimming structures that rarely survive in fossils.
Spinosaurus May Have Spent Most of Its Life Underwater
One of the most striking findings concerns Spinosaurus, a giant prehistoric dinosaur whose relationship with water has generated considerable controversy.
Spinosaurus lived approximately 113 million to 94 million years ago in what is now northern Africa. Although scientists generally agree that it was associated with aquatic environments, exactly how it moved, hunted, and spent its time remains a subject of debate.
Some evidence points to an animal that frequently submerged itself and pursued prey underwater, much like seals or penguins. Other findings suggest a lifestyle closer to that of a modern heron, with Spinosaurus walking and searching for food along shorelines and in shallow water.
The Yale team's analysis provides new support for the more aquatic interpretation.
"Our results shed new light on how much time Spinosaurus spent submerged, which could support the underwater hunting view," Gordon said. "We confidently recovered highly aquatic habits for Spinosaurus, indicating that it spent the vast majority of its time submerged in the water."
Although the findings do not settle every question about how Spinosaurus hunted, they strengthen the case that this enormous predator spent much more of its life underwater than on land.
Ancient Marine Reptiles That Never Fully Left Land
The researchers reached a different conclusion about mesosaurs, small marine reptiles that lived between 290 million and 274 million years ago in regions now forming parts of South Africa and eastern South America.
Mesosaurs have long interested paleontologists because they gave birth to live young, a characteristic some researchers have interpreted as evidence of a fully aquatic existence. However, the new analysis suggests that their limbs were not adapted for a life spent entirely in water.
Instead, their skeletal proportions indicate that mesosaurs regularly moved between aquatic and terrestrial environments.
"They spent a lot of time on land, like a modern-day alligator or platypus does," Gordon said. "Mesosaurs didn't completely leave the land behind."
The findings also suggest a broader pattern among the earliest marine reptiles. According to the researchers, all Paleozoic marine reptiles (all marine reptiles around before the dinosaurs appeared) continued to return to land regularly. None appeared to have evolved a completely aquatic lifestyle, with even the most water adapted species remaining amphibious.
The researchers found that forelimb proportions were particularly useful for distinguishing these lifestyles. Using this information, their models could predict with more than 90% accuracy whether an animal possessed soft tissue flippers and whether it had highly or fully aquatic habits.
A World War II Technique Helps Solve an Evolutionary Mystery
An especially unusual part of the research involved adapting a statistical method developed during the 1940s.
"Caleb resurrected a statistical technique from a bygone era," said co-author Jacques Gauthier, a professor of Earth and planetary sciences at Yale and curator-in-charge for vertebrate paleontology at the Peabody Museum. "It was developed during WWII to estimate the probability that an approaching blip on the radar screen was an enemy plane. Caleb cleverly used it to get at whether or not an extinct animal had limbs modified for swimming."
By repurposing this approach, the researchers could assess the likelihood that an extinct species possessed specialized swimming adaptations, even when direct evidence of those features was missing.
The method could eventually help scientists investigate other major changes in evolutionary history. Potential applications include studying when human ancestors developed the ability to walk on two legs and how the dinosaur ancestors of birds evolved the ability to fly.
A New Way to Understand Extinct Animals
Because most prehistoric vertebrates are known primarily through their fossilized skeletons, reconstructing their behavior is one of paleontology's greatest challenges. Bones preserve valuable information, but they rarely provide a complete picture of how an animal lived.
Traditionally, scientists have interpreted particular skeletal features to make arguments about the lifestyles of extinct species. Those interpretations can differ significantly, especially when fossils are incomplete or several anatomical characteristics point toward different conclusions.
The new approach offers a more systematic way to evaluate that evidence, using patterns observed in living species to make testable predictions about animals that disappeared millions of years ago.
"Bones are all that is left to us of the vast majority of vertebrate animals that have lived on Earth," Bhullar said. "We want to know so very much about these creatures and the succession of lost worlds they inhabited, but we have so little on which to base our conclusions. From skeletal remains, people have tried to discern life habits, generally making an argument on the basis of one preferred set of features or another. Caleb's method removes the subjectivity from this process and allows the data to speak for themselves."
The study's additional co-authors are Lisa Freisem, a doctoral student at Yale's Graduate School of Arts and Sciences, and Christopher Griffin, an assistant professor of geosciences at Princeton University who previously worked as a postdoctoral fellow at Yale.
Research support was provided by the Yale Institute for Biospheric Studies, the International Union for Conservation of Nature's Crocodile Specialist Group, and the National Science Foundation.
