articles.title: A particle from the dawn of time that physicists often ignore may explain why everything in the universe exists
articles.text:
A neglected particle from the dawn of time could explain why everything in the universe exists
A hypothetical particle could have briefly held more energy than everything else in the infant universe combined, which could help explain how matter won out over antimatter.
A neglected "ghost particle" may have dominated the universe right after the Big Bang — changing how the cosmos expanded in its first moments and reshaping the conditions under which matter won out over antimatter, a new study suggests. In other words, it may explain why anything exists at all.
The particle, a hypothetical "right-handed" neutrino, briefly could have held more energy than everything else in the infant universe combined, which would have sped up cosmic expansion and delayed key particle interactions, the study proposes. The research was published Sept. 8 in the journal Physical Review Letters.
Neutrinos are ghostly particles that rarely interact with anything. A typical neutrino from the sun could pass through a slab of lead a light-year thick — about 5.9 trillion miles (9.5 trillion kilometers) — before striking a single atom. Neutrinos come in three types, or "flavors," and switch between them as they travel, making use of a subtle quantum effect that works only if they have mass. Yet the Standard Model of particle physics predicts they should be massless.
One popular fix involves "right-handed" neutrinos. Particles spin a bit like tiny tops, and physicists call them left- or right-handed depending on how they spin relative to their direction of travel. A right-handed particle rotates like an ordinary screw being driven in, turning clockwise as it moves away from you. Every neutrino detected so far is left-handed and turns counterclockwise as it flies away, like a screw with a reverse thread.
"Right-handed neutrinos are hypothetical particles that do not feel the weak nuclear force, "unlike their left-handed counterparts, which are part of the Standard Model," study co-author Rishav Roshan, a theoretical physicist at the University of Southampton in the U.K., told Live Science via email. "They are characterized by having no electric charge and being much heavier."
"Right-handed neutrinos may mix with left-handed neutrinos, helping to explain the mass of the latter" and why they switch flavors, Roshan said.
The cosmic seesaw
In quantum physics, particles that mix can exist as a blend of two identities at once. In a theoretical framework called the seesaw mechanism, each ordinary neutrino carries a faint trace of a heavy right-handed partner, and that trace gives it a tiny mass. The heavier the partner, the fainter the trace and the lighter the ordinary neutrino — hence the name, after the playground ride whose ends move in opposite directions.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
The particles could solve other puzzles, too. They "aim to address several issues, including the origin of neutrino masses, the matter-antimatter asymmetry of the universe, and the nature of dark matter," Roshan said.
The Big Bang should have made equal amounts of matter and antimatter, which would have annihilated each other, forbidding the universe as we know it from ever taking shape. Right-handed neutrinos play a crucial role in models' proposals that the "observed matter-antimatter imbalance arose from processes involving these neutrinos in the early universe," Roshan said.
In this picture, decaying heavy neutrinos left behind a slight excess of leptons — the particle family that includes electrons — that later became today's surplus of matter, he explained.
The seesaw framework usually includes three right-handed neutrinos, but because two are enough to explain the data, physicists often ignore the third, assuming it is too heavy or interacts too feebly with matter.
How the heaviest neutrino took over
In the new study, Roshan and Sudipta Show, a physicist at the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur, examined what this neglected particle — which, in the team's main example, was about 100 trillion times as heavy as a proton — would have done after the Big Bang.
At first, the particle would have zipped around at nearly light speed, so its energy would have faded like that of light, which would have both spread out and stretched to weaker wavelengths as space expanded. But as the cosmos cooled, the particle would have slowed down and most of its energy would have become locked in its mass, which would have been only spread out. Its share of the cosmic energy therefore would have grown until it dominated, and the long-lived particle would have stayed in charge until it decayed into other particles, according to the team's computations.
The study reveals that the neglected right-handed neutrino "significantly impacts the early universe's expansion dynamics, driving a period of early matter domination," Roshan said. This change "affects various Standard Model interactions" that could help to explain the matter-antimatter asymmetry, Roshan added.
Each interaction would have switched on only once it outpaced the expansion of space. Because a universe dominated by the heavy neutrino would have expanded faster, the interactions would have had to wait until it cooled further.
These interactions would have let the early universe distinguish lepton flavors, which would have affected how the matter surplus formed. Thanks to the delay, the team found, a lighter right-handed neutrino about 100 billion times as heavy as a proton could have produced the observed amount of matter before the flavors could be told apart — even after the heavy neutrino's decay diluted part of it.
Hard to test, but not out of reach
Related stories
The heavy neutrino is far too massive to create in any particle accelerator, so tests must be indirect.
Gravitational waves — ripples in space-time — offer one such route. An era dominated by the heavy neutrino would have left a telltale kink in the background of early-universe gravitational waves, such as those from "cosmic strings" — hypothetical thread-like defects in space. The results can be tested through forthcoming facilities such as the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) and the Square Kilometer Array Observatory (SKAO), Roshan noted.
LISA, a space-based European Space Agency mission, is scheduled to launch around 2035, while SKAO, a giant radio telescope project being built in Australia and South Africa, could catch such waves by timing distant pulsars. Tests could come "as these facilities come online and begin data collection," Roshan said. A faint hum from the hot primordial plasma would carry the era's imprint too, but at frequencies beyond what existing detectors could pick up.
Roshan, R., & Show, S. (2026). Delayed charged Lepton Yukawa equilibration in minimal seesaw. Physical Review Letters, 137(11), 111802. https://doi.org/10.1103/nfkx-q6z7
Andrey got his B.Sc. and M.Sc. degrees in elementary particle physics from Novosibirsk State University in Russia, and a Ph.D. in string theory from the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel. He works as a science writer, specializing in physics, space, and technology. His articles have been published in AdvancedScienceNews, PhysicsWorld, Science, and other outlets.

articles.title: Dùng radar quét Nam Cực, thấy "lò phóng xạ" lớn gấp đôi London: Chuyên gia cảnh báo luôn!
articles.text:
Để giải mã những bí ẩn tại Nam Cực - khu vực thách thức nhất trên hành tinh của chúng ta - cần có sự hợp tác quốc tế sâu rộng.
Băng ở Nam Cực chứa các hồ chứa nước ngọt lớn nhất trên hành tinh của chúng ta - chiếm khoảng 70% lượng nước ngọt trên thế giới - và hiện đang mất băng, góp phần làm tăng mực nước biển.
Theo xu hướng chung của hiện tượng nóng lên toàn cầu, Nam Cực được coi là "vùng đất tinh khiết cuối cùng của Trái đất". Hơn 80 nhà khoa học từ khắp nơi trên thế giới đã đệ trình một nghiên cứu toàn diện nhất về sự mất băng ở Nam Cực từng được thực hiện thông qua phân tích dữ liệu vệ tinh.
Nghiên cứu cho thấy, trong 25 năm, từ năm 1992 đến năm 2017, Nam Cực đã mất tổng cộng 3.000 tỷ tấn băng, và mực nước biển toàn cầu đã tăng thêm 7,6 mm! Con số này có vẻ quá nhỏ để người ta dễ dàng nhận thấy, nhưng điều khiến các nhà khoa học lo lắng là lớp băng ở Nam Cực có xu hướng mất đi nhanh chóng trong 25 năm qua và hiện tượng mất băng còn có thể tăng mạnh trong bối cảnh nóng lên toàn cầu càng ngày càng phức tạp.
Nam Cực là một nơi băng giá và đầy tuyết với nhiệt độ tối thiểu là âm 80 độ, khiến nó trở thành nơi lạnh nhất trên Trái đất. Hoạt động địa chất dưới lòng đất ở Nam Cực cũng được coi là yên ắng, với những tảng đá lạnh cũ như xương hóa thạch của khủng long, vẫn không thay đổi trong hàng triệu năm.
Tuy nhiên, mọi chuyện đã khác sau phát hiện của Cơ quan Khảo sát Nam Cực (Anh).
Sử dụng radar để quan sát qua lớp băng sâu 3.000m, nhóm nghiên cứu nhận thấy rằng một số tảng băng - bao phủ một khu vực có diện tích gấp 2 lần London - dường như đã bị mất tích.
Khi nhận thấy nền tảng của dải băng Nam Cực đang tan chảy nhanh chóng một cách khác thường, các nhà khoa học đã đặt câu hỏi và tìm ra được câu trả lời:
Thật bất ngờ, một "lò nóng" bất thường đã được phát hiện dưới lớp băng Đông Nam Cực. Nhiệt độ cực cao của nó đã làm tan chảy một khu vực rộng 5.000 km vuông, trực tiếp dẫn đến sự giãn ra và chảy xệ của tảng băng.
Cụ thể, trong một cuộc khảo sát năm 2018 của Cơ quan Khảo sát Nam Cực của Anh đã phát hiện ra rằng một "lò phóng xạ" khổng lồ, có kích thước gấp đôi London, nằm dưới lớp đá rắn của tảng băng Đông Nam Cực, làm tan chảy cả tảng băng Nam Cực từ dưới đáy, Cơ quan Khảo sát Nam Cực thông tin trên website của họ.
Máy bay Twin Otter của Cơ quan Khảo sát Nam Cực của Anh bay qua Trạm Nam Cực ở Nam Cực. (Nguồn: Tiến sĩ Tom Jordan/BAS)
"Quá trình tan chảy mà chúng ta quan sát được có lẽ đã diễn ra hàng nghìn hoặc thậm chí hàng triệu năm và không trực tiếp góp phần vào sự thay đổi của tảng băng. Tuy nhiên, trong tương lai, lượng nước dư thừa tại tầng băng có thể khiến khu vực này nhạy cảm hơn với các yếu tố bên ngoài như biến đổi khí hậu" - Tác giả chính, Tiến sĩ, nhà địa vật lý Tom Jordan từ Cơ quan Khảo sát Nam Cực của Anh (BAS) cho biết.
Nhà khoa học cảnh báo, "lò phóng xạ" này không chỉ khiến các sông băng tan chảy khiến mực nước biển dâng cao (gây hậu quả khôn lường cho các thành phố ven biển), mà thậm chí còn kéo theo sự sụp đổ của những ngọn núi phủ đầy tuyết, điều này sẽ mang đến nhiều thảm họa tiềm ẩn cho những người yêu thích phiêu lưu mạo hiểm tại Nam Cực; Cao hơn cả là làm ảnh hưởng đến khí hậu của Trái đất.
Nghiên cứu thu thập dữ liệu bằng máy bay của BAS như một phần của dự án PolarGAP. Dự án quốc tế này, do Cơ quan Vũ trụ Châu Âu (ESA) tài trợ, với các nhà nghiên cứu từ Na Uy, Đan Mạch và Anh, nhằm lấp đầy khoảng trống trong dữ liệu vệ tinh xung quanh Nam Cực.
Để giải mã những bí ẩn xoay quanh "lò phóng xạ" khổng lồ này, các nhà nghiên cứu đã bắt tay vào khám phá. Tuy nhiên, điều này không hề dễ dàng, họ chỉ có thể đưa ra một số kết luận suy luận dựa trên dữ liệu duy nhất, đó là, chiếc lò này đã tồn tại ở đó ít nhất là hàng nghìn năm.
Nhóm nghiên cứu tin rằng nguồn nhiệt khổng lồ này là sự kết hợp của các loại đá phóng xạ bất thường có trong thời kỳ Tiền kỷ Cambri và nước nóng từ sâu dưới lòng đất (từ hệ thống chu kỳ địa nhiệt của đứt gãy trong khu vực đó). Cả hai quá trình này ảnh hưởng cùng lúc đến sự hình thành của "lò phóng xạ".
Đồ họa cho thấy hình ảnh về lò đá nóng ở sâu bên dưới Nam Cực. (Nguồn: Tiến sĩ Tom Jordan/BAS)
Ngoài ra, những phát hiện này bổ sung thêm cho chúng ta hiểu biết về thủy văn dưới băng của lục địa Nam Cực.
Nghiên cứu mới này giải thích cách một lượng địa nhiệt cao bất thường đã làm tan chảy phần đế của băng, dẫn đến các lớp băng phía trên bị chùng xuống phía dưới.
"Đây là một dự án thực sự thú vị, khám phá một trong những khu vực hoàn toàn chưa được khảo sát cuối cùng trên hành tinh của chúng ta. Kết quả của chúng tôi khá bất ngờ, vì nhiều người nghĩ vùng Nam Cực này được tạo nên từ những tảng đá cổ và lạnh, ít ảnh hưởng đến lớp băng phía trên. Khám phá cho thấy rằng ngay cả trong nội địa lục địa cổ đại, địa chất bên dưới có thể có tác động đáng kể đến băng" - Tiến sĩ Tom Jordan cho biết thêm.
Trong một thời gian dài, các nhà khoa học phán đoán sự rút lui của các sông băng chủ yếu bằng cách quan sát các sông băng và thềm băng ở các cực từ trên cao thông qua vệ tinh. Tuy nhiên, ngày nay giới chuyên môn biết rằng không chỉ phần trên mặt nước của sông băng bị thu hẹp mà phần dưới nước cũng đang bị thu hẹp lại - một cách âm thầm.
Các phần của băng ở Nam Cực sâu trung bình tới 2.000m. Nếu những sông băng dưới nước này tan chảy, chúng sẽ là mối đe dọa thực sự. Bởi, chỉ một phần nhỏ của sông băng thực sự ở trên mặt biển, và phần lớn nó bị ẩn dưới nước.
Đường phân chia giữa thềm băng nổi bên trên và tảng băng cố định bên dưới nó được gọi là ground line, và được kiểm tra để xác định độ lớn và tốc độ tan chảy của sông băng.
Do độ dày của lớp băng ở đây đã vượt quá 3.000m, các nhà nghiên cứu chỉ có thể thu được dữ liệu liên quan về lớp băng và các lớp đá ngầm bằng cách quét khu vực Nam Cực bằng radar xuyên băng trong không khí.
Sau khi xác định được "lò phóng xạ" bên dưới Nam Cực, các nhà khoa học quốc tế tiến hành lập bản đồ địa nhiệt ở độ sâu hàng nghìn mét.
Bản đồ có độ phân giải cao nhất về địa nhiệt bên dưới lớp băng ở Nam Cực. (Nguồn: BAS)
Dữ liệu được sử dụng đến từ các phép đo từ trường chủ yếu được thu thập bởi máy bay bay qua lục địa và kết quả cho thấy các "điểm nóng" ở Nam Cực và trên Bán đảo Nam Cực, những khu vực thay đổi nhanh nhất của Dải băng Nam Cực.
Bản đồ địa nhiệt mới thoát ra từ bên trong Trái đất này sẽ giúp nâng cao hiểu biết của chúng ta về các điều kiện ở đáy tảng băng, cải thiện khả năng hiểu quá khứ và dự đoán những thay đổi trong tương lai của lớp băng ở Nam Cực và tác động của nó đối với mực nước biển toàn cầu, các chuyên gia tham gia công trình cho biết.
Việc đo trực tiếp nhiệt lượng từ bên trong Trái đất bên dưới lớp băng dày 3-4 km trong điều kiện cực kỳ lạnh giá và khắc nghiệt là vô cùng khó. Đó là lý do tại sao chúng tôi đã sử dụng dữ liệu từ trường để suy ra nhiệt lượng và chúng tôi hài lòng vì những gì chúng tôi có được chính xác hơn 30-50% so với các nghiên cứu trước đây.
Đây là những kết quả bước đầu mang tính cách mạng về việc các nhà khoa học quốc tế làm việc cùng nhau để giải mã những bí ẩn tại khu vực thách thức nhất trên hành tinh của chúng ta.
Bên cạnh việc nghiên cứu băng ở Đông Nam Cực, các nhà khoa học thuộc Cơ quan Khảo sát Nam Cực cũng tiến hành nghiên cứu phía Tay Nam Cực, nơi có sông băng Pine Island Glacier được đánh giá là sông băng tan nhanh nhất ở Nam Cực, gây ra khoảng 25% lượng băng mất đi ở Nam Cực.
Sông băng Pine Island Glacier được đánh giá là sông băng tan nhanh nhất ở Nam Cực. (Ảnh: Internet)
Theo đó, các nhà khoa học đã tạo ra các bản đồ có độ phân giải cao về đáy sông băng Pine Island Glacier, giúp họ dự đoán mực nước biển dâng trong tương lai từ khu vực này. Các cuộc khảo sát bằng radar về vùng đất bên dưới Pine Island Glacier đã cho thấy một cảnh quan đa dạng dưới lớp băng với một số điều bất ngờ.
Phát hiện này rất có ý nghĩa vì Pine Island Glacier không chỉ tan chảy nhanh mà lượng nước từ băng tan của nó còn chiếm tới 10% mực nước biển dâng toàn cầu. Lượng băng tan ra đại dương trong khu vực dự kiến sẽ tăng lên khi khí hậu ấm lên và lớp băng ở Tây Nam Cực tiếp tục mỏng đi.
Nghiên cứu cho thấy bản chất đa dạng của địa hình bên dưới sông băng là yếu tố lớn nhất ảnh hưởng đến dòng chảy của băng qua cảnh quan. Các nhà khoa học sẽ kết hợp những phát hiện mới vào các mô hình máy tính được sử dụng để dự đoán tương lai của sông băng.
Nam Cực có một mạng lưới rộng lớn các sông và hồ dưới băng có ảnh hưởng đến cách tảng băng di chuyển trên chúng. Bất kỳ mô phỏng nào về cách lục địa Nam Cực phản ứng với sự ấm lên trong tương lai đều phải tính đến hệ thống nước trong lòng đất.
Khám phá này có liên quan đến việc khoan tìm lớp băng lâu đời nhất trên lục địa. Các nhà khoa học hiện đang tìm kiếm những bằng chứng có thể ghi lại cảnh tuyết rơi không ngừng ở lục địa Nam Cực cách đây hơn 1,5 triệu năm.
Nam Cực là hồ chứa nước ngọt lớn nhất trên Trái đất. Nếu nó tan chảy, nó có khả năng làm tăng đáng kể mực nước biển toàn cầu. Đối với các quốc đảo và các thành phố ven biển, đây là một mối nguy hiểm thực sự.
Do đó, việc nghiên cứu và hiểu về sông băng ở Nam Cực là cách tốt nhất mà con người có thể làm để đối phó với một trong những kịch bản đáng sợ liên quan đến mực nước biển dâng quy mô toàn thế giới.

articles.title: House-size blocks of ice are falling from permafrost landslides in Canada
articles.text:
'A potential glimpse into the future': Climate change has triggered 'permafrost landslides' with house-size blocks of ice in Canada
For the first time, researchers have identified a new type of landslide of permafrost in Canada's Northwest Territories.
There's a new type of landslide affecting northern latitudes, and it could affect more areas as the planet continues to warm.
These landslides, called permafrost detachment slides, occur in areas with relatively thin permafrost and seem to be a long-term impact of wildfire in these environments, according to a paper published Sept. 23 in the journal Geophysical Research Letters. Such slides have not been observed in the region before and may be unprecedented over the past 10,000 years or more, said study leader Joseph Young, who completed the work as part of his doctoral degree at the University of Alberta.
"It has been stable, and then it just flipped a switch, essentially," Young told Live Science.
Young and his colleagues were doing field observations in Canada's Northwest Territories when they noticed large landslide scars in valleys that have long hosted stable permafrost, which is sediment that remains frozen year-round. They began using satellite imagery to map the changes and also conducted fieldwork, which revealed that the slides weren't standard melting permafrost.
"Typically with permafrost, everything just thaws and melts in a slurry and moves like a mud downslope," Young said. "But with these large landslides, we found blocks of frozen material in the debris."
Some of these blocks were 33 feet (10 meters) tall, the height of a two-story house. The researchers ran an electrical current through the ground to determine the depth of the permafrost on the slopes.
They focused on two slides. One, in the Johnson River Valley, took place in 2017 and moved more than 636 million cubic feet (18 million cubic meters) of soil and rock. The other, in the Redstone River Valley, moved almost 159 million cubic feet (4.5 million cubic meters) of debris in 2018. The smaller slide left a scar three-quarters of a mile (1.2 kilometers) long, while the larger one gouged nearly 2 miles (3.2 km) out of the hillside.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
The researchers then used the data they'd collected to build a model of how these icy slides occurred. The permafrost in this area has been warming by about 0.54 degrees Fahrenheit (0.3 degrees Celsius) per decade since 1980, when monitoring began, and there were also severe wildfires nearby in 1995.
The researchers found that instead of a top-down melting process by which the permafrost thawed to a muddy slurry from above, the slides were instead caused by a combination of fire-related thaw and warming temperatures, leading to cracks near the top of the slopes. These cracks allowed the thaw to penetrate deeper, eventually melting the bottom of the permafrost layer. This propagation can take 20 years to penetrate 66 feet (20 m), which is exactly what happened in the Johnson River and Redstone River valleys.
"We had a fire in '95 and then 20 years later, we start to get a lot of these widespread disturbances," Young said.
Related stories
The two large slides the researchers studied are among more than 150 in the area, Young said. The others are smaller, but they still typically move over 35 million cubic feet (1 million cubic meters) of land apiece. Canada's Northwest Territories are remote, so the permafrost detachment slides have yet to damage any infrastructure. But the two in the study did dam rivers, creating brand-new lakes and rapidly dumping sediment into the waterways downstream, Young said.
There are many other places in Canada and Alaska where the permafrost is 66 to 130 feet (20 to 40 m) deep and thus vulnerable to the same type of slide. This is especially true given the increasing intensity of wildfire at northern latitudes, Young said.
"This is almost a potential glimpse into the future of what we might be able to expect in these areas with changing forest fire dynamics," he said.
Young, J. M., Van Der Sluijs, J., Kokelj, S. V., Gruber, S., Herring, T., Rudy, A. C. A., Alvarez, A., & Froese, D. (2026). Permafrost detachment slides: a distinct High‐Magnitude Permafrost mass wasting process. Geophysical Research Letters, 53(18). https://doi.org/10.1029/2026gl124103
Stephanie Pappas is a contributing writer for Live Science, covering topics ranging from geoscience to archaeology to the human brain and behavior. She was previously a senior writer for Live Science but is now a freelancer based in Denver, Colorado, and regularly contributes to Scientific American and The Monitor, the monthly magazine of the American Psychological Association. Stephanie received a bachelor's degree in psychology from the University of South Carolina and a graduate certificate in science communication from the University of California, Santa Cruz.

articles.title: Oxford scientists discover how viruses build themselves without a blueprint
articles.text:
Oxford scientists discover how viruses build themselves without a blueprint
- Date:
- October 22, 2026
- Source:
- University of Oxford
- Summary:
- Scientists have captured virus-like particles assembling themselves step by step, revealing how a surprisingly simple process of trial and error produces complex structures with remarkable precision. The discovery uncovers a crucial molecular turning point that speeds up assembly and could lead to new ways to disrupt viruses and develop vaccines.
- Share:
Researchers at the University of Oxford have observed virus-like particles assembling themselves one molecule at a time, uncovering the surprisingly simple rules that allow complex biological structures to form with remarkable reliability. The findings, published in Nature, offer a detailed look at a process that scientists have struggled to observe directly for decades.
Understanding how viruses construct their protective protein shells, and how that construction might be interrupted, could lead to new antiviral drugs, improved vaccines, and other medical treatments. The discovery helps explain how individual proteins consistently organize themselves into the correct structures despite having thousands of possible ways to connect.
The researchers found that viral assembly resembles navigating a complicated maze, where only certain paths lead to lasting progress. At first, protein components form weak connections that can easily break apart if the arrangement is unsuccessful. This flexibility allows the molecules to keep trying different combinations until they form particular closed structures. Once multiple connections hold these structures together, they become far more stable.
These stable arrangements serve as molecular checkpoints, narrowing the enormous number of possible assembly routes into a much smaller set of successful pathways. One especially important milestone occurs when five larger protein building blocks connect to form a closed pentagonal ring. This is the first highly stable structure in the assembly process. Once it forms, each subsequent stable stage requires fewer additional building blocks, allowing the particle to grow more quickly.
Co-lead author Dr. Roi Asor (Department of Chemistry and Kavli Institute for Nanoscience Discovery, University of Oxford) explained: "A virus has to solve an extraordinary construction problem. Its components somehow have to find the right arrangement among a huge number of possibilities, without a blueprint or machinery directing the process. We can now watch what happens molecule by molecule and see the physical rules that make it possible."
Watching Virus Particles Assemble Molecule by Molecule
Viruses store and protect their genetic material within organized protein shells known as capsids. Depending on the virus, these shells may consist of tens or even thousands of individual protein components. Remarkably, in many cases, the proteins can arrange themselves into the correct structure without any external machinery directing their assembly.
Although scientists have investigated viral self-assembly for decades, capturing the process as it unfolds has been a major challenge. Many of the intermediate structures exist only briefly and appear in very small quantities. As a result, traditional methods have generally allowed researchers to examine the starting materials and finished particles without clearly showing how one transforms into the other.
To overcome this limitation, the Oxford researchers studied an engineered virus-like particle composed of 60 protein units. They used mass photometry, a technique developed at Oxford that determines the mass of individual molecules by measuring the light they scatter. By combining this technology with a new approach for keeping individual molecules confined and continuously observable, the team could repeatedly measure the mass of a growing particle as additional proteins attached.
This approach allowed the scientists to follow the construction process as it happened, effectively tracking the addition of individual molecular building blocks over time.
Co-first author PhD student Dan Loewenthal (Department of Chemistry and Kavli Institute for Nanoscience Discovery, University of Oxford) said: "This method lets us study the assembly process directly, we just take a video!"
Co-lead author Professor Philipp Kukura (Department of Chemistry and Kavli Institute for Nanoscience Discovery, Oxford University) said: "Until now, much of our understanding of how these structures assemble has had to be reconstructed from snapshots or theoretical models. Being able to both quantify the underlying interactions and follow one particle as it grows changes that. We can see the important intermediate structures appear and deduce a detailed model of the construction process."
The Surprising Trick That Makes Viral Assembly Work
The results help explain how a process involving an overwhelming number of possible molecular arrangements can consistently produce the correct structure. Rather than exploring every possible route, the proteins progress through a relatively small number of stable intermediate stages that guide assembly toward completion.
The findings also clarify why the earliest stage of construction, called nucleation, is particularly difficult and why growth becomes substantially faster after the first stable structure appears.
A key part of this efficiency comes from the ability of protein building blocks to make mistakes without permanently disrupting the process. Weak initial connections allow incorrect combinations to separate, giving the proteins another opportunity to find a better arrangement. When enough components eventually connect in the correct closed configuration, the resulting structure becomes stable enough to support further growth.
Dr. Asor added: "The weak interactions give the system room to make mistakes. Most encounters don't have to be successful: the components can separate and try again. But once enough of them come together in the right closed arrangement, the structure becomes stable, and assembly can move forward. That combination of trial and error followed by locking in successful structures is what makes the process so reliable."
New Possibilities for Antiviral Drugs and Vaccines
By identifying the molecular interactions that control viral assembly, scientists may eventually be able to develop treatments that interfere with the construction of viral protein shells. The same insights could also support efforts to engineer virus-like particles for vaccines and other therapeutic applications.
Co-author Dr. Jack Tan (MRC Weatherall Institute of Molecular Medicine and CAMS-Oxford Institute) noted: "The ability to understand these processes at the molecular level could have important applications in vaccine development and antivirals that disrupt viral assembly."
The implications may extend far beyond viruses. Self-assembly is essential throughout biology, helping create everything from the internal skeletons of cells to specialized molecular compartments and large protein complexes.
By making it possible to observe these intricate construction processes one molecule at a time, the Oxford team's approach offers researchers a powerful new way to investigate how complex biological structures emerge from relatively simple interactions.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Oxford. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Roi Asor, Dan Loewenthal, Diana Melnyk, Tiong Kit Tan, Philipp Kukura. Molecular-level observation of the self-assembly of a virus-like particle. Nature, 2026; 657 (8132): 653 DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-10948-z

articles.title: Ao có nước lâu ngày sẽ có cá? Không ai thả tại sao cá lại có trong ao, chúng từ đâu ra?
articles.text:
Khi kênh ao khô nứt được đổ đầy nước vào thì không bao lâu nữa người ta lại thấy cá nhỏ ở trong đó, dù không ai thả cá vào, vậy cá nhỏ trong ao từ đâu ra?
Có thực sự có trứng cá tồn tại hàng trăm, thậm chí hàng nghìn năm trong đất, cá nhỏ có thể nở được miễn là có một môi trường thích hợp?
Suy cho cùng, ai cũng biết rằng về cơ bản tất cả các loài cá đều không thể tồn tại nếu không có nước. Nhưng nếu bạn đã từng sống ở nông thôn, bạn sẽ biết rằng câu nói "ở đâu có nước, ở đó có cá" không phải là không có căn cứ.
Sau một vài trận mưa lớn, các ao khô này đã được bổ sung nước và hồi sinh. (Ảnh minh họa).
Ở các vùng nông thôn, thường có một số ao hoặc mương khô quy mô nhỏ hơn được đào lên rồi bỏ hoang, sau một vài trận mưa lớn, các ao này đã được bổ sung nước và hồi sinh. Có thể khi bạn đi ngang qua, bạn sẽ thấy rằng có rất nhiều cá nhỏ và chạch trong ao. Rõ ràng không ai thả cá xuống ao, vậy cá ở đâu ra?
Đó là một câu hỏi phức tạp là những con cá nhỏ sống trong ao này đến từ đâu?
Trước hết, phổ biến nhất và là một trong những điều có tỷ lệ thành công cao nhất là "di chuyển". Vào mùa mưa, ao cạn sẽ tích nước, nước trong ao không khô tự nhiên tràn vào một số loài cá có thói quen di chuyển ngược dòng, lúc này chắc chắn là thời cơ tốt nhất. Sau khi mưa lớn, trên mặt đất có rất nhiều nước đọng, kết nối các ao ban đầu bị cô lập, một số loài cá không yêu cầu oxy hòa tan cao trong nước có thể vượt qua chướng ngại vật trên cạn và chạy từ ao này đến cái khác. Điều này tạo ra tình trạng cá xuất hiện trong các ao mới lấp đầy.
Những cơn mưa lớn cũng có thể đem cá đến các hồ nước cạn khô. (Ảnh minh họa).
Hiện tượng thứ hai cần một sự may rủi nhất định, đó là do động vật lây lan. Những người thường xuyên ra đồng, các ao sẽ mang những con vật khác, có thể khi rửa một số trứng cá dính cũng có thể đi sang ao khác theo cách này.
Nhiều loài thủy cầm có thể dính vào trứng cá khi chúng đang uống và nghỉ ngơi bên ao, sông, sau khi bay đi, trứng sẽ được lấy đi và trứng có thể được chuyển đến trong thời gian nghỉ ngơi tiếp theo. Mặc dù những quả trứng rời khỏi mặt nước chỉ có thể tồn tại trong thời gian ngắn, nhưng luôn có những quả trứng may mắn có thể lắng xuống ao khác thành công.
Một cách lây truyền động vật khác là cá chép chi độc quyền. Phương thức đẻ trứng kiểu này của cá có thể gọi là “đẻ và đẻ”, vào mùa sinh sản, cá chép sẽ kéo dài ống dẫn trứng, sau đó tìm cơ hội chích trứng vào vỏ trai. Trai không yên và thường di chuyển, và chúng không hoàn toàn dựa vào nước để di cư. Nhờ sự “quá giang” của trai, nhiều loài cá trứng có thể di chuyển thành công từ ao này sang ao khác để sinh sống.
Nhiều loài thủy cầm có thể dính vào trứng cá khi chúng đang uống và nghỉ ngơi bên ao. (Ảnh minh họa).
Nếu phương pháp di cư thứ hai đòi hỏi một sự may mắn nhất định, thì những quả trứng nở thành công ở một ao khác bằng phương pháp thứ ba chắc chắn là những “đứa trẻ được chọn” thực sự. Cách thứ ba là thông qua phân chim. Đúng vậy, những quả trứng cá này chính là “nhân vật chính” tồn tại rất lâu trong hệ tiêu hóa của loài chim. Đối với phương pháp này, nhiều người tỏ ra nghi ngờ, liệu trứng cá khi đi qua đường tiêu hóa có thực sự sống được hay không?
Một nhóm nghiên cứu từ Đại học Sinos Valley đã từng thực hiện một thí nghiệm như vậy: 650 quả trứng killifish được cho ba con thiên nga hoang dã ăn, và năm quả trứng killifish sống được lấy ra từ phân của chúng. Mặc dù xác suất rất thấp, nhưng có rất nhiều loại chim trong tự nhiên, và vẫn có tính khả thi nhất định.
Những quả trứng cá này chính là “nhân vật chính” tồn tại rất lâu trong hệ tiêu hóa của loài chim. (Ảnh minh họa).
So với ba phương thức di cư "phương tiện" ở trên, phương thức thứ tư có thể được mô tả như một cảnh tượng, đó là "di chuyển bằng đường bay", như tên cho thấy, là bầu trời nơi cá rơi xuống. Điều này là do tốc độ quay cực nhanh của lốc xoáy biển phía trên hồ hoặc đại dương, sẽ đưa hồ hoặc nước biển và các sinh vật khác nhau trong đó lên mây. Dưới tác động của gió mạnh, những sinh vật thủy sinh này sẽ chuyến đi đường dài cuối cùng rơi xuống tạo thành “cơn mưa cá” trong mắt chúng ta. Trong quá trình “mưa cá”, một số cá có thể bị rơi xuống các ao gần đó.
Mặc dù hiện tượng thiên nhiên kỳ dị này khó có thể bắt gặp ở nước ta, nhưng ở Úc và các nước khác thì nó không có gì mới, thậm chí báo chí cũng lười đưa tin bởi chuyện đó chỉ là chuyện cơm bữa. Một số quốc gia thậm chí còn tổ chức lễ hội "mưa cá" đặc biệt để ăn mừng. "Mưa cua", "mưa ốc", "mưa sứa", vân vân đã xảy ra khắp nơi trên thế giới.
Bên cạnh những phương pháp này, nhiều người từng sống ở nông thôn nên nghe lý giải cho câu nói “ở đâu có nước, ở đó có cá”, người ta gọi là “hạt cỏ ngàn năm, hạt cá vạn năm”, có nghĩa là hạt cỏ và cá có sức sống của hạt giống rất mạnh mẽ, thậm chí sau hàng nghìn năm, chỉ cần gặp môi trường thích nghi là chúng có thể mọc lại.
Bỏ hạt cỏ sang một bên, câu nói về trứng cá dường như phù hợp với hiện tượng “ở đâu có nước, ở đó có cá”, và nó cũng giải thích nguyên nhân vì sao cá xuất hiện trong ao. Hầu hết các loại trứng cá về cơ bản không thể tồn tại ngoài nước và sẽ không hoạt động trong một khoảng thời gian rất ngắn. Chỉ một số rất nhỏ trứng cá, chẳng hạn như cá killifish, có thể tồn tại trong môi trường khô ráo trong một khoảng thời gian nhất định, nhưng nhiều nhất chỉ vài tháng. "Trứng cá 10.000 năm tuổi" chỉ là một lời thổi phồng, và nó cũng là một tin đồn được lan truyền từ những đồn đoán về sự thiếu hiểu biết của khoa học cách đây rất lâu.
Dựa vào những cách sinh tồn độc đáo này, chúng đã cho chúng ta thấy rằng có nước là có cá. "Phép màu" của cá thật tuyệt vời, và việc duy trì sự cân bằng giữa con người và thiên nhiên phải là trách nhiệm của tất cả chúng ta.

articles.title: A revolutionary new microscope could reveal the hidden machinery of life
articles.text:
A revolutionary new microscope could reveal the hidden machinery of life
A revolutionary laser-powered microscope could reveal a hidden world inside human cells, opening an entirely new window into life and disease.
- Date:
- October 22, 2026
- Source:
- University of California - Berkeley
- Summary:
- Researchers have developed a revolutionary microscope that uses an incredibly powerful laser to make previously invisible cellular structures easier to see. The technology dramatically improves image clarity, allowing scientists to examine small proteins that conventional electron microscopes struggle to capture. It could eventually reveal how tiny molecular machines interact inside cells, providing an unprecedented look at the hidden workings of life.
- Share:
Almost a century ago, a breakthrough in microscopy gave scientists an entirely new way to examine the inside of cells. Known as phase contrast, the technique made previously faint or nearly invisible cellular structures much easier to distinguish. Its importance was recognized with a Nobel Prize in 1953.
Now, physicists at the University of California, Berkeley, have brought that same principle to electron microscopy, a technology capable of magnifying objects roughly 10,000 times more than conventional light microscopes.
The researchers have developed a device called a laser phase plate that could significantly improve cryoelectron microscopy (cryo-EM). This powerful imaging method has transformed the study of protein structures and helped speed up drug discovery over the past decade. Even so, it has a major limitation: Most human proteins are so small that obtaining clear images of them remains extremely difficult.
The new laser technology could help overcome that obstacle, potentially allowing scientists to image proteins as small as one-third the size of those that challenge current microscopes.
An even greater impact could come from improvements to cryoelectron tomography (cryo-ET). This newer approach combines images captured from multiple angles to construct three-dimensional views of proteins and other molecules. Unlike techniques that study isolated molecules in a solution, cryo-ET can reveal how proteins are arranged and interact within their natural cellular surroundings.
“Cryo-EM has become the new, fastest-growing method for resolving the structure of biological macromolecules, and cryo-ET is expected to show how these molecules work together in their natural, cellular context,” said Holger Müller, a UC Berkeley professor of physics and faculty scientist at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory who led the development effort. “But because of signal-to-noise limitations, the majority of human and animal proteins are too small to be analyzed by these methods. The increase in signal-to-noise ratio provided by this laser phase plate is expected to overcome these important limitations.”
An Extraordinary Laser Reveals Hidden Cellular Structures
The breakthrough relies on what the researchers describe as the world's most intense focused continuous-wave laser. Rather than simply illuminating a specimen, the laser interacts directly with the microscope's electron beam, altering its phase to increase image contrast.
This adjustment makes it easier to distinguish small molecules, including hemoglobin, from their surroundings. It could also improve the visibility of structures inside cells, such as the nucleus and mitochondria.
“With cryo-ET, we're looking at small, very complicated cellular material that’s incredibly crowded inside the cell,” said Bridget Carragher, founding technical director of imaging at Biohub in Redwood City, California. “It’s like a forest of trees, and you’re trying to find one leaf on one tree in there. Cryo-ET needs a dramatic step forward in contrast, so we can start to see what's going on inside the cell. That's what the laser phase plate promises to give us.”
With financial support from Biohub, Müller acquired an advanced cryo-EM instrument and equipped it with the new laser phase plate. He named the resulting microscope Theia, after the ancient Greek Titaness associated with light and radiance.
Meanwhile, Carragher is directing the construction of a related microscope at Biohub's imaging facility in Redwood City. Her team's instrument uses two lasers rather than one, building on theoretical research conducted by Müller and his collaborators.
The two laser beams are arranged at right angles to one another and each operates at approximately half the power. This configuration helps prevent components from burning out while also reducing optical distortions that could interfere with image quality.
Both research teams are working with Thermo Fisher Scientific, the leading manufacturer of cryo-EM instruments.
“Theia is the Formula 1 microscope,” Müller said. “It has extra electron optics that give it better resolution than the standard cryo-EM, even without the laser. With the addition of the laser phase plate, we hope that it really becomes the world's best instrument overall.”
The Berkeley team's latest images and technical findings are presented in the journal Science. Details of Biohub's two-laser design are available in a recently posted preprint.
How a Nobel Prize-Winning Discovery Changed Microscopy
To understand why the new technology matters, it helps to look at a longstanding challenge in biological imaging.
Because plant and animal cells consist largely of water, they are relatively transparent when viewed under an ordinary light microscope. Although this transparency might seem beneficial, it creates a problem. Small cellular structures, including mitochondria and nuclei, scatter very little light and therefore appear only slightly darker than the surrounding material.
Scientists have traditionally addressed this problem by adding stains to create greater contrast. However, staining also kills the cells.
In 1930, Dutch physicist Frits Zernike realized that light passing through biological material changes in more ways than simply becoming brighter or dimmer. When light scatters inside a cell, it also experiences a tiny delay that changes its phase, or the timing of its wave peaks.
Although the human eye cannot directly detect this phase shift, Zernike discovered that it could be converted into a visible difference in brightness. By shifting the phase of the unscattered light by 90 degrees, he made subtle cellular features stand out more clearly against their background when the light reached the viewer's eye.
This innovation became the foundation of phase-contrast microscopy, earning Zernike the 1953 Nobel Prize in Physics.
By the early 1940s, scientists had already recognized how useful phase contrast was for studying cells. They began exploring whether the same idea might improve electron microscopes, which use electrons instead of light to examine structures as small as individual proteins.
Unfortunately, early attempts encountered serious technical difficulties. Devices designed to alter the phase of electron beams often weakened the beam too much, introduced image instability, or reduced resolution.
A possible solution emerged in 2010, when Müller and Robert Glaeser, now a UC Berkeley professor emeritus of molecular and cell biology, proposed using an intense laser to produce the necessary phase shift. Their approach offered a way to improve contrast without sacrificing electron beam intensity.
Overcoming the Limits of Electron Microscopy
Glaeser has played an important role in developing cryo-EM, which offers a potentially simpler way to determine molecular structures than traditional X-ray crystallography.
X-ray crystallography requires researchers to grow crystals of the molecules they want to study and obtain access to an intense X-ray source. Cryo-EM avoids the need to crystallize molecules, but it presents difficulties of its own.
One of the biggest problems is that an electron beam can heat and eventually damage the specimen being examined. This limits how much information can be collected and how detailed the resulting images can become. Covering specimens with metal can reduce damage and improve contrast, but it also makes the images less sharp.
During the 1960s, researchers began investigating whether freezing biological samples could protect them from radiation damage.
Glaeser demonstrated that cooling specimens helped preserve them during imaging. He also proposed using a less intense electron beam to examine thousands of frozen molecules at once, further limiting the damage.
Because the molecules would be positioned at different angles, computers could analyze and combine their images to reconstruct a highly detailed molecular structure.
These advances helped establish the foundations of modern cryo-EM, whose developers received the 2017 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. During their acceptance remarks, the Nobel laureates acknowledged Glaeser's contributions.
The Nobel Committee praised the technology, explaining that cryo-EM “both simplifies and improves the imaging of biomolecules. This method has moved biochemistry into a new era.”
A 15-Year Quest to Harness an Exceptionally Powerful Laser
Turning the laser phase plate concept into working technology required years of engineering.
Following their 2010 proposal, Müller spent 15 years pursuing the idea, with part of the research supported by the National Institutes of Health.
The first major challenge was generating an extraordinarily intense laser beam concentrated into a tiny area. The researchers needed enough light intensity to change the phase of an electron beam by 90 degrees.
It took a decade to develop the necessary system.
Their solution was to confine a continuous laser beam inside a spherical chamber lined with mirrors. As the light repeatedly reflected through the cavity more than 10,000 times, its intensity increased dramatically while the beam became focused into an extremely small spot.
“It’s 75 kilowatts focused to a few microns,” Müller said. “That’s more powerful than what you use for welding. It's more power than a military laser. It builds up the brightest continuous laser focus ever.”
The team first demonstrated that the concept worked by installing a laser phase plate in one of Glaeser's older electron microscopes.
Additional funding from Biohub then made it possible to acquire a customized, state-of-the-art Thermo Fisher Krios cryo-EM microscope and modify it to accommodate the laser technology.
In their latest research, the scientists tested the upgraded microscope using six different samples that varied in size and preparation method. The laser consistently improved image resolution, with particularly important gains for specimens that are difficult to image using standard methods.
“For the most challenging cases — small particles, bad specimens — the laser produces a very considerable advantage,” Müller said.
Sharper Images of Proteins Once Too Small to Study
To demonstrate the new microscope's capabilities, the researchers reconstructed images of two different proteins.
The first was aldolase, a protein found in muscle that modern cryo-EM systems can already image relatively easily. The second was hemoglobin, the protein responsible for carrying oxygen through the bloodstream.
Hemoglobin is much smaller and lies near the lower size limit of proteins that conventional cryo-EM instruments can reliably analyze.
Using the laser phase plate, the researchers improved the resolution of both protein structures. The improvement was especially pronounced for hemoglobin, highlighting the technology's potential to overcome the difficulties associated with smaller molecules.
“The bottom line is, if you have a large protein and a really good sample — a fresh one or one frozen without bubbles, for example — you may not need the phase plate to get a single, high-quality image. But for a small protein and a bad sample, laser-on is best,” Müller said. “This could fill an enormous gap in our knowledge of protein structures that can’t be crystallized or are too small for today’s cryo-EM. And it will be revolutionary for cryo-ET.”
Protein mass is typically expressed in daltons, a unit named after English chemist John Dalton. One dalton is defined as one-twelfth the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
Conventional cryo-EM struggles to image proteins smaller than approximately 70 kilodaltons. That limitation is particularly significant because proteins below this threshold account for about 90% of the human proteome, the complete collection of proteins produced by the human body.
With the laser phase plate, researchers can now image proteins as small as 50 kilodaltons, although doing so remains challenging. Such proteins are even smaller than hemoglobin.
The Next Goal Is to Reveal Even Smaller Proteins
Müller believes the technology could eventually allow scientists to study proteins as small as 17 kilodaltons (the size of the protein myoglobin).
Reaching that goal may require another improvement: using a tightly focused electron beam rather than the defocused beam currently needed to produce sufficient contrast without the laser phase plate.
According to Müller, the laser system should make it possible to obtain contrast directly from phase changes in a focused electron beam.
If successful, this adjustment could double the contrast and signal-to-noise ratio again, adding to the improvement already achieved with the laser phase plate.
Such progress could make it possible to study a far larger proportion of the body's proteins and provide unprecedented insight into how they interact within the complex environment of cells.
“This technology is a step function change for biology,” said Stephani Otte, Biohub’s Vice President of Imaging Science. “We are going to be able to see how molecular machines operate inside the living cell, in context, for the first time. What was once invisible will become visible — and that changes everything about how we understand disease.”
The Berkeley research team also includes Glaeser; postdoctoral fellows and co-first authors Petar Petrov and Jessie Zhang; staff scientist Jonathan Remis; postdoctoral fellow Hang Cheng; and current and former physics graduate students Jeremy Axelrod, Eric Cooper, Ian Hicklin, Shahar Sandhaus, and Cooper Schnurr.
At Biohub, Carragher and David Agard, the organization's founding scientific director of imaging, jointly lead the Dynamic Structural Cell Biology group. Both are co-corresponding authors of the Biohub preprint, alongside Biohub engineer Pavel Olshin.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of California - Berkeley. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Petar N. Petrov, Jessie T. Zhang, Jonathan Remis, Jeremy J. Axelrod, Hang Cheng, Eric S. Cooper, Ian K. Hicklin, Shahar Sandhaus, Cooper Schnurr, Robert M. Glaeser, Holger Müller. Laser phase plate improves structure determination of small proteins by cryo-EM. Science, 2026; 393 (6807): 195 DOI: 10.1126/science.aeh0665

articles.title: Colorectal cancer cases in kids have risen sixfold over past 2 decades — researchers are racing to understand why
articles.text:
Colorectal cancer cases in kids have risen sixfold over past 2 decades — researchers are racing to understand why
While rare, colorectal cancer is becoming more common in kids, teens and young adults, and the disease appears particularly aggressive in this age group.
More children, teens and very young adults are being diagnosed with colorectal cancer in the United States, and new research suggests they often experience aggressive forms of the disease.
While diagnosis rates are rising, the disease is still rare among young people. Colorectal cancer, which affects the lower intestines and rectum, is largely a disease of age: 55% of all colorectal cancers are diagnosed in people over 65, and only 16% occur in people ages 49 or younger, according to a 2026 study published in the flagship journal of the American Cancer Society. Only a few hundred cases per year are diagnosed in people under age 21 in the U.S.
Nevertheless, the numbers of cases in the very young are rising, even as colorectal cancer rates decline or hold steady in older individuals. This increase coincides with an overall rise in colon and rectal cancer rates in people under 50.
The reasons for this schism aren't entirely understood. People over 50 receive routine colonoscopies in which precancerous polyps are removed, and that likely accounts for much of the decline in colorectal cancer diagnoses in older adults. But researchers suspect that environmental factors, such as ultraprocessed foods and sedentary lifestyles, might be behind the growing rates in young people.
"Most of the research has really focused on the gut microbiome," the community of bacteria and other microbes that live in the gut, said Dr. Christopher Lieu, a professor of medical oncology at the University of Colorado Anschutz and a medical adviser to the nonprofit Colorectal Cancer Alliance.
Microbiome disruptions may spur inflammation, which, in turn, may trigger DNA mutations that cause cancer. But these mechanisms are complicated, Lieu told Live Science, and there likely isn't one simple reason young people's microbiomes may be getting disturbed.
"It's going to be extraordinarily more complex than that," he said.
Aggressive disease in young people
What researchers are starting to learn is that colorectal cancer in people in their early 20s or younger tends to be a more aggressive disease than that often seen in older people.
"We do feel like it is a bit of a distinct disease than what we're seeing in older adults," said Dr. Erica Arnold, a pediatric surgery research fellow at Nationwide Children's Hospital in Columbus, Ohio. In October, Arnold presented new research on colorectal cancer in people ages 21 or younger at the annual meeting of the American Academy of Pediatrics.
Arnold and her colleagues analyzed the cases of 84 patients diagnosed between 2012 and 2023. They found that the median age of diagnosis was 16 years old and the median duration of symptoms before diagnosis was only 12 weeks long.
Only about 20% of the patients had a close relative with colorectal cancer, suggesting that for many of these young people, the disease did not necessarily emerge due to hereditary factors.
Eighty percent of the study participants were diagnosed with Stage III or Stage IV disease, meaning the cancer had already spread locally and to lymph nodes or to other, distant organs when the patients were diagnosed. For comparison, in colorectal cancer patients of all ages, 60% are diagnosed in Stage III or IV, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
In addition, Arnold said, one-third of the patients in their study had cellular markers of particularly aggressive cancer.
"Some of that might be related to delays in diagnosis," Lieu said, "but if you want my honest opinion, it does suggest that these cancers are developing differently."
The study's data was not nationally representative, but a recent analysis of CDC data has also found that colorectal cancer rates in youth are on the rise. In 1999, the diagnosis rate in kids ages 10 to 14 was 1 in a million. By 2020, it had risen to 6 in a million. For teens between 15 and 19, the rate of diagnosis went from 3 in a million to 13 in a million in that same time frame.
Unclear causes
There is no definitive reason for this rise, Lieu said. Research on the microbiome has suggested that processed food, antibiotic exposure in childhood, stress, reduced exercise and other lifestyle factors may contribute to this increased risk of colorectal cancer.
Some microbes may play a particularly strong role, at least in some cases of colorectal cancer. For instance, a specific variant of the common gut bacterium Escherichia coli is strongly associated with colorectal cancer; the variant carries a genetic segment and produces compounds that are toxic to genes. But this variant alone cannot explain all colorectal cancer cases in young people. Nor is it clear why the gut microbiome might be undergoing a shift in the first place.
"It may be a combination of food, antibiotic use and environmental exposures," Lieu suggested.
Regardless of the exact causes behind the cases, Arnold's new research pointed to the symptoms that deserve closer scrutiny in young people. Among the 84 patients in the study, 75% reported experiencing back and abdominal pain before their diagnosis, 45% had changes in their bowel movements, 43% experienced unexplained weight loss and 38% had rectal bleeding.
Exclusive to Live Science Pro
These are classic colorectal cancer symptoms, Arnold said, but they might be overlooked in this young age group because these same symptoms can have more common causes.
Parents should know that in most cases, stomach pain and gastrointestinal disruptions in kids are not caused by colorectal cancer, Lieu said, calling the cancer an "extraordinarily rare event." Nevertheless, pain or gastrointestinal upset that doesn't ease or that worsens over time needs a checkup, and symptoms like weight loss and blood in the stool are very unusual in kids and deserve extra attention.
"It's just important to investigate it to make sure we're catching colorectal cancer earlier rather than later in these patients," Arnold said.
This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.
Help us improve Live Science Pro: We're always trying to make our content better. Leave us feedback about Pro here.
Stephanie Pappas is a contributing writer for Live Science, covering topics ranging from geoscience to archaeology to the human brain and behavior. She was previously a senior writer for Live Science but is now a freelancer based in Denver, Colorado, and regularly contributes to Scientific American and The Monitor, the monthly magazine of the American Psychological Association. Stephanie received a bachelor's degree in psychology from the University of South Carolina and a graduate certificate in science communication from the University of California, Santa Cruz.

articles.title: 1,500-year-old pre-Inca burial contains a high-status toddler — but the grave goods are puzzling
articles.text:
Rare burial of elite toddler from pre-Inca culture discovered in Peru
Archaeologists have uncovered the 1,500-year-old burial of an elite toddler from the Moche culture in Peru.
Archaeologists in Peru have found an elaborate 1,500-year-old tomb that may hold the remains of a high-status toddler from a pre-Inca civilization.
The burial, which is from the Moche culture, also contained vessels depicting prisoners with rope around each of their necks and a sculpture of a human-bird deity.
Moche (also known as Mochica) culture developed along the northern coast of what is now Peru from the third to the ninth century. They created agricultural lands in the region's desert landscape, and their archaeological record includes monumental temples, water canals, pottery, metallurgy, textiles and a distinctive form of art. The Moche didn't have a written language, but they left behind thousands of realistic portrait vessels, which are somewhat similar to the prisoner sculptors found in the toddler's burial.
In the newfound tomb, the team unearthed a small skeleton, which is likely the remains of a toddler who was, at most, 2 years old, Carlos Rengifo-Chunga, director of the University of Trujillo's Huacas de Moche Archaeological Project, told Live Science. The child's sex is unknown.
Rengifo-Chunga and his colleagues also found two copper objects in the burial: a mask-like disk covering the child's face, and a half-moon object on their feet. In addition, the burial contained 32 ceramic objects associated with Moche culture, including those depicting the prisoners and the deity.
The tomb was large compared to the child's small size, and could have easily held an adult, Rengifo-Chunga said. It dates to the sixth or seventh century, he added.
The team unearthed the tomb inside the Uhle Platform at the Huacas de Moche archaeological site in northern Peru. The Uhle Platform is a mausoleum, attached to the Huaca de la Luna temple, with a patio archaeologists call the Patio of the Serpents. Of the more than 80 burials previously uncovered there, the tomb represents the only known child to receive this sort of lavish burial.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
The elaborate funerary treatment, including the use of copper, and the location of the tomb all suggest that the child belonged to an elite class of Moche society, Rengifo-Chunga said.
The two prisoner sculptures are associated with the "ritual of combat," a common theme in Moche art. In this sort of imagery, two warriors fight each other, and the loser is stripped of his clothes and weapons, tied around the neck with a rope and offered as a human sacrifice, Rengifo-Chunga said. The prisoners depicted on these two vessels were the losing warriors, and their presence in the burial of a child is rare.
"One would normally presume that these kinds of vessels represent something related to the deceased's life," Rengifo-Chunga said. For example, a vessel like this might signify that the individual took part in combat.
One of the ceramic objects depicts a presumed deity with human and bird features.
An archaeological team discovered a likely elite child burial at the Huacas de Moche archaeological site in Peru.
One of the two ceramics depicting prisoners that archaeologists found in the toddler's burial.
But a toddler couldn't have taken part in such an activity. In general, archaeologists wouldn't expect to see elements of an adult ritual in the burial of a child. "This expands our knowledge on Moche funerary practices," he added.
The sculpture of the presumed deity depicts a human body with bird wings and a bird tail, although for some scholars it might be interpreted as a god in transformation, Rengifo-Chunga said. The deity holds a square shield in one hand and a goblet in the other, and is flanked by two bird "assistants" wearing ceremonial garments.
Related Stories
Researchers will have to investigate whether the deity is a known Moche god, or a newfound addition to the pantheon. Either way, the object joins a contentious debate over whether the Moche pantheon consists of many gods, or just a few that can transform into many different versions, Rengifo-Chunga said.
The artifacts are now in the laboratories of the Santiago Uceda Castillo Museum in Peru, where they will undergo conservation treatment.
How much do you know about the first people to reach the Americas? Find out with our First Americans quiz.
Margherita is a trilingual freelance writer specializing in science and history writing with a particular interest in archaeology, palaeontology, astronomy and human behavior. She earned her BA from Boston College in English literature, ancient history and French, and her journalism MA from L'École Du Journalisme de Nice in International New Media Journalism. In addition to Live Science, her bylines include Smithsonian Magazine, Discovery Magazine, BBC Travel, Atlas Obscura and more.

articles.title: Honey bees are bullying other bees, scientists discover
articles.text:
Honey bees are bullying other bees, scientists discover
- Date:
- October 22, 2026
- Source:
- Anglia Ruskin University
- Summary:
- Honeybees are aggressively pushing wild pollinators away from flowers, with scientists documenting how they chase off rivals and dominate valuable food sources. New research warns that rising temperatures and increasing honeybee populations could intensify this competition, threatening wild bees and other important pollinators.
- Share:
Honey bees are proving to be formidable competitors for food in the UK, and scientists have discovered that they frequently use aggression to drive other pollinators away from flowers. New research has documented how honey bees chase, displace, and intimidate rival insects, providing the first detailed evidence of how extensively they interfere with other species' access to food.
The study, conducted by researchers at Anglia Ruskin University (ARU) and published in Ecological Entomology, followed pollinator activity over two years at five locations in and around Cambridge, England. Each site was situated within 300 meters of an established honey bee colony.
Researchers observed insects visiting bramble (Rubus fruticosus) and ivy (Hedera helix), two flowering plants that provide important supplies of nectar and pollen. Both attract large numbers of insects during their flowering periods, making them useful places to investigate competition for food.
Honey Bees Dominate the Competition for Flowers
To examine how different pollinators interact, the team divided flower visitors into five groups: honey bees, bumble bees, solitary bees, hoverflies, and an 'other' category containing butterflies, beetles, and wasps.
Over 93 hours of observation, the scientists documented encounters in which one insect interrupted another's feeding or prevented it from reaching a flower. Each interaction was classified according to its outcome. A 'win' occurred when one insect gained access to a flower at the expense of another, which experienced a 'loss' of feeding opportunities. A 'share' meant both insects were able to access the flower without conflict.
The results revealed a clear pattern. Locations with greater concentrations of honey bees generally had fewer other pollinators and experienced more competition for flowers. Honey bees also emerged victorious in a larger proportion of their encounters with other insects.
On bramble flowers, doubling the density of honey bees was associated with a 14% decrease in bumblebee abundance. On ivy, higher honey bee numbers were linked to reduced numbers of solitary bees and hoverflies.
Honey Bees Chase Away Rival Pollinators
The honey bees did not simply reach flowers before their competitors. They frequently initiated aggressive encounters, driving other insects away to secure feeding opportunities.
Other pollinators actively avoided honey bees in 28% of observed interactions on bramble and 36% of those on ivy. In at least 20% of the encounters honey bees won on either plant, they physically pushed aside or chased away competing insects.
Aggressive behavior initiated by species other than honey bees was uncommon. However, one insect stood out as an exception.
The ivy bee, a solitary species not native to Britain that was first documented in the country in 2001, was the only pollinator observed actively challenging honey bees. Unlike most other insects, ivy bees sometimes defended their feeding spots by chasing or displacing honey bees, successfully competing for access to flowers.
Climate Change Could Make Competition Worse
The findings are part of a broader research effort to understand competition among pollinators and identify ways to reduce its ecological effects.
The results also come as beekeeping continues to expand across the UK. The number of registered beekeepers increased from 19,000 in 2010 to 47,000 last year, reflecting growing numbers of managed honey bee colonies.
Researchers warn that rising temperatures could add to the pressure on wild pollinators. Their observations showed that competitive encounters became more frequent during warmer conditions.
One possible explanation involves changes in flower nectar production. When plants experience 'heat stress', they can produce less nectar, potentially forcing more insects to compete over a smaller supply of food.
Temperature also affects different pollinators in different ways. Bumblebees and hoverflies are sensitive to high temperatures and may forage more effectively in cooler weather. Honey bees, by contrast, generally become more active as temperatures rise. Previous research found that increasing the temperature by 12°C caused a tenfold increase in the number of honey bees leaving their nests.
Together, these differences suggest that continued warming could give honey bees an even greater competitive advantage over some wild pollinators.
Protecting Wild Pollinators as Honey Bee Numbers Grow
Lead author Victoria Buckle, a PhD student at Anglia Ruskin University (ARU) in Cambridge, England, emphasized that the research is intended to improve conservation efforts rather than discourage people from keeping honey bees.
"The aim of our study was not to discourage beekeeping, but to better understand how competition happens between wild and managed pollinator species with the aim of helping to conserve our wild pollinators, which play such an important ecological role.
"We found that most interactions when competing for food were instigated by honey bees and they had a greater number of 'wins', resulting in a loss of forage for other pollinators. Bumblebees, solitary bees and hoverflies would avoid, be displaced by and on some occasions be chased off by honey bees.
"An interesting exception was the ivy bee, which would win contests more often against honey bees. It is the first time, to our knowledge, such behaviors have been observed and shows ivy bees are able to 'hold their own' in such encounters.
"However, honey bees outcompeted all other wild pollinators and based on our findings, future predicted warming in the UK is only likely to further exacerbate interference competition from dominant honey bees. Therefore, it's important to find ways to ensure honey bees and wild pollinators can continue to coexist, particularly in locations with a high density of hives, such as urban areas."
Story Source:

Journal Reference:
- Victoria A. Buckle, Peter M. J. Brown, Toby Carter, Thomas C. Ings. Honeybees directly outcompete other flower visitors through interference competition on shared resource. Ecological Entomology, 2026; DOI: 10.1111/een.70139

articles.title: Mold gold cape: A 3,900-year-old ceremonial cloak discovered on a skeleton in 'Goblins' Hill,' Wales
articles.text:
Mold gold cape: A 3,900-year-old accessory that's one of the finest examples of prehistoric goldwork ever found
The stunningly detailed gold cape is unique in Europe and may have belonged to a high-ranking woman.
QUICK FACTS
Name: Mold gold cape
What it is: A hammered gold accessory
Where it is from: Bryn yr Ellyllon (Goblins' Hill), Wales
When it was made: Circa 1900 to 1600 B.C.
In 1833, stone quarry workers discovered an ancient burial mound at Goblins' Hill near the town of Mold in Wales. At the center was a stone-lined grave that contained a fragmented skeleton and a gold, cape-like accessory that had been crushed over time. The Mold gold cape has a unique shape and style, and it is one of the finest examples of prehistoric goldwork ever found, according to the British Museum, where the artifact is on display.
The cape dates to Britain's Early Bronze Age (2500 to 1200 B.C.), a time that saw a metalworking revolution as artisans shifted from crafting flint tools to making weapons and jewelry out of gold, copper and bronze.
When the cape was originally unearthed, experts assumed that it had belonged to an ancient warrior, chief or religious leader, due to the spectacular design of the object, Benjamin Roberts, then curator for the European Bronze Age collections at the British Museum, told the BBC in 2010. But after the broken pieces of the cape were put back together, the small size of the artifact suggested it may have been worn by a woman or a child.
The Mold gold cape measures roughly 9.3 inches (23.5 centimeters) tall and 18.3 inches (46.5 cm) wide. It weighs about 1.2 pounds (560 grams) and was probably crafted from a single lump of gold about the size of a ping-pong ball.
The gold ingot was beaten incredibly thin, fashioned into a cape, and then embellished with decorations that mimicked beads or necklaces, according to the British Museum. Additionally, several hundred amber beads were found on the cape in the grave, which likely added to the gilded appearance of the accessory. Perforations around the neck opening suggest the cape originally had a lining made of leather or another perishable material that did not survive.
Because the gold cape, when worn, would restrict a person's upper arm movements, it may have been a ceremonial accessory that conferred religious authority and was worn only on special occasions. But experts are still unsure why the cape was buried in a grave. Nor can they confirm whether the person it was interred with was male or female, as the skeleton was not recovered by the quarry workers in the 19th century.
"The cape is unique — there is really nothing to compare it to in the whole of Europe," Roberts told the BBC. "This makes it more difficult to understand why it was made and what significance it had."

For more stunning archaeological discoveries, check out our Astonishing Artifacts archives.

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

articles.title: NASA’s Curiosity rover reveals a spectacular new view of Mars with a mystery on the horizon
articles.text:
NASA’s Curiosity rover reveals a spectacular new view of Mars with a mystery on the horizon
- Date:
- October 22, 2026
- Source:
- NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory
- Summary:
- NASA’s Curiosity rover has revealed a spectacular new view of mysterious, wind-carved cliffs on Mars that may hold evidence of ancient volcanic activity. With the rover approaching these unusual formations, scientists hope to uncover the secrets behind their strange appearance in 2027.
- Share:
NASA's Curiosity rover has captured a spectacular new panorama of Mars, providing its clearest look yet at a series of mysterious cliffs shaped by wind. Scientists have been eager to examine these distant formations up close, and the latest images offer an exciting preview of what lies ahead. Taken at 8:30 a.m. local Mars time, the scene reveals striking blue tones across the foreground while morning sunlight illuminates rugged cliffs known as yardangs along the horizon.
Curiosity recorded the panorama using its Mastcam on August 11, during the mission's 4,982nd Martian day, or sol. Six separate photographs were transmitted to Earth and combined to create the sweeping view. Unlike most Mastcam photographs, the images were processed without white balancing, allowing the scene to retain the distinctive colors and lighting of the Martian morning.
Curiosity Approaches Mysterious Martian Cliffs
The yardangs stretch approximately 10 miles (16 kilometers) across the northwestern portion of Mount Sharp, a 3-mile-tall (5-kilometer-tall) mountain that Curiosity has been climbing since 2014. The rover recently achieved a major milestone, gaining 0.6 miles (1 kilometer) in elevation, a greater climb than any other rover has completed on Mars.
As Curiosity continues toward these unusual formations, researchers anticipate increasingly detailed views of the cliffs. More importantly, they hope that examining the rocks firsthand will help explain how the remarkable landscape developed.
What Mars' Ancient Rocks Reveal About Its Past
Mount Sharp contains numerous layers of sedimentary rock, each preserving evidence from a different chapter of Martian history. Investigating these layers has helped scientists reconstruct a time billions of years ago when lakes and streams existed in this region of Mars.
As the planet's environment changed, those bodies of water eventually disappeared, leaving deposits of salty minerals behind. Once additional material stopped accumulating on the mountain, powerful winds may have gradually eroded portions of the existing rock, carving out the distinctive yardangs visible today.
Yet the unusual appearance of this particular layer has raised questions about its origins. Its color differs from the surrounding terrain, and its rock layers are tilted in an unexpected direction. Scientists suspect that processes beyond ordinary wind erosion may have contributed to its formation.
"The yardang layer looks out of place. It's the wrong color, the layers tilt at an odd angle, and it almost appears plastered on," said Ashwin Vasavada, Curiosity project scientist of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. "But that's what makes it exciting to reach. No one is sure exactly what created this layer, but one idea is it may be ash deposited by ancient volcanic eruptions."
NASA Plans to Investigate the Cliffs in 2027
Curiosity is now in the second year of its fifth extended mission, which began with an investigation of unusual spiderweb-like boxwork ridges. Over roughly the next year, the rover will continue traveling through rock layers containing abundant sulfates and carbonates, minerals that provide evidence of ancient drying conditions on Mars.
Mission scientists aim to reach the bottom of the yardang formations sometime in 2027. Once there, Curiosity should be able to examine the mysterious cliffs using its robotic arm, gathering unique measurements that could help determine how they formed and reveal more about the environmental changes that shaped Mars billions of years ago.
