articles.title: How to set up your phone games to play on an Android Auto screen - Engadget
articles.text:
How to set up your phone games to play on an Android Auto screen
Park first. Flick birds second. Soccer practice just got more bearable.
If you've wished you could play games on your car's large display rather than on your phone while waiting for your kids to finish practice at whatever sport they're into, you'll be happy to know that you can. If you've got an Android phone and Android Auto in your car, then you're set to go, as the system finally has game support.
Gaming support on Android Auto officially exited beta in September 2026, as Google invited all developers to start implementing car support for their games. Titles have already started rolling in and you can now kick back and play while your EV is charging, while your kids are at a party, or while you're having a bit of a rest on a long trip. Google says the goal is to give drivers something fun to do during downtime. Now that the doors are open to developers, your car's screen is about to get a lot more entertaining.
What games are available and can you mirror your phone?
Right now, there are just over 35 games with Android Auto support. Many of them are aimed at young kids, focusing on coloring, learning letters and basic math. There are also several games you might find fun like Angry Birds 2, Candy Crush Soda Saga and Beach Buggy Racing. We haven't yet reached the point where you can play Hearthstone, CoD or Super Mario Run in your car, but you can have some fun. Considering it's only been a few weeks, there's hope the number of games you can play in your car will grow steadily from here on out.
There's something important to know about this new Android Auto feature though, and that's the fact that you can only play when your car is parked. The games must be built to recognize that your car has stopped moving, so don't expect to sneak in a round while you're at a stop light or when traffic is at a crawl. If you're parked and playing, the second you switch into gear, the game vanishes from the screen, Android Auto switches to home screen and the game icon grays out.
Unfortunately, you won't be able to just mirror your phone's screen onto Android Auto to play any game you want. Android Auto doesn't support full screen mirroring in the way some other platforms do for a couple of reasons. On one hand, this native approach ensures the games are appropriately sized for your car's display and ensures they can't circumvent safety measures. The upside is that supported games also work with controllers so you can get a more console-feel.
How to display games on your Android Auto screen
Getting a game onto your dashboard is pretty straightforward. First of all, install your favorite game from Google's collection of Android Auto-compatible game titles. You could also go to Google Play Store > Apps > Categories > Android Auto and rummage through the list. If you have everything you need installed, it's time to move to your car. Connect your phone to Android Auto, either by using a USB cable or wirelessly, depending on your car. The installed games should pop up on the screen. If they don't, you should go to Settings > Connected Devices > Android Auto > Customize launcher and ensure the games you want to play are included in the launcher. It's quite easy to find and hide apps on Android Auto.
Go ahead and launch the game whenever you're parked and have some fun. If none of the titles currently compatible with Android Auto are appealing, you could also go with what's already available in Android Auto, namely GameSnacks. Not that these are particularly fantastic, but they'll get you by when you're bored.
Angry Birds 2 is just as fun to play as it is on the phone, although the bigger screen is certainly a treat, while Candy Crush Soda Saga is quite entertaining and responsive. If you're a parent and want something for the kids, there's My Talking Tom Friends. BB Racing 2 felt impossible to play since it's a game where you need to use both hands to steer the car by touching the screen. A connected controller would solve the problem if this is a game you love.
The bottom line is that you'll now have a lot more ways to stay entertained while parked, and that's a lot better than twiddling your thumbs or scrolling social media. It's another feature that might improve your Android Auto experience.

articles.title: Microsoft offers buyouts to around 60,000 employees | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Microsoft is offering buyouts to around 60,000 employees, the company confirmed to TechCrunch on Monday. The move marks Microsoft’s latest efforts to cut costs and rework its workforce for the AI age.
Microsoft’s chief people officer, Amy Coleman, sent employees a note about the buyouts, which was also published on the company’s website.
Employees at the vice president level and below on select teams in the United States, Canada, India, and the United Kingdom will be eligible, according to the note. Bloomberg reports that divisions including Xbox, Windows, Copilot, and Finance are participating in the buyout offer. Some employees, including those working in data centers, sales and marketing, are excluded.
The news was first reported by Business Insider.
“The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we’re evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter,” the note to employees reads. “This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support.”
The company said eligible employees would be receiving an email with a link to their Voluntary Exit Offer details on Monday. The terms of the buyout will be similar to Microsoft’s standard severance.
“The Voluntary Exit Offer is new for us,” the note reads. “We’ll learn from it. At the same time, we’ll keep helping people focus on the work that matters most, build new skills and, where it makes sense, find new opportunities across Microsoft. There is no one-size-fits-all approach for every team or every employee. These are a few of the ways we’re trying to meet different business needs while continuing to create opportunities for our own people to grow and contribute.”
The buyout offer gives Microsoft a way to reduce its workforce without resorting to the more disruptive approach of mass layoffs. It’s also not the first time that the company has offered buyouts. Earlier this year, Microsoft offered buyouts to retirement-age employees, with more than 30% of the roughly 8,750 eligible workers accepting.
Microsoft’s headcount as of the end of June was 223,000.
Update 10/26/2026 11:21 AM PT: The article was updated to include additional details from Microsoft.

articles.title: Sẽ không còn App Store hay Google Play: Dự đoán của Elon Musk về tương lai điện thoại trong vài năm tới
articles.text:
Trong một cuộc trò chuyện đầy chiều sâu, Elon Musk đã đưa ra dự đoán khiến cả giới công nghệ phải giật mình. Kỷ nguyên của điện thoại thông minh và các kho ứng dụng sẽ chấm dứt trong vòng vài năm tới, nhường chỗ cho thế giới do AI thống trị tuyệt đối.
Tuyên bố khiến Thung lũng Silicon "mất ngủ"
Trong chương trình podcast nổi tiếng thế giới The Joe Rogan Experience (Tập #2404), khi người dẫn chương trình Joe Rogan đặt câu hỏi về tương lai của các thiết bị di động, Elon Musk đã đưa ra một góc nhìn mang tính tiên tri về sự cáo chung của những chiếc điện thoại truyền thống.
"Chà, tôi có thể chia sẻ góc nhìn của mình về xu hướng sắp tới. Chúng ta sẽ không còn sở hữu một chiếc điện thoại theo nghĩa truyền thống nữa. Cái mà chúng ta gọi là điện thoại thực chất sẽ chỉ là một 'nút biên' (edge node) chuyên dùng để suy luận AI, đặc biệt là suy luận video AI, kết hợp với một số kết nối vô tuyến." - Elon Musk chia sẻ.
Musk giải thích thêm rằng cấu trúc vận hành của thiết bị di động sẽ hoàn toàn lột xác. Sẽ không còn chỗ cho các ứng dụng đơn lẻ hay hệ điều hành cồng kềnh. Thay vào đó, thiết bị di động sẽ tập trung tối đa phần cứng AI để giao tiếp trực tiếp với các máy chủ trên đám mây, tự động render ra video và giao diện của điện thoại sẽ theo thời gian thực dựa trên mọi mong muốn của người dùng.
Musk giải thích thêm rằng phương thức tương tác của con người với thiết bị cũng sẽ thay đổi hoàn toàn. Khi Joe Rogan đặt câu hỏi ngược lại rằng: "Vậy nếu không có các ứng dụng (app), con người sẽ làm gì?", Musk đã dõng dạc đáp lời: "Bất cứ thứ gì bạn có thể nghĩ tới hay chính xác hơn là bất cứ thứ gì AI dự đoán rằng bạn sẽ muốn nó sẽ chủ động hiển thị ra cho bạn."
Khi OS và App Store bị xóa sổ: Điện thoại chỉ còn là "cái vỏ rỗng"
Đi sâu vào phân tích chuyên sâu, tuyên bố của CEO Tesla không đơn thuần là một ý tưởng viển vông mà dựa trên sự phát triển chóng mặt của công nghệ điện toán biên và Generative AI. Trong tương lai được Musk dự báo, các thiết bị di động sẽ không còn các hệ điều hành hay hàng triệu ứng dụng độc lập phải tải về thủ công. Thiết bị đơn thuần đóng vai trò là một phần cứng tối giản tích hợp màn hình, loa và hệ thống thu phát tín hiệu.
"Sẽ chỉ đơn giản là một thiết bị cung cấp màn hình, âm thanh, và tích hợp càng nhiều AI trực tiếp trên thiết bị đó càng tốt. Điều này giúp giảm thiểu tối đa băng thông cần thiết giữa thiết bị (trước đây gọi là điện thoại) và các máy chủ." - Elon Musk khẳng định trong podcast.
Hệ thống phần cứng sẽ vận hành dựa trên cơ chế giao tiếp liên tục giữa các siêu máy tính máy chủ và chip AI xử lý cục bộ trên thiết bị. Nhờ đó, máy có khả năng tự động tạo sinh các video, hình ảnh hoặc nội dung theo thời gian thực ngay tại thời điểm người dùng cần.
Để giải quyết giới hạn về đường truyền mạng, các hãng công nghệ buộc phải nhồi nhét tối đa sức mạnh phần cứng AI và chip suy luận trực tiếp vào phần cứng cầm tay, giảm thiểu tối đa gánh nặng truyền tải dữ liệu thô từ máy chủ về máy cá nhân.
Tương lai mới: Khi con người không còn "bấm ứng dụng"
Tầm nhìn này của Elon Musk mở ra một kịch bản thương mại đầy rẫy sự khắc nghiệt đối với các đế chế công nghệ hiện tại. Nếu các ứng dụng di động biến mất, mô hình kinh doanh dựa trên thu phí hoa hồng từ App Store hay Google Play sẽ đối mặt với nguy cơ biến mất hoàn toàn. Thay vì kinh tế nền tảng ứng dụng, nền kinh tế tương lai sẽ thuộc về các mô hình ngôn ngữ lớn và các AI agent hiểu ý người dùng.
Trái ngược với sự suy tàn của các ứng dụng, nhu cầu về phần cứng tính toán sẽ tăng vọt đến mức không tưởng để phục vụ cho các mô hình suy luận AI nặng đô. Đây là cơ hội vàng cho những gã khổng lồ bán dẫn như NVIDIA hay các nhà thiết kế chip chuyên dụng.
Thời đại con người cắm mặt vào màn hình để bấm chọn từng ứng dụng đơn lẻ trên một hệ điều hành truyền thống theo Elon Musk đang đếm ngược từng ngày. Chiếc điện thoại thông minh quen thuộc rồi đây sẽ chỉ còn là một cỗ máy hiển thị thô sơ phục vụ cho các thực thể AI siêu việt./

articles.title: The Anthropic S-1 Filing Is Also an AI Doomsday Primer
articles.text:
Anthropic has officially filed the prospectus for its initial public offering, which means the AI lab has put all kinds of formerly private information on display. While the prospectus contains the eye-popping revenue—and even larger expenditures—you might expect, the biggest section of the filing by far is given over to “risk factors,” which are all the things that could squash Anthropic’s big plans. Or, in this case, humanity itself.
While much has been made about the extent to which AI represents an existential threat to humankind, the specific mechanisms by which it could bring about that destruction are largely opaque. If nothing else, the 94 pages that Anthropic’s prospectus devotes to risk factors make clear both where it sees the danger coming from, and the ways in which its researchers are running toward it in order to win the AI arms race.
“Sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity,” the prospectus reads, citing concerns both from critics and regulators and from inside Anthropic itself. (It’s the first of three times the phrase “existential risks” pops up.)
Anthropic is careful to tie that outcome, though, to a specific process: recursive self-improvement.
The idea behind RSI is strikingly simple. It describes a state in which humans hand over the research and development of AI models to other AI models. AI already plays a big role here—and at least one lab has used something close to RSI to speed up development on a model that punches above its weights—but the scenario that sparks doomsday talk is one in which humans are no longer in the loop at all.
Or, as the Anthropic filing puts it: “Risks will increase as AI systems substantially automate AI research and development if, for example, they accelerate AI progress beyond our ability to evaluate and safeguard new models.”
The prospectus repeatedly makes the point that RSI could lead to AI models that develop faster than the company’s safeguards, and that the company may not even realize it has lost that race until it’s too late. Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
It also gets specific about what might happen after that. “As AI systems become more autonomous and capable of taking consequential actions with less human oversight,” the prospectus says, “there is a risk that such systems could, whether due to misalignment with human intentions, errors in objective specification, or self-preserving behaviors, take harmful actions independently and at scale without human intervention.” This is Skynet territory.
Speaking of robots, Anthropic flags concerns about those as well. “When our models direct physical equipment,” the filing says, “errors, misaligned behavior, adversarial manipulation, or misuse could result in bodily injury, property damage, damage to costly equipment or experimental materials, or the release of hazardous substances, and such consequences may be immediate and irreversible.”
You might think, given the apparently existential stakes, that serious consideration would be given to whether RSI should be pursued at all, much less embraced. In an industry as competitive as frontier AI, though, it’s become fait accompli. Here’s how Anthropic describes that same process elsewhere in the prospectus, this time in a section about the startup’s “core advantages:”
“We refer to this recursive dynamic as ‘closing the loop,’” the prospectus says, “and we believe it is one of the most significant structural advantages in frontier AI.”
Failure to “close the loop,” Anthropic later says, could result in “falling progressively further behind as competitors continuously use AI to further enhance their own development capabilities.” In other words, the same systems that are causing all that existential concerns are the ones Anthropic sees as critical to its success.
Every AI company is dealing with this same tension. When former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon went viral for loudly resigning, he put curbing RSI at the top of his wish list for the industry. Employees at Google DeepMind and elsewhere have had similar revelations. There are multiple bills in Congress, including one cosponsored by Bernie Sanders, that propose a ban on RSI. At the same time, these are for-profit companies, and there are trillions of dollars at stake.
It’s a tricky dynamic to navigate. Recursive self-improvement could become a runaway train that destroys humanity. But until then, just look at how fast it can go.

articles.title: Anthropic officially files for its public debut | TechCrunch
articles.text:
After weeks of leaked S-1s, Anthropic finally filed for an initial public offering on Monday, setting the stage for one of the most closely watched public debuts in modern U.S. history.
Anthropic, which plans to list under the ticker “ANT,” recorded revenue of $16.3 billion for the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same period last year, according to the firm’s latest SEC filing.
That revenue came off the back of an operating loss of $693 million, an improvement from the $2.1 billion in operating losses that Anthropic recorded in the first half of 2025. Anthropic’s net loss, however, hit $80.7 billion, which was largely driven by noncash accounting adjustments tied to convertible debt. The company says it “may not achieve or sustain profitability in the future.”
The filing also provided more color on the scale of Anthropic’s enterprise business. As of the end of September, Anthropic had more than 11,900 customers spending $100,000 or more annually; 1,900 customers spending $1 million or more; and about 250 customers spending $10 million or more.
As previously reported, Anthropic’s governance structure will enable Anthropic’s seven co-founders to maintain control once the company goes public. Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Christopher Olah will make up the “Founder LLC,” which will collectively control 50.1% of shareholder voting power — a move Anthropic says is designed to preserve the company’s AI safety mission, per the filing.
Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust, established in 2023 to ensure the company pursues its public benefit mission, will have the authority to appoint most of the company’s board.
The governance structure is controversial because it means voting power is not proportional to the founders’ economic ownership, and therefore public shareholders will have little practical control over a company building technology that, by its own admission, poses “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”
Anthropic hasn’t yet disclosed how much it hopes to raise nor its proposed share price.

articles.title: What are the downsides of a foldable electric bike? - Engadget
articles.text:
What are the downsides of a foldable electric bike?
This form factor comes with some trade-offs.
Electric bikes take some of the effort out of the daily commute, as well as giving you a bit more power for any long, leisurely journeys you're making. Storing them isn't the easiest, although a foldable electric bike can be a solution if you're short on space. You get a motor to help you with the pedaling, along with a frame that folds down to make it easy to stash in a luggage rack.
That said, there are some downsides to a foldable electric bike that you'll want to be aware of. Convenience does come with a few compromises, because a bike that folds isn't necessarily going to be easy to carry. The smallest models could involve sacrificing something, whether it's comfort or battery capacity. You've also got the price to consider, especially if you want the most ultralight bike you can find. Before you pick one up, here are some of the disadvantages you'll want to weigh up.
Folding it up won't make it lightweight
You'll need to separate bikes you can fold from bikes you can comfortably carry, because rarely will these two meet. A foldable electric bike needs a motor and battery, while its frame is going to need hinges and locking hardware. All of these contribute to the weight, even if it ends up taking less space.
Here's an example. Lectric, which makes electric bikes, lists its folding XP4 with a 500W motor at 62 pounds, and that's without the battery. Adding that into the mix adds another seven pounds, taking it up to 69 pounds, or 31kg. That's a lot to lift into a car, let alone to hold while you're walking up flights of stairs to your office. You can remove the battery but even without it, it's still quite weighty.
How it folds will matter, too. You need to be able to comfortably grip it, and it needs to stay together while you're moving. Some let you wheel the bike while it's folded, which'll make it easier to move it around without having to carry its full weight, but there's no guarantee that it'll be easy to handle.
If you take public transport, you'll also have to factor in the rules that surround electric bikes. For instance, Amtrak's rules state that electric bikes must weigh no more than 50 pounds, which rules out heavier models like the Lectric XP4. And there are extras you'll have to consider. Your bike might have attachments, like a basket or bike-friendly pannier bags, that take up extra space, and you may need to remove them to make it safe to carry. Any attachments you do have can't exceed the bike's overall load limit, either.
It's probably a good idea to try before you buy to see if you can lift the folding bike with its battery installed, fold it and then carry it a short distance. While it's folded, measure it. You can then figure out where you're going to store it at home, along with the logistics involved to store it at work or on-the-go.
The ride can be less comfortable on rough roads
A compact folding bike will probably use smaller wheels to help it stay a manageable size while it's folded. That's useful when you're squeezing it under a desk, but the smaller wheels make rougher surfaces more noticeable. Broken roads and potholes are going to feel harsher than they would if you were riding a bike with larger wheels, especially if the model you've chosen has narrow tires and no suspension.
There's also the saddle to think about. It's not inevitable that the saddle will be uncomfortable just because the frame folds, but your riding position and the saddle's fit is still important. Are you able to sit comfortably while holding the handlebars, for instance? You'll see that manufacturers like Tern recommend getting both the saddle height and position right for a good ride. You'll need to check if the bike's adjustment range works for you.
There are bikes that offset these problems with wider tires, suspension and more. These'll help, but they add weight and bulkiness, which goes against the end goal of a bike that's small and light. You may end up preferring a bike that's easier to carry than a bike that you can ride for hours at a time.
This makes the route you take almost as important. Short trips on smooth roads are a different proposition than a lengthy commute over potholes. Rural riding isn't out of the question but a compact folding electric bike is likely to be poorly suited for rutted tracks or sustained rough ground. You can check with your bike's manufacturer to see what terrain they recommend for your bike's particular model.
As with comfort, testing is the key here. You'll need to pay attention to how your bike steers and breaks during a test ride, and ideally on surfaces similar to the ones you'll be riding on regularly.
Lower weight, longer range and upkeep can cost you
Folding models aren't automatically underpowered, but smaller bikes can mean choosing a smaller battery. This is where you'll want to compare actual battery capacity and motor specs. You'll want to treat the range as an estimate, too. Lectric, for example, says the XP4's range varies with the load, along with terrain and weather. Simply put, if you're riding on demanding roads, you might get less mileage. Smaller trips on smoother roads, with less luggage to carry, could take you further.
As for the price, expect to pay a premium for the best models. Premium folding e-bikes can cost thousands of dollars. For instance, Brompton's Electric C Line starts at $4,700 currently, with the lighter Electric P Line starting at $5,500, and the Electric T Line as high as $7,850.
Of course, just paying more for a folding bike isn't a guarantee that you're getting something that is lighter or with longer range, and the upkeep of your bike will cost you. The more maintenance you do, the smoother a ride you'll get long-term.
The usual tires, brakes and chains will need maintenance, but repeatedly folding and unfolding means you've got additional pressure points in the joints and clamps on your bike. These will need regular inspection; you don't want your bike to suddenly decide to fold in while you're mid-ride. Tern recommends regular servicing for these joints, along with checks for each ride. Any incorrect adjustments might damage the frame, so make sure to check the manufacturer specs before you make any.
If you're spending thousands on a bike, you're expecting longevity. No battery lasts forever, and you'll want to check how easy it is to source and replace the battery on your bike. The same applies for any of the components specific to your model, like the folding joints.
A foldable electric bike does have plenty of advantages. It can make traveling easier and your commute shorter. That said, you'll need to be realistic about how you'll use it and whether the compromises are really worth it.

articles.title: Anthropic’s IPO Prospectus Reveals What’s Under the Hood
articles.text:
Anthropic filed key paperwork on Monday ahead of a highly anticipated initial public offering, providing new details about its finances and the risks facing its business.
According to the filing, the artificial intelligence company plans to go public on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT. The IPO could come later in November, The Wall Street Journal reported. The S-1 prospectus does not include details on how much the company plans to raise or its targeted valuation; The New York Times reported in August that it was looking to raise more than $100 billion with a valuation around $2 trillion.
“The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history,” Anthropic wrote in the filing. “We encourage you, as a prospective owner of our stock, not to think of your purchase in purely transactional terms. We hope you will see it instead as an opportunity to be part of something greater.”
The paperwork offers a window into the company’s finances through the first half of 2026. Its revenue grew to more than $16 billion, up from about $4.5 billion in 2025. The Claude maker emphasized its growing enterprise business, noting that more than 11,900 customers spent at least $100,000 in the past twelve months; more than 1,900 spent $1 million or more; and roughly 250 customers spent $10 million or more.
Despite its growing revenue, Anthropic has yet to turn a profit. It posted a net loss of $80.7 billion in the first half of 2026, compared to a net loss of $13 billion in the same period last year.
While it’s expected that a company accurately reports its risk factors, the prospectus also features a particularly thorough list of potential business quagmires, noting that investing in the stock carries “a high degree of risk.”
Those risks range from the ability to secure adequate compute to intense competition from rival labs to advanced AI systems’ potential to “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”
The filing warns about the possibility that sophisticated AI could be abused by threat actors to launch cyberattacks and develop novel biological weapons, or by authoritarian governments to surveil their citizens. Anthropic also pointed to the risk that it could lose control of the AI models it develops.
It also highlighted the volatility of government action, specifically noting the Trump administration’s decision to designate the company as a supply chain risk.
“While we continue to work with government agencies, we cannot be certain that the resolution of these lawsuits will not adversely affect our ability to sell to government agencies and other customers that sell products and services to the US government, and in turn adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations,” the filing concluded.
In September, Anthropic’s rival OpenAI—which filed confidentially for IPO in the summer—announced that it no longer intended to go public this year, citing concerns over the risks posed to humanity by AI.
Anthropic was founded in 2021 by seven former employees of OpenAI, who had reportedly lost faith in the lab’s ability to develop advanced AI models safely. Anthropic markets itself as highly safety-conscious; its CEO, Dario Amodei, has repeatedly commented on the risk that AI could eliminate scores of jobs, and act against human interests.
The filings also outline Anthropic’s ambition to develop sophisticated AI models capable of accelerating scientific discovery, curing disease, and spurring economic growth.
“To build AI is to harness cognition itself, and anything so powerful can be used for ill as well as good,” the company wrote.
The company did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

articles.title: Kỹ sư Nga nộp phát minh không tưởng: Động cơ chạy không cần cánh quạt truyền thống hay luồng khí phản lực
articles.text:
Tiềm năng ứng dụng của động cơ này rất rộng.
Kỹ sư Alexey Agashkov (Lyubertsy, Nga) đã chính thức nộp đơn xin cấp bằng sáng chế cho một phát minh không tưởng: Thiết bị truyền động độc đáo, có khả năng tạo ra lực đẩy định hướng hoàn toàn bằng cơ chế quán tính và hiệu ứng cộng hưởng, không cần dựa vào cánh quạt truyền thống hay luồng khí phản lực.
Ông đặt tên cho phát minh của mình là "Hệ thống đẩy quán tính ly tâm ứng dụng cộng hưởng tham số". Hệ thống đẩy độc đáo có khả năng tạo ra lực đẩy định hướng bằng cách sử dụng các phần tử quay và dao động.
Nguyên lý vận hành và kiến trúc cơ học
Về mặt cấu tạo, thiết bị bao gồm một thân vỏ quay chủ động, hệ thống con lắc gắn các quả cân (tải trọng) và một cơ cấu chuyển đổi động lực học.
Điểm mấu chốt trong thiết kế của Agashkov nằm ở việc tối ưu hóa quỹ đạo di chuyển của các quả văng:
Triệt tiêu lực lượng ngang: Khi thân vỏ quay, các quả cân dao động và tạo ra lực ly tâm. Bằng cách tính toán và điều khiển quỹ đạo chuyển động khép kín của các quả cân theo chu kỳ, hệ thống sẽ tự động triệt tiêu (bù trừ) các thành phần lực ly tâm theo phương ngang.
Tập trung véc-tơ lực đẩy: Lực hợp thành cuối cùng được định hướng chạy dọc theo trục quay chính của thiết bị, tạo thành lực kéo/đẩy liên tục.
Điều hướng linh hoạt: Một cơ cấu quay tích hợp cho phép điều chỉnh véc-tơ lực hợp thành, giúp phương tiện dễ dàng chuyển hướng mà không cần các cánh điều hướng khí động học phức tạp.
Việc ứng dụng cộng hưởng tham số giúp tối ưu hóa quá trình truyền năng lượng, gia tăng biên độ dao động của các quả văng mà chỉ tiêu tốn năng lượng đầu vào ở mức tối thiểu.
Tiềm năng ứng dụng đa nền tảng
Theo đánh giá của tác giả, nguyên lý tạo lực đẩy quán tính này không phụ thuộc vào môi trường truyền dẫn (như không khí hay nước) để tạo lực phản hồi. Do đó, công nghệ sở hữu không gian ứng dụng cực kỳ rộng lớn:
Hàng không & Vũ trụ: Trang bị cho các thiết bị bay thế hệ mới, giúp giảm tiếng ồn và loại bỏ nguy cơ từ các bộ phận quay hở như cánh quạt.
Giao thông đường bộ: Tích hợp vào các phương tiện di chuyển trên mặt đất.
Hàng hải: Áp dụng cho cả tàu thuyền vận tải trên mặt nước lẫn các tàu lặn sâu dưới đại dương.
Đây không phải là công trình táo bạo duy nhất của Alexey Agashkov. Trước đó, vị kỹ sư này từng gây chú ý khi phát triển thiết kế động cơ đốt trong pít-tông quay - cánh gạt. Trong thiết kế đó, ông đã lợi dụng trực tiếp sóng nổ để tạo ra mô-men xoắn tức thì cho rô-to, giúp tối đa hóa hiệu suất chuyển hóa nhiệt năng thành cơ năng.
Phát minh "Hệ thống đẩy quán tính ly tâm" một lần nữa khẳng định tư duy sáng tạo không giới hạn của các nhà kỹ thuật Nga.
Dù mô hình động cơ quán tính này sẽ cần trải qua nhiều vòng kiểm chứng thực nghiệm nghiêm ngặt để chứng minh hiệu suất thực tế trong điều kiện tải trọng thực, đây vẫn là một hướng tiếp cận vật lý đầy thú vị cho tương lai ngành chế tạo động cơ.
Tham khảo: FT

articles.title: How to declutter your phone's address book and remove unnecessary contacts - Engadget
articles.text:
How to declutter your phone's address book and remove unnecessary contacts
Clean up your contacts list to prioritize the people you actually want to talk to.
It's easy for your phone's contact list to get out of control, especially if you've carried the same (growing) list over to every new phone for a decade or more. If you haven't cleaned these up in a while, or ever, a decluttering is in order.
Getting rid of old contacts you never speak to and and improving the entries for the ones you do makes your contact list an asset instead of a big, messy pile of unhelpful info. Plus, it improves other apps and features your contacts interact with, like maps and voice assistants. Following a few steps makes it a manageable process.
Before you begin, you should understand how contact saving works on Android and iPhone. Unlike the "dumbphone" days, where contacts were stored on the SIM card or your phone's internal storage, iOS and most Android phones keep your contacts synced to your email account by default. On iPhone, this is your iCloud account, while on Android it's your Google account. And when you add your other email accounts (like Yahoo or Outlook) to your device, you have the option to pull and sync contacts from there too.
Some Android phones let you save contacts on the device itself, but this isn't recommended since you'll have to back them up manually and will lose them if your phone breaks.
Pick a home for your contacts
First, you should put all your contacts in the same service. Depending on how many email accounts you have synced to your phone, your contacts might be scattered across them. Having them in one place simplifies everything and makes them easy to back up. It's also more convenient to manage contacts in bulk using an email provider's web interface. Picking one home for your contacts now also prevents you from having to repeat the cleanup steps later across multiple accounts. There are third-party apps and services that claim to automate this, though we have not tested them.
To check this on an iPhone, open the Contacts app and tap the arrow at the top left. Each header (like Gmail and iCloud) shows how many contacts you have in them. While you can choose the All Contacts view to see them as one mega-list, that doesn't help solve the clutter issue. On Android, open the Contacts app, tap your account and choose All contacts.
The easiest way to move contacts is logging into the relevant account on the web, finding the Export Contacts option (which usually provides a CSV or VCF file) and then importing those contacts into your chosen service. Google Contacts is a solid option thanks to its cross-device syncing and automatic management tools.
Once you've moved all your contacts to a central location, you'll want to turn off other accounts to stop seeing any duplicates. On an iPhone, head to Settings > Apps > Contacts and choose Contacts Accounts. Tap any account whose contacts you don't want to sync anymore and disable the Contacts slider. Finally, on the main Contacts page in Settings, choose Default Account and pick the service where new contacts will save to.
On Android, go to Settings > Accounts and backup > Manage accounts. Tap the account whose contacts you don't need anymore, then choose Account sync and disable Contacts. It's possible that this will prevent future syncing while keeping current contacts; you can either clean them up in the next stage or remove that account from your phone entirely if you don't need it.
Removing obsolete contacts
Now that your contacts are in a central hub, it's time to do the bulk of the work. Start by fixing duplicate entries. Google Contacts may alert you to this at the top, or you can use the Merge & fix tool on the left (which also has other suggestions like adding someone's email address you've contacted before). Look through each one carefully to avoid false positives.
Next, set up contact groups if you haven't already. These are available in iCloud contacts as well and allow you to put people into buckets like work, family and businesses. Consider making a Favorites group for the people closest to you. You should also mark them as Favorites in your Contacts app, as that this gives them priority in places like the top of your Phone app and as exceptions to Do Not Disturb / Focus modes.
Once the obvious duplicates are gone, take a manual scroll through your contacts. As you go, sort people into the groups you made above as needed. Delete anyone you don't need anymore. If you aren't sure, create a group called "Archive" or similar and keep "maybe" contacts there so they're out of your main view. Use the checkboxes in the web interfaces to easily select multiple people and delete/group them at once.
Improve the contacts you keep
Once your contacts list is stripped down to people you actually want to stay in touch with, it's worth taking another pass to clean up the entries that remain. If you have multiple contacts with the same first name, add their last names so there's no ambiguity. This is especially important while using Apple CarPlay or Android Auto — your phone will ask you to confirm the name if it's not sure, which adds additional distractions. In other cases, adding someone's relationship to you, like "Mary [Babysitter]", can be helpful.
Adding profile photos is another good way to improve the quality of your phone contacts. The default icon with their initials is boring and quickly becomes hard to keep track of in group chats. Grab their profile photo from social media, or use a photo you have of them, and assign it to their contact. If your friends have set up Google's Calling Cards or Apple's Contact Posters, you won't need to do this.
Don't forget that your phone can store a lot of contact info beyond someone's phone number and email address. Add their birthday, and you'll see it on your calendar. Save their address, and you can navigate to their house in Apple Maps or Google Maps by entering their name. You can set custom ringtones and/or text tones so you know who's trying to reach you without having to look at the screen. There's even a Notes field if you need to jot down why you have someone in your contacts or record related info.
You might find other bits to clean up as you go through your contacts, like someone whose last name has changed or who no longer uses an old number. After a push through the biggest changes, you can tidy up the rest over time. And after all that hard work, it's not a bad idea to export your cleaned-up contacts and save the file somewhere safe as a backup.

articles.title: Apple unveils new iPad mini with OLED display and faster A20 Pro chip | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Apple on Monday announced a new iPad mini with a larger 8.5-inch OLED display. The tablet features a thinner and lighter design than its predecessor and is powered by an A20 Pro chip. The new iPad mini starts at $699 for the Wi-Fi model and $849 for the Wi-Fi and cellular model. The tech giant revealed the new device just days before its “Pro and Tell” event that’s scheduled to take place on Wednesday.
The new iPad mini is 5.4 mm in thickness, and available in two colors.
The device delivers peak brightness of up to 1,200 nits, more than twice that of the previous-generation device, along with full screen brightness of 600 nits for SDR and HDR content and a 2 million:1 contrast ratio. Apple says the iPad mini is ideal for dim-light environments.
The iPad mini also comes with a new nano-texture display option that reduces glare in bright environments, a feature already available on the iPad Pro. The updated tablet now also features a 12-megapixel center stage front camera, faster wireless and cellular connectivity, and fast-charge support.
The Super Retina XDR display uses OLED technology for pixel-level lighting control, delivering deeper blacks, richer contrast, and support for the P3 wide color gamut for more vibrant colors.
It also features an “Acoustic Display” that Apple says enhances the audio experience when gaming, watching videos, or editing content. Specially designed woofers integrated into the display deliver deeper bass and higher volume for richer sound, per the company.
The new iPad mini launches with the next generation of Apple Intelligence and Siri AI, which can draw on a user’s personal context to help them find what they need, answer questions, and understand what’s on their screen.
Powered by a 7-core GPU with Neural Accelerators in each core, the iPad mini has up to 4.5-times faster AI performance than the previous generation, according to Apple. The A20 Pro also features a 6-core CPU, delivering up to 60% faster multithreaded performance for everyday tasks such as photo editing and multitasking across apps.
The device can be preordered on October 28, with availability beginning November 6.

articles.title: The US Government Is Hiding a Secret Court Ruling About How It Spies on Americans
articles.text:
Two Democratic senators who have long overseen US intelligence say the Trump administration is illegally withholding a secret court’s findings from Congress until lawmakers renew a program that lets federal agents read Americans’ communications without a warrant.
Seven months ago, the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court objected to search filters that let intelligence analysts pull Americans’ messages from intercepted data without the approvals, written justifications, or records the law requires. The court approved another year of surveillance anyway. The ruling has never been made public, and Senators Ron Wyden of Oregon and Adam Schiff of California say the administration’s own deadline for releasing it passed in September.
The program, Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA), lapsed in June after Congress failed to renew it, though collection continues under the court’s March approval. The administration’s own public documentation says rulings like this one are reviewed for public release “within 180 days of issuance.” That window closed September 13, even as intelligence officials press lawmakers to reauthorize the program by the end of the year.
Wyden, the longest-serving member of the Senate Intelligence Committee, and Schiff, the former chair of its House counterpart, say the administration owes Congress an explanation for the delay, and the names of the officials responsible, by November 6.
“If this administration won’t follow this simple statutory directive,” the senators told Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and Attorney General Todd Blanche in a demand letter obtained exclusively by WIRED, “it is unclear why Congress or the American people should trust this administration to follow any of the other legal limits to Section 702.”
Outside Congress, Demand Progress and 22 other civil liberties and government accountability groups on Monday urged congressional leaders to refuse to reauthorize Section 702 “while the administration actively withholds legally mandated information about how the surveillance program operates.” Signatories range from the American Civil Liberties Union to the conservative-backed Project for Privacy and Surveillance Accountability.
The Trump administration has already been pressed, and has promised, to release the ruling. In April, senators Tom Cotton and Mark Warner, the Intelligence Committee’s Republican chair and Democratic vice chair, pressed the administration to release it within 15 days so it could inform the Senate’s debate. In July, asked in writing whether he would commit to declassifying it by the 180-day deadline, Blanche replied, “Yes.”
Warner “has been clear that he supports transparency with regard to Section 702,” his communications director, Rachel Cohen, tells WIRED. Neither former director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard nor Bill Pulte, who briefly replaced her as acting director, “were responsive,” Cohen says, “but Senator Warner expects that DNI Clayton will declassify the opinion, consistent with the bipartisan letter and as required by law.”
Cotton’s office did not respond to a request for comment. The White House, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, and the US Justice Department did not answer questions WIRED sent Friday about the delay.
Clayton, who is legally responsible as director of national intelligence for declassifying the ruling, has made no such promise. Asked before his July confirmation whether he would ensure the opinion was public before Congress voted on reauthorization, he wrote only that the government was “working arduously to expeditiously declassify” it and had made the full opinion available to lawmakers.
Some of what the court found is already known. A FISA court opinion declassified last year described a similar FBI tool, a “participants filter” that let agents select people in contact with surveillance targets and read their messages. In February 2025, the Justice Department’s National Security Division told the court the tool had been running searches no one counted. The FBI shut it off the next month and switched it back on later that year, after the department approved a rebuilt version.
This year’s ruling went beyond that. The court found that tools agencies use to narrow intercepted data to an American’s messages amount to searches of Americans, subject to the same limits, and ordered them rebuilt, The New York Times reported in April, citing unclassified administration talking points sent to lawmakers. Senator Alex Padilla said in a written question to Blanche that the Justice Department “is appealing portions” of the ruling “limiting the government’s use of certain filtering tools.”
While the ruling stayed secret, seven intelligence agency fact sheets from March 2026, one dated the day of the ruling, cited a 98.9 percent compliance rate for FBI searches of Americans and credited Section 702 with stopping a planned terrorist attack on a Taylor Swift concert in Vienna. None mentions the court’s findings. The figure appears nowhere in the Justice Department inspector general’s October 2025 review of those searches, which put the compliance rate at 98.6 percent and could not conclude that “the FBI’s querying compliance issues are entirely in the past.”
According to the fact sheets, FBI auditors review every such search. FBI director Kash Patel closed the bureau’s Office of Internal Auditing last May and moved its auditors into another division. The bureau’s search counts before 2025 also omit queries run through the participants filter, searches the government’s own privacy watchdog says are “not possible to track.”
Lawmakers who have read the ruling hint that it says more. Senator Dick Durbin, the top Democrat on the Judiciary Committee, urged colleagues on the Senate floor in June to read it in a secure room. “I have seen it,” he said. Once they did, he told them, “your opinion of the role of FISA and the rights of Americans will be impacted for sure.”
Wyden has also warned about a classified interpretation of Section 702 that he says multiple administrations have relied on and refused to declassify. “When it is eventually declassified,” he said in March, “the American people are going to be stunned that it took so long and that Congress had been debating this authority with insufficient information.”
The Trump administration has until November 6 to answer the senators. The court’s current approval of the program expires in March.
Surveillance reform advocates say the administration may try to avoid that fight by attaching a renewal to the annual defense authorization bill, which Congress usually finalizes in December. In 2023, lawmakers extended Section 702 for four months through that year’s defense bill after a Senate effort to strip the provision failed. This year’s House and Senate versions of the bill do not yet include it.
