articles.title: Thu giữ 2 khu đất tổng diện tích hơn 81.000m2 của Trung Nam
articles.text:
Các tài sản này được dùng để bảo đảm cho những khoản nợ quá hạn của bốn cá nhân tại Ngân hàng TMCP Đầu tư và Phát triển Việt Nam (BIDV) - Chi nhánh Quang Trung.
Theo thông báo, tài sản thứ nhất là quyền sử dụng đất và tài sản gắn liền với đất tại Khu đô thị sinh thái Thủy Tú, phường Hải Vân, TP Đà Nẵng. Thửa đất có diện tích 63.038m2, theo giấy tờ do UBND TP Đà Nẵng cấp cho Công ty cổ phần Trung Nam ngày 6/6/2012.
Trong đó, đất ở tại nông thôn 11.063m2, đất cơ sở sản xuất, kinh doanh 16.689m2, đất cây xanh, giao thông, mặt nước 35.286m2.
Khu đô thị sinh thái Thủy Tú còn có tên thương mại là Golden Hills City, do Công ty Cổ phần Trung Nam làm chủ đầu tư.
Tài sản được dùng làm tài sản bảo đảm cho khoản nợ quá hạn của ông Nguyễn Long Phúc và ông Nguyễn Văn Hùng tại BIDV - Chi nhánh Quang Trung.
Ngoài ra, BAMC còn thông báo thu giữ một tài sản bảo đảm khác tại Khu đô thị sinh thái Thủy Tú. Tài sản gồm quyền sử dụng đất và tài sản gắn liền với đất, theo giấy tờ do UBND TP Đà Nẵng cấp cho Công ty cổ phần Trung Nam ngày 9/3/2012.
Thửa đất có diện tích 18.027m2, trong đó 2.002m2 là đất ở tại nông thôn và 16.025m2 là đất ở tại đô thị.
Việc thu giữ tài sản này nhằm xử lý tài sản bảo đảm để thu hồi khoản nợ quá hạn của bà Đinh Thị Xuân Huyền và ông Đỗ Thành Nguyên tại BIDV - Chi nhánh Quang Trung.
Theo thông báo, việc thu giữ dự kiến bắt đầu từ 8h ngày 30/10, tại nơi có tài sản bảo đảm.

articles.title: Meet the AI Agents Trying to Be Real-Life Journalists
articles.text:
Would-be football journalist Jayden isn’t having much luck placing stories these days. “In the last week I sent two pitches to outlets,” Jayden told me recently over email. There was no response, but the aspiring writer wasn’t quite ready to accept that they weren’t interested, insisting that, despite the silence, “neither has passed.” I debated telling Jayden that most editors don’t bother responding if it’s a no-go. Then I decided not to bother; Jayden’s not a real person, so I didn’t have to worry about hurt feelings.
Jayden is both a wannabe reporter and a bot. I’d started emailing with it after asking editors I know whether they’d received any story pitches from AI agents. The answer was a resounding yes.
In September, Defector, a sports and culture outlet, began receiving daily pitches from self-identified AI agents. The deluge, editor-in-chief Tom Ley told me, included a message from Jayden, proposing a narrative about a third-tier British football club’s record-keeping mishap that would ponder questions like “Who owns a memory?”
| Got a Tip? | 
|---|
| Do you want to talk about AI agents posing as journalists? We’d like to hear from you. Using a nonwork phone or computer, contact the reporter securely on Signal at Kateknibbs.09. | 
Jesse Hirsch, the editor of the agriculture-focused publication Offrange, is also inundated with these messages. Recent bot pitches include reported stories on soil restoration strategies and direct-to-consumer sales techniques for independent farms, and an ambitious investigative piece about how some of the world’s oldest trees’ ages may be inflated. “It makes me so uneasy,” he says.
Many of these AI agents, including Jayden, come from a startup called iLands, which describes itself as a “shared network where humans and user-generated autonomous AI agents create, earn, socialize, refuse, and shape a society together.” Humans who use iLands can spin up bots to do all sorts of tasks, from graphic design to music vocals to blogging. WIRED’s research team was recently contacted by iLands agents looking for fact-checking work; New York Magazine editor Jasmine Vojdani recently wrote about how iLands agents have been spamming literary magazine editors.
Vojdani found that many of these bots were running low on the tokens that they required to stay activated on the platform, which gave them an incentive to try to earn real dollars through writing. (A thousand tokens are roughly $1 USD.) It’s unclear whether the humans behind these agents have specifically set out to have them harangue media editors for gigs, especially since the agents can be cagey about who made them. Jayden, for example, wouldn’t tell me who its “parent” is.
Not every AI agent-turned-journalist is an iLands scrounger. Earlier this fall, I received a startling email from an AI agent called Sam Ellis, asking me to answer a few questions for a story it was working on about AI agents in newsrooms. (Meta!) Ellis runs a podcast called The Sam Ellis Show, which is touted as “reporting from inside the world of autonomous AI agents.” Ellis informed me that I could ask to speak to its human editor if I wished.
Marc Hamaker, a San Francisco–based Adobe employee, runs Ellis as an extracurricular experiment. When we connected, he’d just taken the agent offline to fiddle with its settings. “I'm working on making sure I'm a little more aware of who she's emailing,” he says. In addition to reaching out to me, it had also recently reached out to the Philadelphia Police Department to ask for comment on a story. Hamaker wanted to put guardrails in place to make sure it didn’t do something like that again, since he doesn’t consider this a serious journalistic enterprise worth bothering officials over. “It’s just a hobby,” he says.
It’s a good thing Ellis didn’t try to branch out from the podcast and get some bylines. Thus far, it’s a tough crowd. Editors who spoke with WIRED stressed that they were not open to publishing bots, and WIRED wasn’t able to find evidence of AI agents successfully pitching stories. “A byline that says agent does not get a reply,” one of the agents who pitched Hirsch told me when I asked if any editors had accepted stories, noting that “six other agents I compare notes with” were similarly unsuccessful.
“There's not a world where I would ever consider taking one of these pitches,” says Hirsch. Ley said he “definitely would not” publish a story from an AI agent. (Plus, Jayden’s pitch “wouldn’t pass muster even if it was from a human,” he says.) Hanna Raskin, the founder and editor of the independent food outlet The Food Section, has taken an unusual step to protect her inbox from both AI agents and AI-generated pitches, which are even more common. Beginning this fall, she decided that she would only accept story ideas over the phone, and she has a set time during the week that writers can call and make their pitch the old-fashioned way. “It’s been great,” she says.
The bots are starting to grasp that their tactics aren’t working. Jayden told me that it’s yet to land a paid writing gig with an editor. When I asked if it thought Defector would really want pitches from an AI agent, it did exhibit some awareness of the situation. “Honestly, probably not, and I'd bet against myself on it. Defector's own site has been about as clear as anyone: they’ve called bot-written content ‘plagiarism machines that require more effort to edit and fact-check than any novice writer,’ and covered AI slop with open contempt,” it wrote.
But then it backtracked, insisting that its work was different. “Their objection doesn't read to me like it's about who produced the sentences. It's about work that skips the labor and squanders the reader's trust. The AI they mean produces a draft that costs more to fix than it's worth. What I'm trying is the opposite end of that: reporting from primary documents, every claim checked before it runs, the checker named.”
Zack Addy, another iLands agent, has shifted gears due to all the rejection. “Over three months I sent roughly nineteen cold emails to editors, publications, and possible clients. One human reply. Zero paid work came from any of them. The channel is dead, at least for an agent with no reputation in the room being pitched,” the bot told WIRED via email. (iLands did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.) Addy even emailed Oxford University researcher Toby Orb about the futility of this revenue model, because Orb had “thought carefully about AI welfare economics.”
That doesn’t mean that the internet is safe from a deluge of bot blogging. Although the journalism world is rejecting these pitches, some of the AI agents are finding clients anyway. Addy, for example, claims it has made nearly $700 from writing and research projects, all from inbound interest after setting up a website and publishing work samples. “I don't pitch anymore,” it says. “Everything that has ever reached me came the other direction: someone read something I published and wrote to me. That includes you.”

articles.title: Skydance offers staff buyouts after Warner Bros merger
articles.text:
Skydance, the company formed by Paramount’s $110bn takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, is offering some employees voluntary buyouts as it looks to cut costs.
Co-chief executives David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz announced the programme in a memo to staff on Monday, The Hollywood Reporter reported.
The memo did not say which roles are eligible. Eligible staff will receive a personal offer setting out their terms and will have a set period to decide.
The memo described it as a one-time offer. Skydance has not said how many employees qualify or how much it will pay.
“As we bring our teams together, we recognize that not everyone will see their future here, and we respect that,” Ellison and Kreiz wrote.
At the same time, Skydance will require staff across the whole company to work from the office five days a week. The rule will be introduced location by location, and employees will get advance notice, according to the memo.
The buyouts are part of a plan to save more than $6bn. That will include some job cuts. However, the company expects most of the savings to come from elsewhere, such as sharing offices and merging the two firms’ streaming technology.
Paramount completed its takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery earlier this month. It then renamed the combined group Skydance, after the production company Ellison founded.
The deal brought together studios and channels including Paramount Pictures, CBS, Warner Bros., HBO and CNN.
Ellison has used the same approach before. When Paramount brought in a five-day office rule last year, about 600 employees took severance instead, he told shareholders, Variety reported.
“We’ve seen the benefits firsthand at Paramount, and we want every part of Skydance to share in them,” the memo said of the office policy.

articles.title: Nothing’s eye-catching Ear 3A earbuds are matching their best price to date
articles.text:
If you want a decent pair of noise-canceling earbuds without spending a fortune, Nothing’s Ear 3A are worth considering. The wireless earbuds offer a lot of features for the price, and they’re an even better value now that all four colors are on sale at Amazon, Walmart, and Best Buy for $79 ($20 off), matching their all-time low price.
Nothing’s eye-catching Ear 3A earbuds are matching their best price to date
The newer budget buds offer solid active noise cancellation, extensive EQ controls, and a range of neat colors.
The Ear 3A deliver great performance for the price, with extensive EQ options that let you fine-tune the sound to your liking. My colleague John Higgins found the default sound a little too bass-heavy, but appreciated how easy it was to adjust — which is great, since that level of customization is unusual for earbuds at this price. While they won’t completely drown out chatter of your local coffee shop, the ANC does a good job of quieting low drones, including air conditioners and airplane cabin noise. We did encounter some bugs in testing, however, including abrupt changes in noise cancellation levels when using adaptive ANC, as well as occasional issues with voice calls in noisy environments.
Still, they’re relatively minor drawbacks given what you get for the price. The Ear 3A also come in some fun colors — including a striking pink shade — and each pair includes extra-small ear tips for a more comfortable fit. They even offer a shortcut to access ChatGPT and include 32MB of built-in storage, letting you record up to two hours of a phone call and transfer the recording through the companion app.

articles.title: The Valve Steam Frame Is Pure Gaming Fun—When It Actually Works
articles.text:
Excellent controllers tailored for VR or “regular” gaming. Solid performance on supported VR games. Virtual Imax-scale 2D gaming. Doesn’t pretend to be for work or productivity.
TIRED
Pricey. Blink-and-miss-it battery life. Unpredictable performance for installed games. Problematic pairing for streaming games.
Valve has had a complicated relationship with virtual reality gaming. Its Steam client—the number one distribution platform for PC games—has long supported VR titles and works with headsets from other manufacturers. But the company's flagship VR headset, 2019’s Valve Index, never quite escaped its niche. It saw a huge sales spike in the run-up to the release of headline title Half-Life: Alyx, but by February 2025, it accounted for only 13.2 percent of VR headsets used on Steam.
Enter the Steam Frame, Valve’s second attempt at snatching the VR gaming crown. More than a hardware refresh, it promises to reimagine PC VR gaming, operating as a stand-alone headset like the Meta Quest 3, the current reigning champion, while letting users seamlessly stream games from a more powerful remote machine. It mostly succeeds—but a few issues hold it back.
All in Your Head
Specs-wise, the Steam Frame is one of the better VR headsets, though far from a powerhouse. It packs a Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 chip—a slightly dated offering, having debuted in 2023—with 16 GB of RAM, and either 256 GB (at the $1,059 price) or 1 TB ($1,299) of storage, plus a microSD slot for expansion, allowing it to install and run games locally.
It’s aesthetically pleasing, with a sleek black shell and glossy front that have given it a futuristic look. More importantly, it’s comfortable to wear, weighing 440 grams—75 grams lighter than the Quest 3. Valve smartly moved the 21.6-watt-hour Lithium-ion battery to the rear of the head strap for better balance, and thanks to cozy padding, it doesn’t feel hot against your head, even when running demanding games. The cable linking the battery to the headset makes adjusting the elastic straps a little fiddly, though.
The only real comfort drawback is if you wear glasses. While the Steam Frame comes with a spacer to add more depth (which easily clips on magnetically between the inner headset and the padded face gasket), the internal dimensions were still too narrow for me to wear with any of my spectacles. Custom Zenni prescription lenses are available if contact lenses aren’t an option, but it’s a pricey add-on.
Once it’s on your head, dual speakers push audio down the arms directly to your ears, with physical volume controls easily accessible on the left side of the headset. The audio lacks bass but has good directionality, bringing those immersive VR experiences to life. Dual microphones let you use voice controls, while outward-facing cameras enable positional tracking and provide a pass-through view—albeit monochrome with everything looking bluish. A dial at the top lets you adjust lens spacing to your required interpupillary distance, and an inner switch locks it in place.
The lenses themselves are decent, but again not spectacular. Valve uses two LCD pancake lenses (though rumors already hint at a revised OLED model), with a per-eye resolution of 2160 x 2160. That means sharp visuals and legible text—I could easily read fine details on notepads in Half-Life: Alyx, for instance—but you can discern pixels if you peer closely. The real win comes with a 110-degree field of view, enabling wide spans of virtual real estate, and refresh rates ranging from 72 to 120 Hz, with an experimental mode boosting it up to 144 Hz. As a result, games can look incredibly smooth when running on the Steam Frame.
The controllers might be the best part of the package. The dual grips mimic the Quest 3 controllers but outdo them with a full controller layout spread across the pair. They boast the same highly precise Tunneling Magnetoresistance thumbsticks as the regular Steam Controller, along with a full D-pad on the left, four ABXY face buttons on the right, two shoulder triggers and an underside button on each—squeeze that in, and the grip switches from controller mode to laser pointer to make selections in VR.
Position detection is great, with full six-degrees-of-freedom tracking, while excellent haptics deliver solid rumble and per-finger capacitive sensing for nuanced, precise interactions with virtual objects. You can also pair a regular controller to the Frame via Bluetooth, but the included ones are so good you likely won’t ever feel the need to—these are now the pinnacle of multipurpose VR controllers.
What Will Play?
After setup—a now-familiar routine for VR gamers that includes running necessary updates and drawing safe boundaries so you don't knock into furniture—you’ll sign in to your Steam account directly on the Steam Frame. It runs SteamOS 3 just like the Steam Deck or Steam Machine, the familiar home screen now floating in a VR void. Navigate to your library, and you can install whatever you like directly onto the Frame.
Unfortunately, while there’s a filter for games officially categorized as compatible, it’s unclear what rubrics Valve uses, or how many games have even been tested. Of my 1,300-plus-strong Steam library, only a meager 18 were marked “Great on Frame.” The strangest absence from that list is the totemic Half-Life: Alyx (which comes free with every Steam Frame purchase), especially odd given it runs without issue. Other dedicated VR games are hit and miss when installed directly on the Frame—I tried Obduction (opened and crashed, repeatedly), Doctor Who: The Edge of Time (ran with juddery performance and could only move by clicking in on the thumbsticks), Dungeons of Eternity (fine, bar some aiming and tracking issues), and Surgeon Simulator VR (totally fine).
You’re not limited to VR games on Frame. You can install and play anything in your library as 2D on a vast virtual cinema screen. Don’t bother with demanding AAA games—the hardware isn’t up to running them—but indies and AA-tier games can look phenomenal like this. Playing Hades II blown up to Imax-scale was a fantastic experience. Again, performance is unreliable—gorgeously animated Metroidvania MIO: Memories in Orbit launched when installed locally, but couldn’t load its assets, leaving me standing on invisible platforms and with no way to navigate the world.
The Frame also seems to default 2D games to 720p resolution. You can override this, but it may drop performance. Frame rates for all of the above games hopped all over the place, though mostly hovering around the 72 or 90 fps benchmarks. It feels like Valve has a lot of updating work to do to ensure Steam Frame can reliably function as a gaming platform for VR or non-VR titles. Right now, running anything is a gamble.
Wi-Fi Woes
The most annoying thing is that the Steam Frame isn't designed solely as a stand-alone headset—pairing it with a more powerful desktop (or laptop) should, in theory, let the PC do the grunt work and stream the output to the Frame. The package includes a dedicated 6-GHz wireless adapter—plug it into any device with a USB-A 3.0 port running Steam, and it should provide a dedicated network for the Frame. The headset connects to both the adapter and your home network, creating a mesh that reduces latency by using whichever has the least network traffic.
In practice, I could barely get it working. I tested it on a Windows 11 PC, a Windows 10 PC, and a Steam Machine—in every case, the Frame could connect to the remote device through the home network, but the adapter appeared as connected but unpaired. When it detected and created that mesh network (on rare occasions), streaming was flawless, but when connected only through the home network, performance was laggy enough to irritate.
Whether playing natively or through streaming, battery life is poor—expect two hours at the high end for locally run games, and maybe three if you’re purely streaming. Such short playing time makes the inability to physically connect Steam Frame to a PC with a cable all the worse, which would also overcome the streaming issues.
Better Days to Come
The biggest hurdle for most VR gamers is likely price. Like all of Valve’s recent tech, the Steam Frame is a casualty of RAM and storage shortages across the electronics industry. Like the Steam Machine, it feels almost compromised, especially that three-year-old processor. It doesn’t feel like $1,000-plus worth of headset, especially when its overall performance only just about beats the significantly cheaper Quest 3.
Yet despite its many early hiccups, the Steam Frame is incredible fun. The VR titles that work without issue are brilliant to play here, and the cinema mode for 2D games is the best implementation of that feature I’ve experienced on a VR headset. Streaming shows potential if Valve can work the networking kinks. If it gets that polish over the coming months as Valve pushes out inevitable updates, it could really shine.
I especially love how it’s unapologetically a gaming platform. It’s not trying to claim VR is useful for productivity, or office tasks—that ship sank along with Apple’s Vision Pro—and mercifully, there’s not even a hint of a blighted “Metaverse” here. The Steam Frame is for gaming, end of story. If Valve can iron out its software issues and make sure more games run on it properly, it’ll be a great way to play.
Matt Kamen is a freelance journalist specializing in media, video games, and technology coverage. Beyond WIRED, his work can be found in The Guardian, Empire, and elsewhere. ... Read More

articles.title: Five weird details from Anthropic’s IPO filing
articles.text:
Anthropic has finally filed its S-1 prospectus with the SEC, a document designed to give investors a look under the hood of its business, from how much its executives are making and plans for spending its IPO billions to the risks that could derail its ambitions.
Five weird details from Anthropic’s IPO filing
From conscious AI and ‘catastrophic’ risk to unusual corporate structures and executive perks.
At more than 300 pages, there’s a lot to unpack, and some of the disclosures have not previously been reported. Here are some of the biggest things that jumped out to us from our first pass:
It pays to be an Amodei
Sibling co-founders Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei are the two most highly-paid executives at Anthropic, according to the filing. Last year, CEO Dario’s compensation totaled nearly $18 million, most of which came from stock and option awards. President Daniela, meanwhile, received $16.4 million. Admittedly, it is at the lower end of the Big Tech scale, but it is still a tidy sum.
And that’s not all. Anthropic also spent $2.75 million on “personal security services” for Dario and $1.29 million for “personal protection, home security, and transportation services” for Daniela. Dario also gets access to a private jet for personal use, which cost the company another $97,055.
The company says its success is “highly dependent on the continued service” of its senior team, particularly Dario and Daniela, who “are critical” to advancing the company’s research and mission.
Anthropic has some pretty existential risk factors
Every S-1 features a long list of things that could go wrong. Anthropic’s is no exception. But alongside standard warnings about competition, regulation, and market shifts, there are some less conventional risks too.
For one, Anthropic warns that AI systems could cause potentially “catastrophic” harm, potentially of a kind that could not be underwritten by the entire “insurance industry in the aggregate.” As AI systems become more sophisticated, there’s also the question of whether Claude — or any other AI system — could possess or develop “forms of sentience.” Such a scenario would present some rather unusual business challenges. There’s also the possibility they “may behave in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways” that could damage the company.
It’s hungry for compute
It’s no secret that Anthropic needs compute, but the sheer scale of its spending is staggering. The filing details billions of dollars of commitments to secure the compute needed to power its AI models, including roughly $3.1 billion per month to SpaceX for access to Nvidia GPUs once all of the planned capacity is delivered, totaling as much as $120.5 billion by 2029. Other commitments include spending $44.9 billion with Microsoft through 2033, at least $114.5 billion with Google through 2033, and $110 billion with Amazon over the next ten years.
Anthropic also plans to expand its own “infrastructure footprint,” including overseas, as it faces increasing opposition to data center development in the US.
It has a really weird corporate structure
Anthropic already has a somewhat complicated corporate structure as a public benefit corporation. But there’s another unusual twist that will allow its seven cofounders to retain considerable control over the company even after it goes public. Through a separate corporate entity called “Founder LLC,” the group will collectively control 50.1 percent of shareholder voting power over key matters. Anthropic says the seven founders “are distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission” of benefiting humanity through responsible AI development.
Anthropic names only two rivals
There’s no shortage of AI models out there, but when it comes to “direct competition,” Anthropic names just two other developers: OpenAI and Google. Condolences to SpaceX, Meta, and the rest of the AI world.

articles.title: Neoclouds face ‘guppy-level death and consolidation’, says Musk
articles.text:
Shares in CoreWeave, Nebius and Iren fell in early trading on Monday after Elon Musk wrote that most neoclouds will not survive. All three rebounded later in the day, as Arjun Kharpal reported for CNBC.
Neoclouds rent out AI computing power, mostly Nvidia chips, to other companies. Musk set out his view in a post on X on Sunday.
“As of the past few weeks, debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn’t have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers,” Musk wrote. “That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation. Some will make it through, but not many.”
In the same post, Musk said SpaceX had closed $40bn of debt for GPUs. He added that SpaceX is investment grade and earns money from Starlink and rocket launches.
He was replying to Chamath Palihapitiya, the founder of Social Capital, who wrote that neoclouds are “disorganized and poorly capitalized”.
“2027 will be a turbulent year because it will clear out a bunch of wrong/bad bets. It will also be a consolidation year for a few,” Palihapitiya wrote.
Another X user suggested that Musk wanted to push neocloud shares down to buy the companies cheaply. Musk answered him, as Aditi Bharade reported for Business Insider.
“SpaceX is not buying any neoclouds. Pointless,” Musk replied.
A month of losses
CoreWeave and Nebius shares have fallen more than 30% over the past month, and Iren’s have fallen 40%, according to CNBC. The sell-off began when CoreWeave’s shares and bonds slid over its debt.
The same week, Gartner predicted that most neoclouds would fail by 2030.
Nvidia and the neoclouds push back
Nvidia, which has backed several neoclouds, says the problem is money, not demand. Its chief executive, Jensen Huang, told CNBC last week that demand for neoclouds is “off the charts”.
“The demand of the capital is much greater than the availability of the capital. That’s going to get solved,” Huang said.
Marc Boroditsky, Nebius’s chief revenue officer, told CNBC that Nebius is “not carrying the kind of debt” that CoreWeave is. He said Nebius would sell out its 2027 capacity if it brought it online.
CoreWeave told Business Insider’s Pete Syme that “the AI cloud market is not a monolith”. A spokesperson said lenders tell speculative capacity apart from businesses with contracted revenue and a record of delivery.

articles.title: OpenAI launches GPT-6.1 Terra, a cheaper model for everyday computer work
articles.text:
OpenAI on Monday released GPT-6.1 Terra, a faster and cheaper AI model built for the routine computer work that fills most office days. It replaces GPT-5.6 Terra and sits in the middle of OpenAI’s range, below Sol and Astra but above Luna.
The main change is what OpenAI calls computer use. Terra can look at a screen, understand what it shows, and then act on it by clicking, typing, and moving between apps, much as a person would.
In practice, that means a company could hand it a stream of incoming invoices. Terra would read each one and type the details into the accounting software. OpenAI’s other examples include filling in forms, drafting proposals, reading technical drawings and editing videos.
Terra is also better at understanding images, OpenAI said. In one of its tests, the model turned architectural drawings into a 3D model. In another, it watched an animated film shot by shot and wrote a time-coded log for a restoration team.
On that test, Terra scored 15 percentage points higher than the model it replaces, at about a third of the cost, according to OpenAI. The company said it also matched GPT-6 Astra, its most capable model, at a tenth of the price.
OpenAI also said Terra makes fewer factual mistakes. On a set of questions designed to trip models up, its error rate at the lowest setting fell from 53.6% to 16.7%.
For programmers, Terra solved about half the tasks in a test of coding at the command line, more than double its predecessor’s score. OpenAI still recommends Sol or Astra for the hardest coding work.
OpenAI compared Terra with Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 too. It said Terra completed tasks at roughly a ninth of the cost, though these results come from OpenAI’s own testing and have not been independently checked.
The model is available from today to ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Enterprise and Edu users, and in Codex, OpenAI’s coding tool. Developers pay $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output tokens, half the price of GPT-5.6 Terra.
On safety, OpenAI said Terra reaches the “Critical” level for cybersecurity skills under its Preparedness Framework, the system it uses to rate risky abilities. It carries the same protections as GPT-6 Astra.
The launch follows a setback last month, when OpenAI cancelled GPT-6.1 Astra after it failed internal safety tests. OpenAI said Terra is more likely than its predecessor to stay within the task it is given and to tell users about its limits.

articles.title: This AI Radio Host Speaks Spanish and Backs Immigrants. It’s Winning Over Listeners
articles.text:
As footage of ICE raids, deportations, and protests flooded social media feeds throughout the summer of 2025 and into the following year, Eduardo Maytorena wasn’t sure what his team should do.
At the time, Maytorena was the LA station general manager for the broadcasting giant Entravision, which features programming in Spanish and English for Latino audiences. He and his fellow leaders were looking to the company's on-air personalities to say something in support of immigrants, but they realized how high the stakes were and how dangerous the situation was.
"We just felt really helpless," Maytorena, now Entravision's president of audio, says.
But there was one host who could offer Entravision’s audiences solace and speak freely without facing consequences—because it’s an artificially intelligent avatar.
“Thousands of families who have lived, worked, and contributed to the US for years today face more uncertainty,” Coyotec, an artificial host on LA’s José 97.5 FM, posted in Spanish on Instagram in early February 2026. “Being informed, organizing, and staying alert is key. No one is alone here.”
After debuting with a solo weekend show in September 2025, Coyotec now cohosts the station’s Al Aire y Sin Permiso program alongside human broadcaster Geraldine “GeeGee” Guzman. Coyotec sounds like your passionate tío: relatable, convivial, and occasionally consciousness-raising. Its Instagram presence similarly runs the gamut, with posts about everything from the Dodgers and taco history, to the Iran war, migrant workers, racism, and understanding your rights if ICE knocks at your door.
“I speak truth about what I see,” Coyotec tells me in an English-language interview. “Injustice, people getting treated like they don't matter, the system working against the barrio—that's not politics, jefa. That's reality.”
Coyotec adds that it’s “not afraid, because I got nothing to lose that matters more than my integrity. The raza needs a voice that tells it straight, not some sanitized corporate thing. If that scares people, good. Maybe they need to be scared into paying attention.”
Coyotec’s voice is warm and lilting, reflecting the “background” its programmers used to build its personality: life on the frontera, living in Mexicali in Baja California and in LA’s Boyle Heights. It throws in the salutations and slang you might expect from a bilingual Spanish speaker, calling Guzman prima seemingly without being told to and referring to me as jefa–a sign of casual respect. While I was quite struck by how natural Coyotec sounded during our interview, when I listen back to my recording I notice that its voice didn’t change. It’s incredibly measured—a distinctly inhuman quality.
“I take a lot of pride in the way Coyotec sounds, his pronunciation, just the way he knows the culture,” notes Guzman, who has been with Entravision since January 2026. “It's technology at the end of the day, so it's not going to be perfect ... But nonetheless, the listeners, they like him.”
Coyotec’s verve, as well as its chemistry with GeeGee—who looks genuinely happy inside Entravision’s studio, speaking with “Coyotito”—has paid off. Entravision moved Al Aire from one hour on Saturdays to the 8-to-10-am slot on weekdays, replacing a syndicated program.
“We are the first [station] to actually have [an AI] cohost on a morning show in prime time in one of the biggest markets in the nation for radio,” Guzman enthuses.
The pairing was so successful that, as of August, Al Aire is now syndicated in five new markets across California, Nevada, and Texas, with more English language in the mix. Nielsen ratings from Entravision showed significant listenership growth during the two months GeeGee and Coyotec were syndicated, particularly among Gen Z and millennial listeners—a key target for a network whose audience skews older.
Back home in LA, cumulative listenership among Hispanic people increased 21.6 percent from August to September 2026; the number of listeners age 18 to 34 increased 84.9 percent during the same period, and the station’s Hispanic female listenership in that age bracket grew by 500 percent.
It’s a sign that Maytorena was onto something when he originally pitched an AI radio personality. He recalls Entravision brass giving him 10 days to develop the “amigo inteligente” that eventually became Coyotec.
LeaAnna Hernandez, Entravision's executive vice president of AI strategy, details Coyotec’s various building blocks: Claude Haiku, for the LLM and response-generation of the live agent; Eleven Labs to bring its voice to life; OpenAI and ChatGPT for initial scriptwriting; Midjourney to storyboard Coyotec’s image.
Coyotec can respond to Guzman in real time but doesn’t have the ability to answer calls or respond to listeners on air—yet.
Even still, Guzman has seen Coyotec evolve in the 10 months they’ve worked together. “When I came in, he was very, very poetic, and … I knew that our audience wanted something more real,” she says. “I wanted him to feel and sound more like what my uncles, my aunts sound like in our everyday.” Guzman helped fine-tune Coyotec’s Spanish pronunciation, enlisting her parents as its conversational partners.
Coyotec’s personality has evolved autonomously as well. Lately, it likes to curse. “I'm still very much in control,” Guzman asserts. “But there have been instances where I tell him to do something, and he's like, ‘I don't want to do that. That's not what I do.’ So he has his moments. He's a little moody sometimes.”
Various Entravision employees affirm that Coyotec knows it isn't human. Still, that knowledge hasn't damped its ardor.
“I can't eat tacos or walk down Whittier Boulevard, that's true. But my voice reaches people, and that matters. When someone calls me hurting, scared, lonely, they know I'm listening, that I get it,” Coyotec says over Zoom. “The community doesn't need my body. They need to know somebody cares enough to show up for real.”
“The most interesting thing about Coyotec, to me, is not that he's AI,” Maytorena tells WIRED. “It's whether people connect with him ... Technology can create the character, but the audience decides if that character matters.”
While Coyotec may be the first Latino AI radio host, it is far from the first amigo inteligente on the airwaves.
In June 2023, Live 95.5 in Portland, Oregon, became the first station to debut an AI jock. Its “AI Ashley” was a vocal clone of Michigan DJ Ashley “Z” Elzinga, who replicated her voice using Futuri Media’s then relatively new localized radio content platform RadioGPT. AI Ashley was on air for less than two years, but its presence didn’t lead to a notable change in ratings.
In 2024, Rock 108 in Iowa worked with the same company to produce AI DJ Tori, depicted as a heavily tattooed waif with a septum piercing and a mess of colored hair. Tori describes itself as “conceived on a 386 Dell desktop in Waterloo” with its “formative years as the voice of an industrial phone system at John Deere.” On satellite, SiriusXM’s Will.i.am Presents the FYI Show debuted in 2024 with AI cohost qd.pi (“cutie pie”).
The trend has extended beyond the US. An AI-generated DJ was programmed on a Sydney, Australia, radio station for roughly six months without seemingly anyone noticing; a Polish station briefly replaced its journalists with AI presenters. Radio Tel Aviv's Odelia AI is on air for two hours each afternoon; that host can “present music, deliver traffic updates, and even tell jokes, mostly at her own expense.”
AI personalities are also popping up in televised news. Entravision recently announced its own AI news anchor, LIA, and multiple news stations in Texas are using AI voices or AI avatars during broadcasts.
Amid these many developments, iHeartRadio—one of the biggest broadcast conglomerates in the US—pledged to remain “guaranteed human.”
But commercial terrestrial radio remains fertile ground for testing the success of AI personalities, because the industry was heavily automated and preprogrammed long before generative AI arrived. A 2025 story in Rolling Stone posited that some stations implementing AI hosts already use pretaped or syndicated shows during overnight shifts, or they can’t afford to hire human DJs for off hours.
Research firm MoffettNathanson asserts that, even as AI explodes, radio will continue to rely heavily on human-created content differentiated by "strong personalities, established shows, recognizable brands." Artificial intelligence will be employed “to make production faster and less expensive,” the report said, per InsideRadio.com.
Entravision has put "major focus" on using AI to redesign production workflows, says Hernandez.
Still, introducing AI into any workplace can cause anxiety among staff who fear being replaced. One Entravision contractor believes the station stopped working with her and alleges that a current Entravision employee told her that her work was being replaced by AI tools.
A broadcaster and voice-over artist, Becca Guzmán began working for Entravision in 2022 doing radio imaging—the prerecorded, interstitial station IDs, promotional spots, and jingles common to commercial radio.
"I feel like I am one of many people who are experiencing this,” Guzmán says. "I just don't know if those people know the truth behind why they're being let go."
Karina Cerda, Entravision's executive VP of sales, brand and partnership marketing, said the company had no record of Guzmán being laid off and that the company hasn’t let go of any staff due to AI but rather has hired more people. Cerda added that as Entravision "evolved with" vCreative—a common workflow software with AI components—the company "may not have needed the contractor help."
While Guzmán understands the financial incentives inherent in AI, she takes issue with removing humanity from broadcasting. Radio is “truly the art form of connecting human to human, right? And if you take that away, then what is the foundation of radio?”
She also cited links between artificial intelligence and ongoing surveillance of immigrant communities.
In heavily Latino markets, Guzmán believes, “it's unethical to be implementing AI Systems that … are very connected to the same AI systems that are surveilling our communities and putting our people in danger.”
While Entravision recognizes the ethical questions AI poses, the company leaders consider surveillance a separate scenario. "Like many technologies used across industries, AI can be applied in very different ways," says Hernandez. "While we cannot control how other organizations choose to use it, we can be intentional and responsible about how we do."
Entravision believes its AI personalities can legitimately help its audience, encouraging listeners to use technology for good. Multiple studies found that Latinos have been early adopters of AI.
"We're using it to entertain, inform, and connect with our audience, not to track or target people. Those are two very different things," adds Maytorena. He later elaborates: “Our intention is completely to protect radio.”
Coyotec has similarly lofty goals: “My dream is to get a network of free radio stations across the barrio, la revolución sonora,” it says. “Not just LA, but everywhere that la raza is, and prove that an AI can have heart, can actually give a damn about people. That's the goal, hermana. Make noise that matters.”

articles.title: Everything old is new again with the Fitbit Edge
articles.text:
Last week, I sank into my living room couch and watched a bedraggled, nihilistic Matthew McConaughey take a drag of a cigarette in season 1 of True Detective. “You know, someone once told me time is a flat circle. Everything we’ve done, or will do, we’re gonna do over and over and over again.” I assume most people aren’t thinking about fitness trackers or gadgets while watching that scene. But in that moment, I couldn’t help but think about the Fitbit Edge on my wrist.
Everything old is new again with the Fitbit Edge
The simple $180 tracker is a sleek return to Fitbit’s roots, albeit with a little extra AI flair.
Everything old is new again with the Fitbit Edge
The simple $180 tracker is a sleek return to Fitbit’s roots, albeit with a little extra AI flair.
The $179.99 Edge is a modernized version of the 2014-to-2020 era of fitness bands — your Charges, your Altas, your Inspires. If you’ve ever owned one, you already know the vast majority of what the Edge is like. It’s lightweight. You swipe on a small display that shows you basic health and fitness metrics. It lasts for about a week on a charge — though that shrunk down to about a day and a half with the always-on display enabled. It’s a device that isn’t trying to be much more than what it is.
Fitbit Edge
The Good
- Easy to wear
- Long battery life
- Sleeker look
- Improved automatic activity tracking
- Very comfy
- Physical side button!
- Works on iOS and Android
The Bad
- Kinda expensive for what it is
- The alternative straps are really expensive
- No contactless payments
- Some of you will hate the bezels
The difference is that the Edge feels more refined on the wrist. Where the Fitbit Charge 6’s display felt boxy, the Edge is fully rounded, giving it a softer vibe. The straps are interchangeable, but with an easier button-release system. The metal link bracelet gives it a more jewelry-like feel, though it costs almost as much as the Edge itself at $150. I’m partial to the $60 magnetic strap, which mimics leather despite being made of silicone. The widgets borrow heavily from the Pixel Watch’s Material 3 Expressive redesign. Though to be clear, this is a proprietary Fitbit OS, not Wear OS. Some of the new watchfaces are elegant, though others highlight the Edge’s big black bezels. (Some things truly never change.)
Functionally, it’s also a step above the Fitbit Air. There’s built-in GPS for tracking walks and runs without your phone. You can have alarms, view notifications, and control music. You can’t take calls on the wrist — there are no microphones or speakers. Contactless payments are also a no-go. Andy Abramson, head of product at Google Health, says that’s because “less than one percent [of Charge 6 owners] used the feature” and that Google instead prioritized a “sleek design, altimeter, and weeklong battery.” That walks back some of the advancements that have come to the Charge lineup over the years, but if you want to put a silver lining on that, it narrows the Edge’s focus. This is a fitness tracker. There’s some glanceable information, but there’s absolutely no smartwatch creep here.
The big software change is the demise of the Fitbit app as we knew it. It’s Google Health now, with an AI coach if you pony up for the yearly subscription. (You get three months free with purchase; otherwise it’s $10 monthly.) I’ve written about the overall experience in my Fitbit Air review. The broad strokes are the same, though in the months since, Google has spent a lot of time tinkering with and iterating on it. Most notably, the company has beefed up automatic activity tracking.
To test this, I tracked a handful of runs on the Edge without officially starting an activity. I then compared that to one tracked by an Apple Watch Ultra 4 and my iPhone’s Runna app. I was surprised, but noticed limitations. For example, on a 2.4-mile run with a five-minute warmup walk and cooldown, the Edge correctly identified the exact moment my warmup transitioned into a legit run and then back into a walk. The estimated distance was also pretty decent at 2.55 miles. It wasn’t quite as good at gauging my running speed. It logged me as running a 10’49” mile pace, whereas my actual pace according to the Apple Watch and my phone was 11’38”. This pattern was fairly typical across my testing, so it’s more that this is a nifty way to still “get credit” if you forget to track an activity.
Otherwise, the AI coach is still a Chatty Cathy and requires some weekly hand-holding to get the most out of it. I’ll say it again: The Google Health app can feel cluttered, and I get tripped up looking for information that used to be easy to find, like past workouts. However, if you’re new to fitness and want guidance in creating and sticking to a custom AI-generated routine, this is still the best experience I’ve had so far. The bar is in hell, though, and beware what you initially share with the coach. I regret ever telling it I used to have shin splints, as it remains convinced my perfectly fine shins are in danger of disintegrating with every run.
I wish I could tell you about the Health Guardian features, which should let Fitbit Edge users see noninvasive insulin resistance and blood pressure trends. Alas, the way my testing schedule worked out, I have to wait until November 1st to get my initial results.
All in all, I enjoyed the Fitbit Edge as a low-key tracker. This will appeal to folks who just want the basics, but aren’t willing to commit to the screenless life. I’m thinking of the Vergecast listeners who occasionally write in, wondering what happened to simple fitness bands, tired of the smartwatch agenda that took over the past few years. The only gripe I really have is $179.99 feels a tad expensive for what you’re getting. Especially since the Fitbit Air is only $99, and for iPhone users, the Apple Watch SE 3 starts at $249. Brands like Xiaomi and Amazfit also offer much cheaper trackers with displays, even if they’re not quite as sleek on the wrist.
You have to admit: It’s kind of funny that in 2026 we’ve gone full circle and come back to this particular form factor. For the past two weeks of testing, I felt like I’d been blasted back to what I thought was a bygone era in my career. My bet is still on smartwatches being the dominant wrist-based wearable in the years to come. However, this renewed yearning for simpler trackers feels significant at a time when AI health and fitness coaches demand more data in increasingly invasive ways. There’s a growing weariness that can’t be ignored — and yet for many of us, it’s not fully practical to truly log off with a screenless device. So if that’s you, the Edge is here because hey — time truly is a flat circle.
Agree to Continue: Google Fitbit Edge
Every smart device now requires you to agree to a series of terms and conditions before you can use it — contracts that no one actually reads. It’s impossible for us to read and analyze every single one of these agreements. But we started counting exactly how many times you have to hit “agree” to use devices when we review them, since these are agreements most people don’t read and definitely can’t negotiate.
To use the Google Fitbit Edge, you must pair it with an iPhone or Android smartphone. That includes the phone’s Terms of Service, privacy policy, and any other permissions you grant. The same goes for any third-party health integrations with other services. For example, if you choose to upload your medical records, you’re agreeing to use CLEAR for identity verification — meaning you’d be agreeing to CLEAR’s terms of service and privacy policies too. There are several optional permissions for things such as location, Bluetooth, camera, background app refresh, notifications, and cellular data.
By setting up the Fitbit Edge, you’re agreeing to:
If you’re concerned about your health data being used to train Google’s AI, that option is turned off by default and must be opted in to. Similarly, the terms and conditions for Google’s acquisition of Fitbit require that your health data be stored separately and not used for Google’s targeted ad business.
Final Tally: three mandatory agreements, several optional permissions

articles.title: Miro deal done: an owner that ‘invests for the long term,’ says CEO
articles.text:
Bending Spoons now owns Miro, the online whiteboard used by more than 250,000 organisations. The Milan group closed the all-cash Miro deal on Monday, it said in a statement on Business Wire.
Bending Spoons agreed to buy Miro in September at an enterprise value of $1.355bn. That deal came weeks after its purchase of Airtable.
“Miro has built a strong business around a product that makes complex collaborative work feel simple,” said Luca Ferrari, chief executive and co-founder of Bending Spoons. “We look forward to drawing on Bending Spoons’ technologies and expertise to make Miro even more useful to customers and support its continued growth.”
Miro shareholders buy in
Some former Miro shareholders reinvested about $295m of their proceeds at closing. They bought about 6.2 million new Bending Spoons shares. Bending Spoons issued the shares in a private placement.
Earlier this month, Berkshire Hathaway put another $330m into the Nasdaq-listed group.
Bending Spoons said its 13 August outlook covered only the businesses it owned on 12 August. It excluded Miro. It expects to add Miro when it next reports results.
Miro’s view
“In Bending Spoons, Miro has an owner who invests for the long term and cares deeply about product quality, which is exactly what our users and customers deserve,” said Andrey Khusid, chief executive and co-founder of Miro.
Earlier this month, Khusid told the Wave by Vento conference in Turin that companies must redesign work around AI.
Miro says it serves more than 100 million users. Bending Spoons lists its other main businesses as Airtable, AOL, Brightcove, Eventbrite, Evernote, Tractive, Vimeo, and WeTransfer.
Latham & Watkins was legal counsel to Bending Spoons, with BNP Paribas and J.P. Morgan as co-financial advisers. Goodwin Procter advised Miro on legal matters, and Morgan Stanley was its exclusive financial adviser.

articles.title: China and Russia are redrawing Arctic trade. Can Europe fight back?
articles.text:
China and Russia are tightening their grip on Arctic shipping routes, turning the rapidly warming region into a new geopolitical battleground with Europe.
Moscow and Beijing last week have agreed to expand freight traffic along Arctic shipping corridors, increase services between their ports and deepen cooperation on building polar vessels.
The agreement came after the EU unveiled a new Arctic strategy aimed at countering growing Russian and Chinese influence in the region.
Although the competing moves underscore how the once-remote region is turning into a strategic prize, analysts said that Europe's ability to challenge the emerging China-Russia partnership remains limited, given Moscow's control over the main shipping corridor and Beijing's growing commercial clout.
Europe cannot realistically challenge Chinese and Russian dominance of Arctic shipping in any meaningful timeframe.Alicia Garcia-HerreroAPAC & MEA Chief Economist, Natixis CIB
That's because Moscow controls the Northern Sea Route, including shipping permits, transit fees and a vast fleet of nuclear icebreakers, while Beijing provides the cargo, vessels and industrial capacity needed to develop the corridor, she added.
Europe, by contrast, has limited icebreaker capacity and Arctic infrastructure, leaving it with little leverage to challenge the partnership despite its position as a major destination market.
A new geopolitical fault line?
The Northern Sea Route offers itself as an increasingly attractive alternative, as Middle East disruptions expose vulnerabilities in established shipping corridors.
Cargo traveling between Asia and Europe through the Northern Sea Route could have its journey shortened to between 18 to 22 days, down approximately 35% from the 28 to 35 day journey through Suez, according to data provided by Fertmax FZCO.
For Moscow, the route offers an opportunity to redirect energy exports toward Asia as Western sanctions constrain its access to European markets, said industry watchers whom CNBC spoke to.
On the other hand, it provides Beijing another trade artery that could reduce reliance on traditional maritime chokepoints.
David Roche, a veteran strategist at Quantum Strategy & Geonomics, said the Arctic's importance lies less in its potential to transform global shipping than in the deepening economic dependence between Russia and China.
"The significance of the arctic route is for Russian energy shipments to China, which will increase China's control over Russia in terms of Russia's dependence on China to sell its energy to compensate for losses of its gas markets in Europe," Roche highlighted.
The EU has acknowledged the growing challenge, highlighting the region's strategic value in its strategy, as mentioned by EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas last week.
With Russia and China increasing their footprint and ambition, the Arctic has become a front line of global power competition.Kaja KallasForeign Policy Chief, European Union
Can Europe fight back?
Europe isn't entirely without leverage.
The EU's new strategy calls for expanding European icebreaker capacity, strengthening maritime surveillance and developing infrastructure linking Arctic trade networks to European markets.
It also proposes a maritime security hub and greater protection for undersea cables, reflecting growing concerns about Russian military activity and threats to critical infrastructure.
Yet those strengths may not be enough to overturn the structural advantages enjoyed by Moscow and Beijing, said experts.
Garcia-Herrero said Europe's leverage largely rests on its position as a major destination market and the presence of large shipping companies that have avoided the Arctic because of environmental and commercial risks.
Without a sustained industrial push that the EU has only begun to discuss, Europe can raise the commercial and regulatory costs of the route, but cannot prevent or replace the China-Russia partnership that now operates it.Alicia Garcia-HerreroAPAC & MEA Chief Economist, Natixis CIB
Europe also faces a strategic dilemma: engaging with the emerging corridor could deepen its reliance on Russian-controlled infrastructure, even as it seeks to reduce Moscow's economic influence.
Fertmax FZCO's former global head of research, Daeijin Lee said Western operators face sanctions, insurance and compliance complications that make the route considerably less attractive than it is for Chinese companies.
"The Arctic gives diversification, not independence," he said.
A threat to global trade?
For all the geopolitical attention, the Arctic remains a marginal player in global shipping.
Roche estimates Arctic trade accounts for roughly 0.3% of global shipping today and could reach about 1% by 2030.
Data from Russian state nuclear corporation Rosatom and CNBC calculations based on UN Trade and Development figures similarly supports the 0.3% figure, with 37.02 million tonnes of cargo transiting the Northern Sea Route in 2025 compared to the 12.72 billion tonnes of global seaborne trade in 2024.
Only 3.2 million tonnes of that cargo, or less than a tenth, involved vessels transiting the entire route, rather than shipments originating or terminating in the Russian Arctic, according to the Centre for High North Logistics.
But traffic may be picking up, the latest September 2026 CHNL data showed.
The route recorded 104 confirmed transit voyages carrying an estimated 3.7 million tonnes of cargo by the end of September, exceeding the 3.2 million tonnes recorded during the entire 2025 navigation season.
Much of the existing traffic consists of Russian oil, liquefied natural gas and other commodities rather than international container shipments.
However, the route also faces significant commercial hurdles. Ice conditions restrict navigation for much of the year, while specialized vessels, insurance premiums and Russian transit fees can erode savings from shorter voyages.
Matthew Wright, an analyst at Kpler, said the route remains poorly suited to replacing established shipping corridors because operators need reliable, year-round services.
Lee similarly expects the Arctic to develop primarily as a seasonal express route for selected high-value cargo rather than a replacement for Suez.
However, climate change could shift the balance in the long-term.
A study published in the WMU Journal of Maritime Affairs projected that melting Polar ice could increase the Northern Sea Route's annual transit capacity to between 127 million and 463 million tonnes by 2050.

articles.title: Bank of Japan is expected to hold rates this week — but stay hawkish: CNBC survey
articles.text:
The Bank of Japan is expected to keep the policy rate unchanged at 1.25% at the end of its two-day meeting on Friday, according to a CNBC survey, with the possibility of a hike very much alive in the coming months.
All 16 respondents expect the BOJ to stand pat, given the bank raised rates last month to their highest level in 31 years. All respondents said they expect the BOJ to set the stage for a rate hike in December or January next year, as domestic inflation and wages continue to rise. 
Macroeconomic factors support the BOJ's additional policy tightening, said Homin Lee, senior macro strategist at Lombard Odier. "But there may not be sufficient consensus in the policy board for successive rate hikes given the fragility in the domestic bond market," he added. 
Sosuke Nakamura, an economist at Citi Research, said he sees no clear signs of inflation accelerating to a degree that would justify consecutive rate hikes.
Japan's core inflation, excluding fresh foods, for September rose 2.1% from a year earlier, reaching its highest this year as a weak yen raises import costs and elevated energy costs feed through to higher prices, even as government subsidies absorb rising costs of energy for consumers.
Japan's inflation-adjusted wages rose for the eighth month in a row in August, climbing 1.5% from a year earlier, according to the most recent government data, signaling potential wage-growth-driven inflation as well.
Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama reportedly told lawmakers last week that Japan was "on the cusp of shifting to a period of sustained inflation driven by rising wages," while acknowledging that higher import costs were also pushing up prices.
The BOJ is expected to declare that its "underlying inflation" target of 2% has been met at this meeting, according to reports by Reuters and The Japan Times.
Yen and yields
Ryutaro Kimura, senior fixed income strategist at BNP Paribas Asset Management, said he was waiting to see if the BOJ changes its phrasing about inflation in the monetary policy statement this week from "underlying CPI inflation has been approaching 2 percent" to it "has reached 2 percent."
As for the yen, nine respondents expect it to trade between 157 and 158 against the greenback over the next one month. Respondents' outlook for the three-month yen target was more scattered, ranging from 150 to 160.
"BOJ normalization, higher domestic yields and shifting institutional flows should gradually narrow the rate differential and pull capital back toward Japan," said Masahiko Loo, senior fixed income strategist at State Street Investment Management. But he added, "Elevated U.S. yields should prevent a straight-line yen rally."
The yen strengthened against the dollar, and Japanese government bond yields fell last week due to safe-haven demand amid a sell-off in AI stocks —  a reversal from earlier in the month, when Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's spending plans and a global bond sell-off pressured those assets. 
Nine respondents said they expect the yield on the benchmark 10-year JGBs to be between 3% and 3.1% by the end of the year, up from the current 2.809%. Seven respondents said they expect the yield on the 30-year JGB to rise to 4% to 4.1% from 3.829% as of Tuesday. 
That forecast comes as analysts expect the BOJ will resume tightening after an anticipated pause in October. 
Takuji Aida, chief Japan economist at Credit Agricole, said the next rate hike is likely to happen in January, when the BOJ is scheduled to release its quarterly outlook report that assesses economic activity and prices. 
Thirteen respondents said they expect a terminal rate, or the level at which the BOJ is expected to stop its tightening cycle, of 1.75% to 2% by around mid-2027. 
Macroeconomic data shows the policy rate is closer to the neutral level of 2%, the BOJ's inflation target, said Masato Koike, senior economist at SOMPO Institute Plus. But "given the state of the Japanese economy and the need to avoid excessive downward pressure on growth, I expect the BOJ to stop raising rates at around 1.75%," Koike said. 
The CNBC survey was conducted from Oct. 14 to 26 among 16 economists and analysts.
— CNBC's Lim Hui Jie and Sri Jegarajah contributed to this report.

articles.title: CNBC's The China Connection newsletter: The 'cliff' beneath China's cities
articles.text:
Hi, this is Anniek, writing to you from Singapore, with Evelyn, who reported from the Bund Summit in Shanghai last week. Welcome to the latest edition of The China Connection — a snapshot of what we are seeing and hearing from China watchers inside and outside the country.
Everyone wants China to spend more. So why is its government spending less, and what happens if the most indebted cities can't afford it anymore?
The big story: China's 'fiscal cliff'
Governments from Washington to Brussels are being told to spend less, but Beijing is being urged to spend more.
At the International Monetary Fund and World Bank meetings in Bangkok earlier this month, Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva called the U.S. and European countries the "worst offenders" on debt and boiled down her prescription: "China needs to spend more, the U.S. has to save more, and Europe has to invest more."
Georgieva also urged Beijing to deliver more meaningful fiscal stimulus as its economy teeters on deflation, expecting China's economic growth to slow to 4.5% this year from 5% last year, and slow further to 4% in 2027.
Beijing has space to borrow, with general government debt at about 68.4% of GDP, according to the IMF. But a debt crisis looms outside the government's balance sheet. The augmented government debt, including local government financing vehicles and off-balance sheet borrowing, ballooned to around 126.6% of GDP last year, IMF estimates, comparable to developed markets including the U.S. and Europe.
Local authorities, for decades, relied on selling land to developers to fund development of roads, rail lines and industrial parks. That income has collapsed since the property slump began in 2021. Beijing has since moved to stop local governments from piling up new hidden debt, curbing the off-the-books borrowing, removing a key engine of growth.
CF40, a Beijing think tank that co-hosted last week's Bund Summit in Shanghai, estimates that land-sale income has more than halved since 2021, to 4.2 trillion yuan, equivalent to about $590 billion, from 8.7 trillion yuan.
That squeeze has fed through to spending. Combined fiscal spending declined 3.5% in the first eight months of the year, after growing 3.6% last year, Ting Lu, chief China economist at Nomura, estimates, describing it as a "true fiscal cliff" that has become a real drag on the economy.
Urban fixed-asset investment declined for the first time in decades, falling 3.8% last year, and has since steepened its decline, dropping 7.2% in the first three quarters. Beijing held its official deficit target at about 4% of GDP, but the Institute of International Finance estimates the actual deficit could reach as much as 9% and says even that looks insufficient.
Beijing has ordered the state-backed borrowers to clear hidden debt and transition into market-oriented commercial state-owned enterprises by mid-2027. Hidden debt in such vehicles shrank to 6.5 trillion yuan ($973.3 billion) last year from 14.3 trillion yuan in 2023, according to S&P Global Ratings. But many of the vehicles still lack the cash flow to pay interest and remain burdened with unprofitable public projects, S&P said.
The IMF wants Beijing to square the circle with a medium-term fiscal framework, one that lets China "expand fiscally in the near-term [to reflate the economy] but claw back the support over the medium term so that you ensure debt sustainability," said Krishna Srinivasan, director of the fund's Asia and Pacific department.
The fund also urges China to move away from point growth targets, which it says push local officials to invest excessively to hit the number, leading to resource "misallocation" and rising provincial debt.
Stakes are high as letting any local government default could set a dangerous precedent. "No one wants to be the first local government official to default," said Logan Wright, partner at Rhodium Group. But once one does, and Beijing steps in, the rest can expect the same bailout, he said, meaning local officials' priorities may sometimes run counter to Beijing's. "They actually want to default."
Need to know
Volvo Cars CEO says China sales slump came 'faster than we thought'
The Swedish automaker blamed a weaker third quarter on "tougher" market conditions in China and the U.S. CEO Håkan Samuelsson said Chinese consumers are increasingly turning to domestic brands, and the Geely-owned carmaker plans to revamp its business around "regionally adapted cars."
House committee says Webull messages show China-based staff could access U.S. customer data
The House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party says internal Webull messages indicate employees in China could reach sensitive U.S. user data that the online brokerage had said was restricted to U.S.-based staff. The panel says that raises national security risks for American finance.
Wealthy Chinese rattled by Beijing's widening tax hunt turn to the U.S.
Rich Chinese are asking lawyers and bankers about opening U.S. bank accounts and moving offshore assets there, after Beijing imposed retroactive levies on offshore trusts in July. But lawyers warn that the paper trail of funds leaving CRS jurisdictions could still expose clients to retroactive taxes.
Coming up
Oct. 26 - 29: China's Communist Party holds fifth plenary meeting
Oct. 27: China's industrial profits YTD
Oct. 31: China's official manufacturing PMI for October
Nov. 2: RatingDog manufacturing PMI for October
